title: The Prior-Force Family of Implicit Denoiser Priors and Its Decisions in Linear Inverse Problems
summary: Implicit priors given by Gaussian denoisers successfully regularize a wide range of inverse problems in approaches such as plug-and-play (PnP), regularization by denoising (RED) and score-based methods. Such a prior depends on the noise level, and how it selects among signals consistent with the data remains largely uncharacterized. To put implicit and explicit priors on the same footing, we define the prior-force family $W_t=t^{-1}(D_t^{-1}-I)$ of any Gaussian denoiser $D_t$ at noise variance $t>0$ (inverse in the graph sense), the normalized denoising residual as an operator on clean signals. At a common effective prior weight, the equilibrium equations differ only in their prior terms: PnP uses $W_t$, RED/score-based methods the score force (the normalized residual as an operator on noisy inputs), and maximum a posteriori (MAP) estimation the MAP force (the negative log-prior gradient). For the minimum mean-square error (MMSE) denoisers of a prior $\pi$, we compare the corresponding energies at three levels. Without observation, raising the noise level favors PnP minima that retain more posterior variance. On signals consistent with the data, the leading-order PnP energy for separated modes is the proximal hull of the MAP energy, which lets PnP select signals between modes; modes of equal data fit are ranked by peak height at small noise levels and by mass at large ones. For recovery, $W_t$ at the truth bounds the local bias, and an oracle noise level balances this bias against denoiser error. These results show that the noise level is a parameter of the prior rather than a step size. Experiments with exact priors support these predictions, including the mixture components that PnP selects on unseen data.

AI.tldr: The paper defines a prior-force family W_t = t^{-1}(D_t^{-1} - I) for any Gaussian denoiser D_t, putting implicit denoiser priors (PnP, RED, score-based) and explicit priors on the same footing, and shows that the noise level acts as a parameter of the prior rather than a step size.
AI.motivation: Implicit priors given by Gaussian denoisers regularize inverse problems well, but how they select among signals consistent with the data, and how this depends on the noise level, remained largely uncharacterized.
AI.method: Each method's equilibrium equations are written with a common effective prior weight, differing only in the prior term: PnP uses W_t, RED and score-based methods use the score force, and MAP uses the negative log-prior gradient. For MMSE denoisers of a prior, the corresponding energies are compared at three levels, and the bias-error trade-off of an oracle noise level is analyzed for recovery.
AI.result: Without observations, raising the noise level favors PnP minima that retain more posterior variance. For separated modes, the leading-order PnP energy is the proximal hull of the MAP energy, so PnP can select signals between modes, ranking equal-fit modes by peak height at small noise and by mass at large noise. Experiments with exact priors support these predictions, including the mixture components PnP selects on unseen data.
AI.conclusion: The noise level must be treated as a parameter of the prior, which clarifies when and how implicit denoiser priors select among modes and how they trade bias against denoiser error in recovery.

title: Model Collapse Is Avoidable Even as Real Data Vanishes: A Sharp Criterion for Iterative Gaussian Estimation
summary: Large generative models are commonly trained on data collected from the open web, which may contain data produced by previous generations of the same model. Previous work has shown that recursively training on model-generated data can progressively degrade model performance, a phenomenon known as model collapse. Yet, generative models continue to improve dramatically over time. Existing theory suggests that this is enabled by the availability of new real data at each iteration, kept separate from generated data. However, exact separation is not realistic, and uncurated data is still commonly used. We bridge this gap by considering a more realistic setup in which real and generated data are not handled differently during training. Specifically, we present a comprehensive theoretical study of iterative estimation of the mean and covariance of a multivariate Gaussian distribution. At each iteration, samples are drawn from a mixture of the real data distribution and the estimated distribution from the previous iteration, but are used indistinguishably. We provide a single equivalent condition for consistency of the mean and covariance estimators in Euclidean norms, and convergence to zero of the expected squared 2-Wasserstein distance between the estimated and true distributions. Using this result, we show that consistency holds, i.e., model collapse is avoided, for any fixed real data fraction above zero, and even for a fraction that vanishes across iterations, provided it does not vanish too quickly. However, more real data (or data curation) remains important at practical finite times: the convergence rate of the mean estimator deteriorates as the real data fraction approaches zero. We support our results with an empirical investigation of the theoretical setup, and with experiments on iterative training of a diffusion model on CIFAR-10 that correlate with our theory.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that model collapse in iterative Gaussian mean and covariance estimation is avoided when real data and generated data are mixed without distinction, provided the real data fraction stays positive or vanishes slowly enough.
AI.motivation: Prior theory explains continued improvement of generative models by assuming new real data is kept separate from generated data, but exact separation is unrealistic and uncurated web data is commonly mixed in.
AI.method: At each iteration, samples are drawn from a mixture of the real distribution and the previous iteration's estimated distribution and used indistinguishably. The authors derive a single equivalent condition for consistency of the mean and covariance estimators in Euclidean norms and for convergence of the expected squared 2-Wasserstein distance to zero.
AI.result: Consistency, and hence avoidance of model collapse, holds for any fixed real data fraction above zero and even for fractions that vanish across iterations, provided they do not vanish too quickly. The mean estimator's convergence rate deteriorates as the real data fraction approaches zero. Experiments on iterative training of a diffusion model on CIFAR-10 correlate with the theory.
AI.conclusion: Collapse is avoidable without strict data separation, but more real data or data curation still matters at practical finite times because it governs the convergence rate.

title: Outstrumental Variable Regression
summary: Estimating the causal effect of a treatment $X$ on an outcome $Y$ from observational data in the presence of unobserved confounding requires additional structure or assumptions. Existing identification strategies such as instrumental variable regression exploit exogenous variation in only the treatment. We show that the causal effect can also be identified if the outcome mechanism varies across a finite set of environments, even if the treatment distribution is unchanged. Concretely, we introduce Outstrumental Variable Regression (OVR), which proceeds in three steps: (i) compute the conditional expectation of $Y$ given $X$ in each environment; (ii) form the vector of differences in these conditional expectations between all environments and a reference environment (we call this vector contrast); and (iii) regress $Y$ on $X$ while adjusting for the contrast and environment. We prove that this yields the true causal effect if the following two conditions hold: inclusion restriction, i.e., the contrast determines the conditional confounding bias; and positivity, i.e., the treatment varies sufficiently strongly after adjustment. We prove that a finite-sample version of OVR is consistent under regularity conditions and demonstrate the procedure's effectiveness on synthetic and real-world data.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes Outstrumental Variable Regression (OVR), which identifies the causal effect of a treatment on an outcome under unobserved confounding by exploiting variation in the outcome mechanism across a finite set of environments, even when the treatment distribution is unchanged.
AI.motivation: Instrumental variable regression identifies causal effects only through exogenous variation in the treatment, so it cannot handle cases where the treatment distribution is fixed but the outcome mechanism varies across environments.
AI.method: OVR computes the conditional expectation of Y given X in each environment, forms a contrast vector of differences between each environment's conditional expectations and a reference environment, and then regresses Y on X while adjusting for the contrast and environment.
AI.result: The authors prove that OVR yields the true causal effect under an inclusion restriction, where the contrast determines the conditional confounding bias, and a positivity condition, where the treatment varies sufficiently after adjustment. A finite-sample version is proven consistent under regularity conditions, and its effectiveness is shown on synthetic and real-world data.
AI.conclusion: Causal effects can be identified from environment-dependent outcome mechanisms alone, which extends identification beyond instrumental-variable strategies.

title: Transformer-Based Reinforcement Learning for Phase I Dose Allocation
summary: Phase I dose-finding trials must learn from sparse toxicity observations while limiting exposure to overly toxic doses. We develop a single reinforcement-learning policy for trials with different numbers of ordered dose levels. Each dose is represented as a token containing its normalized position, accumulated patient count, observed dose-limiting toxicities (DLTs), and current-dose indicator. A Transformer encoder summarizes the dose tokens, trial-conditioned cross-attention produces a fixed-dimensional trial representation, and a three-action policy chooses de-escalation, staying, or escalation. The final maximum tolerated dose (MTD) decision is deliberately kept outside the learned policy: after the planned sample size, weighted isotonic regression and a prespecified safety cap select the dose closest to the target toxicity probability. In the simulations, toxicity-penalized policies reduce DLT burden while unpenalized policies improve selection accuracy at the cost of greater toxicity. These results demonstrate a controllable safety--accuracy trade-off but do not establish superiority over conventional dose-finding designs.

AI.tldr: The paper develops a single Transformer-based reinforcement learning policy for Phase I dose-finding trials with varying numbers of ordered dose levels, with the final maximum tolerated dose (MTD) decision made outside the learned policy.
AI.motivation: Phase I dose-finding must learn from sparse toxicity observations while limiting patient exposure to overly toxic doses, and existing designs need a policy that generalizes across trials with different numbers of dose levels.
AI.method: Each dose is encoded as a token with its normalized position, accumulated patient count, observed dose-limiting toxicities (DLTs), and a current-dose indicator. A Transformer encoder summarizes the dose tokens, trial-conditioned cross-attention produces a fixed-dimensional trial representation, and a three-action policy chooses de-escalation, staying, or escalation. After the planned sample size, weighted isotonic regression with a prespecified safety cap selects the dose closest to the target toxicity probability.
AI.result: In simulations, toxicity-penalized policies reduce DLT burden, while unpenalized policies improve selection accuracy at the cost of higher toxicity. The results show a controllable safety-accuracy trade-off but do not establish superiority over conventional dose-finding designs.
AI.conclusion: The approach offers a tunable safety-accuracy trade-off for dose allocation, but its advantage over established designs remains unproven.

title: Representative Learning for Distributed Support Vector Machines
summary: Distributed support vector machine (SVM) learning is challenging under heterogeneous local data and limited communication. We develop a Representative Learning framework based on Lifted Empirical Risk Minimization, replacing each covariate by a local Gaussian distribution. For linear SVMs, the resulting expected hinge loss has an exact closed form, is smooth for nondegenerate lifting covariances, and converges to the ordinary hinge loss as the covariance vanishes. The lifted formulation enables clouded representatives that encode both location and covariance. We study a model-independent Mean Representative (MR) and a Score-Matching Representative (SMR) that matches the class-wise lifted gradient at its construction parameter. We show that SMR covariance scaling is stable with respect to within-group heterogeneity and that the gradient discrepancy between full data and frozen representatives is controlled by the maximum within-group diameter. Under strong convexity and smoothness, this yields an inexact-gradient convergence guarantee. Experiments under heterogeneous class allocation show that lifted representatives remain competitive with centralized solutions, while SMR more closely recovers the centralized lifted-SVM optimizer. We further extend the framework to nonlinear SVMs through a shared kernel dictionary, with experiments on Ionosphere and Australian Credit Approval showing analogous behavior. These results provide a distributional representative framework for communication-efficient distributed SVM learning under heterogeneity.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a Representative Learning framework for distributed linear and nonlinear SVMs, in which each local covariate is replaced by a Gaussian distribution, yielding an exact closed-form expected hinge loss that converges to the ordinary hinge loss as the covariance vanishes.
AI.motivation: Distributed SVM learning is difficult under heterogeneous local data and limited communication, so an approach is needed that summarizes each group compactly while preserving the centralized optimum.
AI.method: Lifted Empirical Risk Minimization replaces each covariate with a local Gaussian. Two representatives are studied: a model-independent Mean Representative (MR) and a Score-Matching Representative (SMR) that matches the class-wise lifted gradient at its construction parameter. Nonlinear SVMs are handled through a shared kernel dictionary.
AI.result: SMR covariance scaling is stable with respect to within-group heterogeneity, and the gradient discrepancy between full data and frozen representatives is controlled by the maximum within-group diameter, giving an inexact-gradient convergence guarantee under strong convexity and smoothness. Under heterogeneous class allocation, lifted representatives remain competitive with centralized solutions, and SMR more closely recovers the centralized lifted-SVM optimizer. Ionosphere and Australian Credit Approval experiments show similar behavior for kernel SVMs.
AI.conclusion: Distributional representatives give a communication-efficient route to distributed SVM learning under heterogeneity, with SMR preferred for recovering the centralized solution.

title: Pricing Today, Shaping Tomorrow: Contextual Dynamic Pricing in Purchase-Driven Evolving Systems
summary: Across diverse markets, it is important for firms to balance attracting customers with managing operational conditions, such as workloads and delivery times. Dynamic pricing plays a central role in this tradeoff, as the orders generated today can change the conditions faced by future customers. We develop a novel framework for contextual dynamic pricing with an observed shared state and unknown purchase-driven transitions. The valuation model allows unknown mean functions of customer covariates and state, unknown state-specific scales and a common unknown standardized noise distribution. We propose Shadow-Adjusted Pricing in Evolving Systems (SHAPE), which incorporates a purchase's future revenue consequences into current pricing. Purchase-shadow adjustment and scale standardization reveal a common one-dimensional oracle price map across states, allowing SHAPE to retain its pricing history across value updates without repeating coarse exploration. The same active sales records support price-map learning and joint updates of continuation values and purchase shadows, without fitting the noise distribution or full transition matrices. To support this reuse under purchase-driven feedback, we establish pricing guarantees for history-dependent inputs and stability bounds for the joint updates. Under regularity, coverage and design conditions, we obtain sublinear expected regret against a finite-horizon dynamic oracle for linear, Hölder and sparse linear mean models. For affine valuations at fixed state and feature dimensions, SHAPE matches the static semiparametric minimax time exponent up to logarithmic factors for every fixed noise-tail smoothness order $\beta\ge2$. Numerical experiments further demonstrate the appealing performance of SHAPE.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes SHAPE, a contextual dynamic pricing method for evolving systems in which each purchase changes future states, incorporating the purchase's future revenue consequences into current prices and achieving sublinear regret against a dynamic oracle.
AI.motivation: Dynamic pricing must balance attracting customers against operational conditions such as workload, and today's orders alter future customers' conditions, while existing contextual pricing methods do not account for purchase-driven state transitions.
AI.method: SHAPE combines a purchase-shadow adjustment with scale standardization, which reveals a common one-dimensional oracle price map across states. Pricing history is retained across value updates, and continuation values and purchase shadows are updated jointly from the same active sales records, without fitting the noise distribution or the full transition matrix.
AI.result: Under regularity, coverage and design conditions, SHAPE has sublinear expected regret against a finite-horizon dynamic oracle for linear, Hölder and sparse linear mean models. For affine valuations at fixed state and feature dimensions, it matches the static semiparametric minimax time exponent up to logarithmic factors for every fixed noise-tail smoothness order beta at least 2. Numerical experiments show good performance.
AI.conclusion: Accounting for purchase-driven feedback in contextual pricing is feasible with sublinear regret and near-minimax rates, without repeated coarse exploration.

title: Model-Based Learning of Latent Euclidean Embedding from Relational Data
summary: Visualizing and interpreting the dependence structure in relational data often benefits from geometric representations via low-dimensional Euclidean embeddings. However, existing approaches are typically restricted to specific response types, rely on burdensome high-dimensional nonconvex optimization, or lack uniform theoretical guarantees for simultaneous coordinate recovery. To address these limitations, we introduce a unified, distance-based latent space framework for both unipartite and bipartite relational data---accommodating continuous, binary, ordinal, and count-valued observations---via a modular two-stage procedure that decouples signal estimation from geometric recovery. First, we estimate the low-rank signal matrix using spectral denoising. For models with nonlinear link functions, we further apply one-step row- and column-wise refinement to achieve uniform entrywise accuracy. Second, we recover the latent configurations through direct spectral analysis for unipartite data and a low-dimensional alignment optimization for bipartite data. We establish uniform recovery guarantees that characterize the propagation of error from signal estimation to the embedding space. To illustrate the scalability and interpretability of our approach, we apply the proposed method to two real-world datasets: a statistician citation network and European Parliament voting records.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a distance-based latent space framework for unipartite and bipartite relational data with continuous, binary, ordinal, and count responses, with a two-stage procedure that estimates the signal matrix by spectral denoising and then recovers the latent Euclidean embedding, with uniform recovery guarantees.
AI.motivation: Existing relational-embedding methods are limited to specific response types, rely on burdensome high-dimensional nonconvex optimization, or lack uniform guarantees for simultaneous coordinate recovery.
AI.method: The low-rank signal matrix is estimated by spectral denoising, with one-step row- and column-wise refinement for nonlinear link functions to obtain uniform entrywise accuracy. Latent configurations are recovered by direct spectral analysis for unipartite data and by low-dimensional alignment optimization for bipartite data.
AI.result: The authors establish uniform recovery guarantees that characterize how estimation error propagates into the embedding space. The method is applied to a statistician citation network and to European Parliament voting records.
AI.conclusion: The modular decoupling of signal estimation from geometric recovery yields a scalable and interpretable embedding method with theoretical guarantees across response types.

title: Sampling Design and Confidence Tubes for Integral Curves on Riemannian Manifolds
summary: We estimate the integral curve of an unknown vector field from noisy tangent vector field on a known compact Riemannian manifold. We consider two sampling settings: independent observations at random locations that have already been collected, and a fixed response budget that allows subsequent locations to be chosen using pilot information. Under suitable regularity assumptions, the passive kernel estimator has curve error of order $n^{-2/(d+3)}$ in probability, with sample size $n$ and manifold dimension $d$. Its functional central limit theorem has a limit characterized by a linear stochastic differential equation. For active sampling, an independent pilot directs one new batch of measurements to neighborhoods of the target curve. Under localization, smoothness and design conditions, this concentration yields expected maximum curve error of order $N^{-1/2}$, including the pilot in the total response budget $N$. Both methods provide simultaneous geodesic confidence tubes with asymptotically exact coverage under mild conditions. Simulations show narrower active tubes in most reported settings, with improved small-sample coverage in some three-dimensional examples. Ocean-drifter observations illustrate mean-flow reconstruction on the sphere, and a canopy-flow LDA application uses retrospective active sampling to quantify lateral and vertical departures of local mean streamlines.

AI.tldr: The paper estimates the integral curve of an unknown vector field on a compact Riemannian manifold from noisy tangent observations, with passive and active kernel estimators that give simultaneous geodesic confidence tubes with asymptotically exact coverage.
AI.motivation: Recovering flow curves from noisy tangent measurements on manifolds requires both uncertainty quantification and efficient use of a limited response budget, which fixed designs do not provide.
AI.method: A passive kernel estimator uses independent observations at random locations. An active method uses an independent pilot to direct one new batch of measurements to neighborhoods of the target curve, with the pilot counted in the total budget N. A functional central limit theorem for the passive estimator has a limit characterized by a linear stochastic differential equation.
AI.result: The passive estimator has curve error of order n^{-2/(d+3)} in probability, and the active method achieves expected maximum curve error of order N^{-1/2}. Both yield simultaneous geodesic confidence tubes with asymptotically exact coverage. Simulations show narrower active tubes in most settings, and ocean-drifter and canopy-flow applications are illustrated.
AI.conclusion: Active sampling directed by a pilot tightens both estimation error and confidence tubes relative to passive sampling, with practical value for geophysical flow reconstruction.

title: Unbiased Low-Rank Approximation for Repeated Matrix-Vector Multiplication: Stability and Optimal Sampling
summary: Replacing the matrix in an iteration with random low-rank matrices can reduce the cost of matrix-vector multiplication. However, even if the sampled matrices equal the original matrix in expectation, the expected squared norm of the random iterates may grow while the original iteration converges. Under a fixed rank bound, we study how to choose the distribution of these random matrices to minimize this growth when sampling independently at each step. We derive an exact formula for the optimal asymptotic growth factor and use it to determine when the expected squared norm can converge to zero. We then characterize precisely when a fixed sampling distribution achieves this optimal factor and construct finite-support optimal distributions in every attainable case. These results determine the minimum rank required for stability and provide optimal sampling designs under the prescribed rank constraint.

AI.tldr: The paper characterizes the optimal sampling distribution for random low-rank replacements of a matrix in an iteration, minimizing the growth of the expected squared norm, and determines the minimum rank needed for stability.
AI.motivation: Replacing the matrix in an iteration with random low-rank matrices reduces cost, but even unbiased replacements can make the expected squared norm of iterates grow while the original iteration converges.
AI.method: Under a fixed rank bound, the authors derive an exact formula for the optimal asymptotic growth factor when samples are drawn independently at each step. They characterize when a fixed sampling distribution attains this optimum and construct finite-support optimal distributions in every attainable case.
AI.result: The exact optimal growth factor determines when the expected squared norm converges to zero, and the paper identifies the minimum rank required for stability and the optimal sampling designs under the rank constraint.
AI.conclusion: Stability of randomized low-rank iterations is determined by a precise rank threshold, and optimal finite-support sampling designs achieve it.

title: Bootstrap Inference for Riemannian Optimization Problems
summary: We develop an online multiplier bootstrap for manifold-valued parameters estimated by averaging the iterates of Riemannian stochastic approximation. The method runs weighted iterations alongside the original algorithm, with each path using the same observations while updating its own state and intrinsic average. The weighted averages provide uncertainty assessments without a plug-in asymptotic covariance estimator. Under local stability and regularity conditions, we establish bootstrap consistency and show that a fixed number of paths suffices for asymptotically valid Student intervals and intrinsic confidence regions. The theory accommodates samplewise nonsmooth scores and identifies a critical oracle-bias regime in which the estimator's limiting distribution shifts, but the centered bootstrap distribution does not. Applications include spherical means, positive-definite matrix means and medians, and principal-subspace estimation. Simulations show coverage close to nominal in regular settings, and an analysis of North Atlantic storm locations illustrates descriptive online inference for a spherical center.

AI.tldr: The paper develops an online multiplier bootstrap for manifold-valued parameters estimated by averaging iterates of Riemannian stochastic approximation, giving uncertainty assessments without a plug-in asymptotic covariance estimator.
AI.motivation: Inference for manifold-valued estimators from Riemannian stochastic approximation usually requires an asymptotic covariance estimate, which is difficult to obtain in this setting.
AI.method: Weighted bootstrap iterations run alongside the original algorithm, each path using the same observations while updating its own state and intrinsic average. A fixed number of paths is used to form Student intervals and intrinsic confidence regions.
AI.result: Under local stability and regularity conditions, bootstrap consistency is established, and a fixed number of paths suffices for asymptotically valid intervals. The theory allows samplewise nonsmooth scores and identifies an oracle-bias regime in which the estimator's limit shifts while the centered bootstrap does not. Simulations show near-nominal coverage in regular settings, and an analysis of North Atlantic storm locations is given.
AI.conclusion: The online bootstrap provides valid descriptive inference for Riemannian estimators, with a known failure regime under oracle bias.

title: Riemannian Newton Methods with Statistical Inference
summary: We develop online statistical inference for Polyak-Ruppert averages of inexact Newton iterates on Riemannian manifolds. A local asymptotic representation separates observation noise, solver randomization, and accumulated implementation bias, and yields one-pass covariance estimators and asymptotically valid Wald regions under local regularity and centering conditions. Independent fresh solves add a positive semidefinite term to the score-sandwich covariance; averaging solver replicas reduces this term in inverse proportion to their number. Slowly varying predictable gains instead cancel from the first order law. Product torus simulations show how Newton scaling shortens an ill-conditioned transient and how retaining solver variation restores coverage. Intrinsic means and principal subspaces provide geometric applications, with a streaming data illustration.

AI.tldr: The paper develops online statistical inference for Polyak-Ruppert averages of inexact Riemannian Newton iterates, with one-pass covariance estimators and asymptotically valid Wald regions.
AI.motivation: Inexact Newton solves on manifolds introduce solver randomness and implementation bias in addition to observation noise, and standard inference does not separate these sources.
AI.method: A local asymptotic representation separates observation noise, solver randomization and accumulated implementation bias. Independent fresh solves add a positive semidefinite term to the score-sandwich covariance, which decreases in inverse proportion to the number of averaged solver replicas. Slowly varying predictable gains cancel from the first-order law.
AI.result: Asymptotically valid Wald regions are obtained under local regularity and centering conditions. Product-torus simulations show that Newton scaling shortens an ill-conditioned transient and that retaining solver variation restores coverage. Applications include intrinsic means and principal subspaces, with a streaming example.
AI.conclusion: Solver variability must be retained in the covariance to achieve nominal coverage, and replicated solves reduce its contribution.

title: Self-Normalized Inference from Riemannian Stochastic Gradient Paths
summary: Riemannian stochastic gradient paths estimate constrained parameters, but confidence regions usually require estimating the Hessian and gradient-noise covariance. We develop self-normalized inference from one path by expressing retained iterates in a common random tangent space. Their average and centered partial sums share an unknown covariance factor that cancels in a Brownian bridge pivot. Under suitable regularity conditions, a joint expansion of the averaged estimator and integrated path controls nonlinear coordinate errors using conditional second moments. The procedure uses fixed-dimensional memory and extends to nondegenerate smooth functionals and alternative local coordinates. Numerical studies show competitive coverage relative to plug-in Wald inference while avoiding Hessian and residual-density estimation.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes self-normalized inference for Riemannian stochastic gradient paths, using a Brownian bridge pivot so that confidence regions avoid Hessian and gradient-noise covariance estimation.
AI.motivation: Confidence regions for constrained parameters estimated by Riemannian SGD usually require estimating the Hessian and the gradient-noise covariance, which is costly and unstable.
AI.method: Retained iterates are expressed in a common random tangent space. Their average and centered partial sums share an unknown covariance factor, which cancels in a Brownian bridge pivot. A joint expansion of the averaged estimator and integrated path controls nonlinear coordinate errors, using fixed-dimensional memory.
AI.result: Under regularity conditions the procedure extends to nondegenerate smooth functionals and alternative local coordinates. Numerical studies show coverage competitive with plug-in Wald inference while avoiding Hessian and residual-density estimation.
AI.conclusion: Self-normalized path inference offers a memory-light alternative to plug-in Wald intervals for Riemannian SGD.

title: Lower Bounds on Inference Complexity for Polyak-Ruppert Averaged Stochastic Gradient Descent
summary: In this paper, we establish sharp lower bounds for Gaussian approximation of Polyak-Ruppert averaged stochastic gradient descent with polynomially decreasing step sizes. For every fixed exponent $\gamma\in(1/2,1)$, a single one-dimensional smooth, strongly convex example has approximation error with the limiting variance of order $n^{1/2-\gamma}+n^{\gamma-1}$ in Kolmogorov and convex distances. This matches the existing upper bound throughout the range of $\gamma$. The nonlinear bias contributes $n^{1/2-\gamma}$ even when the Gaussian reference uses the finite linearized variance. We also derive a lower bound of order $n^{-(1-\gamma)/2}$ for the relative mean error of estimating the limiting variance from one SGD trajectory, uniformly over a scalar quadratic family. With the limiting variance known, achieving approximation error $\varepsilon$ on this example takes order $\varepsilon^{-4}$ iterations for the best choice $\gamma=3/4$. Achieving both Gaussian approximation and relative mean variance-estimation errors at most $\varepsilon$ uniformly over the model class requires at least order $\varepsilon^{-6}$ iterations for every fixed $\gamma$.

AI.tldr: The paper proves sharp lower bounds for Gaussian approximation of Polyak-Ruppert averaged SGD with polynomially decaying step sizes, and shows that the variance-estimation and iteration costs for both tasks are of matching order.
AI.motivation: Existing upper bounds on the Gaussian approximation error of averaged SGD lacked matching lower bounds, so the true inference complexity was unknown.
AI.method: For each exponent gamma in (1/2, 1), a one-dimensional smooth strongly convex example is constructed. The authors bound the approximation error in Kolmogorov and convex distances, and derive a lower bound for the relative mean error of estimating the limiting variance from one trajectory over a scalar quadratic family.
AI.result: The approximation error has order n^{1/2-gamma} + n^{gamma-1} in the limiting variance, matching the known upper bound across the range. The nonlinear bias contributes n^{1/2-gamma} even with the linearized Gaussian reference. With known variance, error epsilon needs order epsilon^{-4} iterations at gamma = 3/4. Uniform accuracy epsilon for both tasks needs at least order epsilon^{-6} iterations for every fixed gamma.
AI.conclusion: The inference complexity of averaged SGD is established as sharp, and variance estimation dominates the cost of uniform guarantees.

title: Adaptive Optimizers Can Get a Policy Ranking Wrong: Momentum, Dependent Data, and a Two-Run Remedy
comment: 64 pages, 1 figure, 5 tables; includes an electronic companion with proofs and supplementary experiments
summary: Operators choosing among decision rules, such as when a battery charges or where an idle taxi goes, rank them by estimated long-run value. A standard estimator, linear temporal-difference (TD) learning, fits values from one stream of correlated observations. Large fits often use an adaptive optimizer, such as adaptive moment estimation (Adam), with fixed averaging rates. We show that these rates can change what is estimated, not just how fast: the same observations drive the updates and the optimizer's step-size scaling, moving the fit away from the intended TD value. The shift differs across rules, so it need not cancel in a comparison, and more data only makes a wrong ranking look more certain. Our remedy refits the same data at a second averaging rate that halves the effective gain, the number to which the leading shift is proportional. Twice the new fit minus the original removes that shift. In New York taxi and battery models calibrated to real data, common optimizer settings leave the selected rule unchanged but order close rules wrongly and misstate its value. Our remedy corrects nearly every wrong ordering, with one extra fit when the shift is moderate and two when it is larger.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that adaptive optimizers such as Adam, with fixed averaging rates, can bias linear TD value estimates and so change the policy ranking, and proposes a two-run remedy that cancels the leading shift.
AI.motivation: Operators rank decision rules by long-run value estimated from correlated data, and large fits often use Adam with fixed averaging rates, whose effect on the estimand is not usually considered.
AI.method: The optimizer's step-size scaling depends on the same observations as the updates, so the fit shifts away from the intended TD value. The remedy refits the same data at a second averaging rate that halves the effective gain, and computes twice the new fit minus the original to remove the leading shift.
AI.result: In New York taxi and battery models calibrated to real data, common optimizer settings leave the selected rule unchanged but misorder close rules and misstate its value. The remedy corrects nearly every wrong ordering, using one extra fit for moderate shifts and two for larger ones.
AI.conclusion: Optimizer hyperparameters can alter the estimand rather than only the convergence speed, and a cheap second-rate refit can correct the resulting ranking errors.

title: Infinite Quantiles Inference under Local Differential Privacy
summary: We study simultaneous quantile inference under local differential privacy for a number of target probabilities that grows with the sample size. Each user participates once, so learning unknown quantile locations and calibrating their joint uncertainty must share the same private information. We fuse complementary cumulative distribution function (CDF) scores from a single tree report using their exact covariance; the variance at the correct anchor is no larger than that of either score, and anchor error incurs only quadratic excess variance. Three consecutive cohorts then localize the quantiles, estimate their densities, and supply fresh scores for a one-step correction and joint multiplier calibration. Under mild conditions, a uniform representation controls localization and density errors and yields asymptotically valid simultaneous coverage. A fixed-privacy regime permits every polynomially growing target grid. Simulations show consistent same-report precision gains, while comparisons with CDF-band inversion expose the sample cost of learning target locations. Census microdata illustrates how the resulting joint intervals support wage-percentile ratios.

AI.tldr: The paper develops simultaneous quantile inference under local differential privacy for a growing number of target probabilities, using three consecutive user cohorts from a single tree-based report and a joint multiplier calibration for asymptotically valid simultaneous coverage.
AI.motivation: Under local differential privacy each user reports once, so learning unknown quantile locations and calibrating their joint uncertainty must share the same private information, which existing CDF-band inversion handles with a high sample cost.
AI.method: Complementary CDF scores from a single tree report are fused using their exact covariance. Three cohorts localize the quantiles, estimate their densities, and supply fresh scores for a one-step correction and joint multiplier calibration.
AI.result: The variance at the correct anchor is no larger than that of either score, and anchor error adds only quadratic excess variance. Under mild conditions, asymptotically valid simultaneous coverage holds, and a fixed-privacy regime permits every polynomially growing target grid. Simulations show precision gains, and census microdata illustrate wage-percentile ratios.
AI.conclusion: Joint quantile intervals are feasible under local differential privacy with sample costs lower than CDF-band inversion.

title: Principled Human-AI Collaboration in Agentic Workflows
comment: 44 pages, 4 figures. Includes supplementary material with proofs and experimental details
summary: Organizations adopting AI face the challenge of deciding which outputs can be released without human review while meeting the quality standards of human experts. We develop a statistical framework for delegating tasks between experts and black-box generate-verify workflows, in which AI-generated answers are verified and revised over multiple rounds. Before deployment, human experts evaluate selected outputs, and their judgments are used to calibrate the verifier threshold and number of attempts. Our method selects the policy with the highest estimated automation rate among statistically approved candidates, without modifying the generator or verifier. We establish finite-sample control of the error rate among released outputs, characterize the expert evaluations sufficient to attain a target automation rate, and derive a minimax lower bound establishing rate optimality in the quality margin and required confidence. In a MultiHiertt financial question-answering case study, average held-out automation increases from 2.50% to 24.17% as expert evaluations accumulate, while released-output error rates remain around 1.20%. In contrast, heuristics that release answers after consistently high verifier scores either violate the 5% error tolerance or automate at most 1.30% of tasks. Synthetic experiments further examine these theoretical predictions under controlled settings.

AI.tldr: The paper gives a statistical framework for deciding which outputs of a black-box generate-verify AI workflow can be released without human review, calibrating the verifier threshold and number of attempts from expert evaluations, with finite-sample control of the error rate among released outputs.
AI.motivation: Organizations need to know which AI outputs can skip human review while meeting expert quality standards, and heuristics based on verifier scores do not provide reliable error control.
AI.method: Before deployment, experts evaluate selected outputs, and their judgments calibrate the verifier threshold and attempt count. The policy with the highest estimated automation rate among statistically approved candidates is selected, without modifying the generator or verifier.
AI.result: On a MultiHiertt financial question-answering case study, average held-out automation rises from 2.50% to 24.17% as expert evaluations accumulate, while released-output error stays around 1.20%. Heuristics either violate the 5% error tolerance or automate at most 1.30% of tasks. A minimax lower bound establishes rate optimality, and synthetic experiments support the predictions.
AI.conclusion: Error-controlled automation of agentic workflows is achievable with modest expert labeling, and it substantially outperforms score-threshold heuristics.

title: When Does Sparse Routing Help? The Geometry of Expert Separation in Mixture of Experts
summary: Sparse mixtures of experts combine multiple prediction models while evaluating only a small subset for each input. Although this architecture reduces computation, how expert separation and routing sparsity jointly govern expert recovery remains an open problem. In this paper, we address this question for location Gaussian mixtures of experts with a fixed number of experts by establishing how expert separation and spatial arrangement determine recovery rates. For dense models, our results reveal that when experts form well-separated clusters, the separation geometry is governed by the size of the largest cluster; without a prescribed cluster structure, this geometry is instead driven by the total number of experts. For sparse models, the separation geometry on retained routing regions is determined by the number of active experts, while the contribution of omitted regions is controlled by their total probability. Consequently, activating fewer experts reduces the separation complexity in these bounds. Furthermore, Top-1 routing yields a particularly striking result: experts can be recovered at a rate independent of the separation quantity. Our technical approach combines polynomial interpolation and Gaussian reproducing-kernel Hilbert space (RKHS) test functions with quantitative restriction inequalities that extend pointwise comparisons to expert functions.

AI.tldr: The paper analyzes when sparse routing helps in Gaussian location mixtures of experts, showing that top-1 routing lets experts be recovered at a rate independent of the separation quantity, while the separation geometry of dense and sparse models is governed by cluster size, expert count, or the number of active experts.
AI.motivation: It was an open question how expert separation and routing sparsity jointly govern expert recovery in sparse mixtures of experts, which reduce computation but whose statistical behavior was not well understood.
AI.method: For location Gaussian mixtures of experts with a fixed number of experts, recovery rates are derived using polynomial interpolation and Gaussian RKHS test functions, together with quantitative restriction inequalities that extend pointwise comparisons to expert functions.
AI.result: For dense models with well-separated clusters, the geometry depends on the largest cluster size, and otherwise on the total number of experts. For sparse models, the geometry on retained routing regions depends on the number of active experts, and omitted regions are controlled by their total probability. Fewer active experts reduce separation complexity, and top-1 routing achieves recovery independent of the separation quantity.
AI.conclusion: Activating fewer experts reduces the statistical difficulty of expert recovery, with top-1 routing offering the strongest guarantee.

title: Surrogate Losses for Fairness-Aware Classification: Fisher Consistency and Calibration
summary: Fairness-aware classification seeks to balance predictive accuracy and fairness across demographic groups. Although surrogate losses facilitate the optimization of fairness-aware objectives, it remains unclear when minimizing these losses yields optimal decisions under the original fairness-aware risk. This paper investigates the statistical validity of surrogate-based fairness-aware classification under demographic parity and equal opportunity, considering both attribute-blind and attribute-aware settings. We introduce fairness-aware Fisher consistency and characterize it through conditions on the derivatives of the surrogate losses. The characterization shows that consistency depends not only on the individual loss functions but also on their interaction within the fairness-regularized objective. We further establish a calibration inequality that relates the excess fairness-aware risk to the excess surrogate risk, providing a quantitative connection between surrogate optimization and the original classification objective. Numerical experiments illustrate how deviations from the consistency conditions affect fairness-aware excess risk and how the regularization parameter influences the well-posedness of surrogate optimization. An application to consumer credit default prediction demonstrates that appropriately calibrated fairness regularization can substantially reduce demographic disparities while maintaining predictive performance.

AI.tldr: The paper characterizes Fisher consistency of surrogate losses for fairness-aware classification under demographic parity and equal opportunity, in attribute-blind and attribute-aware settings, and gives a calibration inequality linking excess fairness-aware risk to excess surrogate risk.
AI.motivation: Surrogate losses make fairness-aware objectives tractable, but it was unclear when minimizing them yields optimal decisions under the original fairness-aware risk.
AI.method: Fairness-aware Fisher consistency is defined and characterized through conditions on the derivatives of the surrogate losses, which depend on their interaction within the fairness-regularized objective. A calibration inequality is derived relating the two excess risks.
AI.result: Numerical experiments show how deviations from the consistency conditions affect fairness-aware excess risk and how the regularization parameter affects well-posedness. In a consumer credit default application, calibrated fairness regularization substantially reduces demographic disparities while maintaining predictive performance.
AI.conclusion: Consistency depends on the joint structure of the surrogate and the fairness regularizer, and the calibration inequality gives a quantitative bridge from surrogate optimization to the original objective.

title: Sharp Generalization for Nonparametric Regression in Interpolation Space by Shallow Over-Parameterized Neural Networks with Channel Attention
summary: We study nonparametric regression using an over-parameterized two-layer ReLU neural network with fixed covariance-based channel attention, trained by gradient descent with both layers updated simultaneously. The spherical covariates follow an arbitrary fixed non-atomic distribution, and the target function lies in an interpolation space with spectral bias widely studied in the statistical learning literature. We prove that early-stopped training achieves regression risk $\cO(\eps_n^2)$, where $\eps_n$ is the critical population rate of the attention kernel $\Kattn$. Its positive eigenvalues are $\lambda_j^{s'}$, where $\lambda_j$ are those of the ReLU feature covariance kernel $K$ and $s'=2s+3$ for $s\ge1$. Under polynomial eigenvalue decay $\lambda_j\asymp j^{-2\alpha}$ with $\alpha>1/2$, the regression risk bound $\cO(\eps_n^2)$ specializes to the minimax optimal rate $\cO(n^{-2\alpha s'/(2\alpha s'+1)})$. Our analysis is based on two new technical results on the optimization and generalization of the attention network. First, the neural network function after every gradient descent iteration admits a decomposition into a function with bounded Reproducing Kernel Hilbert Space (RKHS) norm and a uniformly small residual. Second, local Rademacher complexity converts this decomposition into a regression risk bound. Kernel gradient descent on the same ball attains the same rate, while our theorem gives explicit sufficient width and auxiliary-sample conditions for simultaneous network training. Our analysis is further extended to covariates supported on $\RR^d$ through a novel normalization method. Under a sub-Gaussian covariate distribution, the attention network achieves a nearly optimal regression risk $\cO((\log n)n^{-s'(d+3)/(s'(d+3)+d)})$ without a density assumption.

AI.tldr: The paper proves that early-stopped gradient descent on an over-parameterized two-layer ReLU network with fixed covariance-based channel attention achieves the minimax optimal regression rate for target functions in an interpolation space with spectral bias.
AI.motivation: Existing sharp generalization results for nonparametric regression do not cover over-parameterized networks with attention trained by simultaneous gradient descent on both layers, with spherical or R^d covariates.
AI.method: The network function after every gradient descent iteration decomposes into a bounded-RKHS-norm function plus a uniformly small residual. Local Rademacher complexity converts this decomposition into a regression risk bound, and kernel gradient descent on the same ball is compared as a baseline.
AI.result: The risk is O(eps_n^2), where eps_n is the critical rate of the attention kernel. Under polynomial eigenvalue decay with alpha > 1/2, this specializes to the minimax rate O(n^{-2 alpha s'/(2 alpha s' + 1)}) with s' = 2s + 3. Under sub-Gaussian covariates on R^d, a nearly optimal rate is obtained without a density assumption, and explicit width and auxiliary-sample conditions are given.
AI.conclusion: Over-parameterized attention networks trained by gradient descent can attain minimax optimal nonparametric rates, matching kernel methods on the same RKHS ball.

title: Beyond Imputation: Mask-Adaptive Conformal Prediction via Tree Embeddings on General Missing Data Mechanisms
summary: Conformal prediction (CP) provides a distribution-free framework for uncertainty quantification with finite-sample marginal coverage guarantees. Yet, missing values introduce distributional heterogeneity, where marginal coverage can hide systematic undercoverage for certain missingness patterns. At the same time, existing methods based on distances or smoothness require a continuous representation of partially observed covariates. Although imputation restores continuity, it obscures the missingness patterns and introduces task-dependent overhead. We develop a new CP framework that is \emph{adaptive to missingness patterns}, without imputing covariates. We rely on data augmentation by feature embedding that accounts for missingness. Our framework represents each input with missing values by a tree embedding together with its raw missingness mask, and then learns a regularized quantile score function. Varying the choices for the penalty function and the augmentation enables us to characterize three practically relevant validity levels: exact coordinate-wise validity, exact validity on observed masks, and approximate missingness-conditional guarantees for general mechanisms (MCAR, MAR, MNAR). Experiments on synthetic and real datasets support these guarantees and show that the proposed method reduces miscoverage risk while maintaining informative intervals, especially in non-MCAR settings. These results highlight the practical value of uncertainty quantification that adapts to missingness.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a conformal prediction framework that handles missing covariates without imputation, using tree embeddings of inputs together with their missingness masks and a regularized quantile score, with three levels of validity for general missingness mechanisms.
AI.motivation: Missing values create heterogeneous distributions in which marginal coverage can hide systematic undercoverage for certain missingness patterns, while existing distance- or smoothness-based methods need continuous covariates, which imputation distorts.
AI.method: Each input with missing values is represented by a tree embedding together with its raw missingness mask, and a regularized quantile score function is learned. The choice of penalty and augmentation yields exact coordinate-wise validity, exact validity on observed masks, and approximate missingness-conditional guarantees under MCAR, MAR and MNAR.
AI.result: Experiments on synthetic and real datasets support the guarantees and show reduced miscoverage risk with informative intervals, especially in non-MCAR settings.
AI.conclusion: Uncertainty quantification that adapts to missingness patterns is practical without imputation, with the strongest gains when missingness is not completely at random.

title: Convex Regression at Scale: Geometry-Preserving Constraint Sparsification
summary: Convex regression provides a flexible nonparametric estimation framework while incorporating appropriate shape information. However, its standard least-squares formulation has $O(n^2)$ supporting-hyperplane constraints creating a computational bottleneck as the sample size $n$ increases. We study a $K$-nearest-neighbor (KNN) localized relaxation for convex regression where we for each sample, we only maintain the $K$ nearest hyperplane constraints. Under mild regularity conditions, we establish statistical guarantees for our modified estimator in every fixed dimension $d\ge2$. In particular, for $d>4$, the population risk of our modified problem can be shown to have equivalent convergence rates as the original least square convex regression estimator of $\widetilde O(n^{-2/d})$ using neighborhoods sizes (i.e. $K=K_n$) of order $\widetilde O(n^{2(d-1)/(2d-1)})$ for general convex functions and $\widetilde O(n^{(d+1)/(d+2)})$ for strongly convex functions. To corroborate our theory, we implement iterative optimization methods to compare the prediction accuracy of the KNN relaxation with those of the full estimator across synthetic convex benchmarks. Our experiments demonstrate that KNN prediction risk approaches the full-estimator prediction risk at neighborhood sizes matching the theoretical scale.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a K-nearest-neighbor relaxation of convex regression that keeps only K nearest supporting-hyperplane constraints per sample, reducing the O(n^2) constraint count while matching the rates of the full least-squares estimator for d greater than 4.
AI.motivation: The standard convex least-squares estimator has O(n^2) supporting-hyperplane constraints, which becomes a computational bottleneck as the sample size grows.
AI.method: Each sample keeps only its K nearest hyperplane constraints, and the modified estimator is analyzed in every fixed dimension d at least 2. Neighborhood sizes of order n^{2(d-1)/(2d-1)} for general convex functions and n^{(d+1)/(d+2)} for strongly convex functions are used, with iterative optimization for experiments.
AI.result: For d > 4, the population risk of the relaxed estimator has the same convergence rate as the full estimator, of order n^{-2/d} up to logarithmic factors. In synthetic convex benchmarks, the KNN prediction risk approaches the full-estimator risk at neighborhood sizes matching the theoretical scale.
AI.conclusion: Localized constraint sparsification makes convex regression scalable without sacrificing the statistical rate in higher dimensions.

title: Direct Knowledge Transfer for Offline Q-Learning
summary: Data-driven sequential decision making in marketing and healthcare can benefit from observations collected in related environments, particularly when data in the environment of interest are limited. Transferring such information requires accounting for differences in rewards and transition dynamics across environments. We study knowledge transfer for offline reinforcement learning through a joint estimation framework that directly integrates source information into target value-function learning. We propose Direct Transfer Fitted Q-Iteration (DFQI), which updates the target Q-function while simultaneously borrowing the source information through an L1 penalty that links the target coefficients to a weighted aggregate of source coefficients, with both determined jointly within each Bellman update. Using sieve approximation, we establish statistical guarantees for target estimation and policy learning in stationary discounted environments with common or heterogeneous transition kernels. Empirical studies further demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed DFQI framework in transferring source information to improve policy learning with limited target data.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes Direct Transfer Fitted Q-Iteration (DFQI), an offline reinforcement learning method that borrows source-environment information through an L1 penalty linking target and aggregated source coefficients within each Bellman update.
AI.motivation: Decisions in marketing and healthcare benefit from related environments, but reward and transition differences across environments must be accounted for when transferring information, and target data may be scarce.
AI.method: The target Q-function is updated while source information is integrated through an L1 penalty, with target and source coefficients determined jointly within each Bellman update. Sieve approximation is used for the estimation.
AI.result: Statistical guarantees are established for target estimation and policy learning in stationary discounted environments with common or heterogeneous transition kernels. Empirical studies show that DFQI transfers source information and improves policy learning with limited target data.
AI.conclusion: Joint estimation with an L1 coupling is a practical way to transfer offline RL knowledge across related environments with limited target data.

title: Rare Event Constrained Reinforcement Learning with Large Deviations
summary: We study finite-horizon reinforcement learning with a safety constraint on the probability of reaching a failure set. In contrast to the well-studied safe reinforcement learning literature, we consider problems where the probability of reaching the failure set is vanishingly small, but the consequences of reaching the failure set are catastrophic. Direct simulation and estimation of the optimal policy is naturally ineffective when the failure probability is extremely small. Moreover, on a real system the controller can only choose actions, and this is not enough to make failures frequent. In contrast to the rare event simulation literature, our goal is not to estimate the probability of the rare event occurrence, but to upper bound it such that the failure constraint is satisfied. Thus, instead of sampling failures, we use the large deviations principle. We define a damage variable that on exceeding a certain threshold indicates failure. We study the cumulant generating function (CGF) as its positive root provides an upper bound on the failure probability via Cramer's theorem. We extend this approach to Markov decision processes with hitting times through state-action CGFs, and give finite-horizon and state-dependent versions of the bound. The state-action CGFs do not depend on the policy and can be estimated from regular transitions, so the bound can be checked for any policy a priori. This gives a policy improvement algorithm in which every policy satisfies the failure constraint with high probability.

AI.tldr: The paper bounds the probability of rare failure events in finite-horizon reinforcement learning using the cumulant generating function of a damage variable and Cramer's theorem, and gives a policy improvement algorithm in which every policy satisfies the failure constraint with high probability.
AI.motivation: Failures in safety-critical control can be vanishingly rare but catastrophic, so direct simulation or estimation of failure probability is ineffective, and the controller can only choose actions rather than make failures frequent.
AI.method: A damage variable is defined that signals failure when it exceeds a threshold. The positive root of the cumulant generating function upper-bounds the failure probability via large deviations rather than sampling. The approach is extended to Markov decision processes with hitting times through state-action CGFs, which are policy-independent and can be estimated from regular transitions, giving finite-horizon and state-dependent bounds.
AI.result: The bound can be checked a priori for any policy, which yields a policy improvement algorithm in which every policy satisfies the failure constraint with high probability.
AI.conclusion: Large-deviation bounds offer an a priori certificate for rare-event safety constraints in RL without requiring rare failures to be observed.

title: Reduced Cost Influence Functions for Predict-then-Optimize under Noisy Data
summary: Machine learning models deployed in decision-making pipelines, from vehicle routing to dynamic pricing to clinical decision support, must remain reliable in the face of low-quality training data. We study a predict-then-optimize setting in which an upstream model predicts the cost vector of a downstream linear program, with a large pool of noisy training data supplemented by a small curated set of clean data. We introduce Reduced Cost Influence Functions (RCIFs), which combine influence functions from robust statistics with the geometry of linear optimization to estimate how each training point shifts downstream decisions. Building on this, we propose a reweighting algorithm that uses RCIFs to downweight harmful training points and reduce downstream regret. Experiments on random linear programs and shortest-path problems show that our approach reduces regret, and accompanying theory characterizes properties of RCIFs and identifies regimes favorable to our method relative to baselines.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Reduced Cost Influence Functions (RCIFs) that estimate how each noisy training point shifts the decisions of a downstream linear program, and uses them to reweight training data and reduce regret in predict-then-optimize settings.
AI.motivation: In predict-then-optimize pipelines, an upstream model predicts the cost vector of a linear program from a large pool of noisy data, and standard robust methods do not account for how errors affect downstream decisions.
AI.method: RCIFs combine influence functions from robust statistics with the geometry of linear optimization. A reweighting algorithm uses RCIFs to downweight harmful training points, with a small curated clean set also available.
AI.result: Experiments on random linear programs and shortest-path problems show reduced regret, and theory characterizes RCIF properties and identifies regimes where the method outperforms baselines.
AI.conclusion: Decision-aware influence estimation is a practical route to reducing downstream regret caused by noisy training data.

title: Multiclass Classification with Rare Useful Features: Fundamental Limits and the Optimality of Diversity Pursuit Higher Criticism Thresholding
comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026. 43 pages, including references and supplementary material
summary: We consider classification in high-dimensional feature spaces where only a vanishing fraction of features are useful and the number of classes may be large. While this rare-and-weak useful-feature regime is well understood in the binary setting, its multiclass version raises new questions: a feature can be useful for class discrimination without separating any specific pair of classes. We focus on a rare feature diversity model, in which most features are useless, but a small fraction promote discrimination among classes in a way that can be detected by a per-feature diversity test, such as one-way ANOVA or the Kruskal-Wallis test. For this setting, we propose Diversity Pursuit Higher Criticism Thresholding (DP-HCT), a feature-screening procedure that applies a higher-criticism threshold to the collection of p-values obtained from per-feature diversity tests. We justify DP-HCT under a Gaussian multiclass Rare-and-Weak Useful Feature model with class-mean contrasts of fixed magnitude in random directions, extending the binary model of Donoho and Jin (2008). When the number of classes is fixed, our model recovers the binary phase transition. When the number of classes grows logarithmically with the number of features, however, we derive a new and strictly harder phase transition, driven by the growing degrees of freedom and their effect on the useful-feature tail rate. We show that whenever classification beyond chance is possible, DP-HCT with ANOVA, followed by a simple classifier based on similarity to class means, achieves asymptotically perfect accuracy. Experiments on real multiclass classification benchmarks demonstrate substantial improvements, and numerical simulations confirm that the derived phase-transition curve accurately predicts the finite-sample behavior of DP-HCT in the growing-class regime.

AI.tldr: The paper develops Diversity Pursuit Higher Criticism Thresholding (DP-HCT), a feature-screening method for multiclass classification with rare useful features, and shows a new, strictly harder phase transition when the number of classes grows with the number of features.
AI.motivation: In multiclass problems a feature can be useful without separating any particular pair of classes, a case the binary rare-and-weak feature theory does not cover.
AI.method: Per-feature diversity tests such as one-way ANOVA or Kruskal-Wallis produce p-values, to which a higher-criticism threshold is applied. Justification is given under a Gaussian multiclass rare-and-weak useful-feature model that extends the binary model of Donoho and Jin (2008).
AI.result: With a fixed number of classes the binary phase transition is recovered. When the number of classes grows logarithmically with the number of features, a new, strictly harder phase transition emerges. Whenever classification beyond chance is possible, DP-HCT with ANOVA followed by a similarity-to-class-means classifier achieves asymptotically perfect accuracy. Real benchmarks show substantial gains, and simulations match the predicted phase-transition curve.
AI.conclusion: Multiclass feature screening with diversity tests is asymptotically optimal in the rare-feature regime, and the growing-class regime is intrinsically harder.

title: On Stochastic Continuous-Time Linear System Identification for Adaptive Stabilization
summary: Learning to stabilize an unknown continuous-time stochastic linear system is a central problem in control theory and reinforcement learning. This paper numerically studies data-driven identification of such systems with possibly unstable dynamics for the purpose of stabilization. We present a method that learns a stabilizing gain from observed trajectories, and examine how the failure probability, namely the probability that the learned gain does not stabilize the system, depends on the amount of data, dimension, noise intensity, excitation, and controllability. Numerical experiments on an unstable batch-reactor benchmark show that the squared identification error decays inversely with the aggregate observation time, that is, the combined length of all trajectories, while the failure probability decays exponentially in the same quantity. Hence, despite instability, a single long trajectory can achieve similar stabilization performance to that of many short trajectories of the same total length. We also observe \emph{signal saturation}: stronger excitation improves stabilization only logarithmically with the excitation strength. Finally, we show experimentally that accurate identification of the full dynamics is \emph{not} necessary for successful stabilization.

AI.tldr: The paper numerically studies data-driven identification of unknown continuous-time stochastic linear systems for stabilization, finding that the failure probability decays exponentially in the aggregate observation time, so a single long trajectory performs about as well as many short ones of the same total length.
AI.motivation: Learning a stabilizing gain for an unknown, possibly unstable, continuous-time stochastic system requires understanding how the failure probability depends on data amount, dimension, noise, excitation and controllability.
AI.method: A method learns a stabilizing gain from observed trajectories, and its failure probability and identification error are measured numerically on an unstable batch-reactor benchmark while varying data amount, dimension, noise intensity, excitation and controllability.
AI.result: The squared identification error decays inversely with the aggregate observation time, and the failure probability decays exponentially in the same quantity. Stronger excitation improves stabilization only logarithmically, which the authors call signal saturation. Accurate identification of the full dynamics is not necessary for successful stabilization.
AI.conclusion: For stabilization, total observation time matters more than trajectory count, and full model accuracy is not required.

title: Specification-Aware Predictive Uncertainty Decomposition
summary: Classical decompositions of predictive uncertainty, such as the information-theoretic one, are defined for a fixed representation $x$ of the input object. They do not consider that $x$ may be incomplete, nor do they measure how much the missing information can affect the prediction. In Large Language Models, users can clarify an underspecified input without any retraining. The clarified input can describe the user's unobserved intent $z^*$ more accurately and change the predictive uncertainty about the outcome. In this paper, we formalize this setting probabilistically and derive a three-term decomposition of prediction risk into specification, residual aleatoric, and epistemic uncertainties. We show that at the original information level, when only $x$ is available, the aleatoric uncertainty, represented by a Bayes risk, has two components. The first, which we call specification uncertainty, is the expected reduction in this Bayes risk from revealing the intent. The second is the residual aleatoric uncertainty, i.e., the Bayes risk that remains once the intent is known, averaged over its possible values $z$ given $x$. The distinction is important, as specification uncertainty informs the decision to request clarification before making a prediction. We build approximations of these components and connect them to existing uncertainty measures. Our experiments across different domains and modalities show distinct roles for the three components. Specification uncertainty is the most informative for detecting underspecified inputs, while residual aleatoric uncertainty is the most informative for detecting in-distribution prediction errors.

AI.tldr: The paper decomposes predictive risk into specification uncertainty, residual aleatoric uncertainty and epistemic uncertainty, to separate underspecified inputs from intrinsic ambiguity, and shows that specification uncertainty signals when clarification should be requested.
AI.motivation: Classical uncertainty decompositions assume a fixed input representation and do not account for incomplete inputs or how much missing intent could change the prediction, which matters for LLMs that can be clarified without retraining.
AI.method: The setting is formalized probabilistically with a latent user intent z*, and prediction risk is split into three terms. Specification uncertainty is the expected reduction in Bayes risk from revealing the intent, and residual aleatoric uncertainty is the remaining Bayes risk averaged over intent values given x. Approximations are built and connected to existing uncertainty measures.
AI.result: Across domains and modalities, specification uncertainty is most informative for detecting underspecified inputs, and residual aleatoric uncertainty is most informative for detecting in-distribution prediction errors.
AI.conclusion: Separating specification from aleatoric and epistemic uncertainty gives a principled basis for deciding when to ask for clarification versus when to predict.

title: Causal discovery needs explicit epistemic standards
comment: This paper was accepted to the position paper track of NeurIPS 2026
summary: There are many causal discovery algorithms, but few guiding principles for choosing between them. Methods are usually compared through three lenses: identifiability, consistency, and benchmarks. Each introduces assumptions about the data-generating process that are often untestable. We argue that there are no shared standards for comparing, prioritizing, or even discussing those assumptions. We support this claim by showing that (i) identifiability assumptions are often preferred by convention rather than by principle, (ii) uniform consistency requires further untestable assumptions, while the weaker pointwise consistency has arguably narrowed algorithm design, and (iii) benchmarks are not neutral tests but carry an epistemic role of their own: they quietly fix which regimes matter, which guarantees come into play, and what counts as success. In doing so, they shape what algorithm comparisons are taken to show and thus perform some of the same epistemic work as theory, but less transparently. In this position paper we argue for a more transparent, integrated practice: Make the epistemic standards for discussing identifiability and consistency assumptions explicit, especially their failure modes and scope conditions; design benchmarks to operationalize those standards, by stress-testing and ablating both. Then, theoretical and empirical results jointly clarify when, why, and how algorithms may work rather than accumulate as disconnected advances.

AI.tldr: This position paper argues that causal discovery lacks shared epistemic standards for identifiability, consistency and benchmark assumptions, and calls for explicit standards, with benchmarks designed to stress-test them, so that theory and experiments jointly clarify when algorithms work.
AI.motivation: Causal discovery methods are compared through identifiability, consistency and benchmarks, each relying on often untestable assumptions, and there is no shared standard for comparing or discussing them.
AI.method: The paper argues that identifiability assumptions are often chosen by convention, that uniform consistency needs further untestable assumptions while pointwise consistency has narrowed algorithm design, and that benchmarks carry an implicit epistemic role in fixing regimes and success criteria. It proposes explicit standards and stress-testing and ablation of benchmarks.
AI.result: The paper is a position argument and reports no new experimental results.
AI.conclusion: Algorithm progress in causal discovery requires integrating theory and benchmarks under transparent epistemic standards rather than accumulating disconnected advances.

title: Poisson Super Learning For Survival And Competing Risks On A Discretized Time Scale
summary: We introduce the Poisson Super Learner, a scalable ensemble method for survival and competing risks prediction with right-censored data. The approach exploits the correspondence between the likelihood of piecewise-constant hazard models and the Poisson likelihood. After expanding the data over a chosen time partition, candidate hazard learners are trained under a common Poisson loss, and cross-validated log-hazard predictions are combined by a Poisson meta learner. The resulting ensemble is a geometric combination of candidate hazards, and can be used to estimate survival probabilities and cause-specific absolute risks. The Poisson Super Learner framework is modular and can in principle incorporate any learner that can estimate interval-specific hazards, including parametric, penalised, additive, and other machine-learning hazard models. Training targets the cause-specific hazard directly and does not require explicit modelling of the censoring distribution. For competing risks, separate cause-specific ensembles are fitted and subsequently combined to obtain individualised cumulative incidence predictions.
