We illustrate the approach using data from the Steno Diabetes Center collected between 2005 and 2022 to predict cardiovascular disease risk in patients with type 1 diabetes from detailed covariate information. The applied analysis is complemented by simulation studies designed to reflect key features of the data and to examine the behaviour of the method under controlled settings. All analyses were implemented using the freely available R software package poissonsuperlearner.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Poisson Super Learner, an ensemble for survival and competing-risks prediction with right-censored data that trains piecewise-constant hazard learners under a common Poisson loss and combines them with a Poisson meta-learner.
AI.motivation: Survival ensembles need a scalable method that models cause-specific hazards directly without explicitly modeling the censoring distribution, and that can incorporate any interval-hazard learner.
AI.method: After expanding the data over a time partition, candidate hazard learners are trained under a Poisson likelihood, and their cross-validated log-hazard predictions are combined by a Poisson meta-learner. The result is a geometric combination of hazards used for survival and cause-specific absolute risks, with separate ensembles for each cause in competing risks.
AI.result: The method is illustrated on Steno Diabetes Center data (2005 to 2022) for cardiovascular risk in type 1 diabetes, complemented by simulation studies. The implementation is released as the R package poissonsuperlearner.
AI.conclusion: The Poisson super learner offers a modular, scalable route to survival and competing-risks ensembles that avoids modeling censoring explicitly.

title: EventGPT: Next-Event Pretraining on Banking Customer Histories
comment: 43 pages, 12 figures, 15 tables. Code: this https URL. Weights: this https URL
summary: A model pretrained to predict a customer's next event can estimate the probability of future events without training on their labels and provide a reusable representation for supervised downstream banking tasks. We pretrain EventGPT, a hierarchical causal transformer, by next-token maximum likelihood estimation on the public Multimodal Banking Dataset (MBD-mini: 100,224 clients, 38.8 million transactions and 66.3 million geolocation pings). Keeping one state per event, EventGPT trains in about two hours on one L4 GPU at windows up to 8,192 tokens. From its next-event distribution, with no labels, EventGPT scores five targets of the form "the client makes a transaction of a given kind for the first time next month" at ROC-AUC 0.79 to 0.92. Gradient boosting on 114 engineered features needs 10,000 to 300,000 labeled client-months to match it on four targets and stays below it on the fifth. For product prediction, frozen EventGPT embeddings score below the engineered features (mean ROC-AUC 0.787 against 0.808 over five test folds), and a rank-averaged ensemble of EventGPT, profile fields and token counts with the engineered features adds 0.014 to 0.017, of which 0.007 to 0.016 is EventGPT's own. The code and pretrained weights are released.

AI.tldr: The paper pretrains EventGPT, a hierarchical causal transformer, on customer event histories from the Multimodal Banking Dataset, and shows that its next-event probabilities predict future banking events without labels, with a small gain when combined with engineered features.
AI.motivation: A model that predicts a customer's next event may provide label-free estimates of future events and a reusable representation for supervised banking tasks, which had not been tested against strong engineered-feature baselines.
AI.method: EventGPT is pretrained by next-token maximum likelihood on MBD-mini, with 100,224 clients, 38.8 million transactions and 66.3 million geolocation pings, using one state per event and windows up to 8,192 tokens, trained in about two hours on one L4 GPU. It is compared with gradient boosting on 114 engineered features.
AI.result: Without labels, EventGPT scores five first-time-transaction targets at ROC-AUC 0.79 to 0.92. Gradient boosting needs 10,000 to 300,000 labeled client-months to match it on four targets and stays below it on the fifth. For product prediction, frozen embeddings score below engineered features (mean ROC-AUC 0.787 vs 0.808), while a rank-averaged ensemble adds 0.014 to 0.017, of which 0.007 to 0.016 comes from EventGPT. Code and weights are released.
AI.conclusion: Next-event pretraining gives strong label-free predictions for banking events and a modest complementary signal for supervised tasks, though frozen embeddings alone do not beat engineered features.

title: Neural Actor--Critic Learning with Minimax Critics and Reflected Langevin Sampling
summary: Actor--critic methods rely on critic gradients to improve continuous-action policies, yet finite-sample guarantees must control both value and gradient errors and their propagation through the actor. We develop a neural actor-critic procedure that combines a regularized minimax Bellman estimator over sigmoid networks with a finite reflected Langevin sampler driven by the fitted critic gradient. Under uniform Bellman regularity and covered reset sampling, a positive high-order action-derivative penalty yields value and action-gradient risk bounds with classical nonparametric minimax exponents up to logarithmic factors. We propagate estimation, mixing, discretization, temperature, and policy-iteration errors to obtain return guarantees, with refinements for bounded multimodal potentials and strongly concave regimes. Empirical studies across controlled simulations, logged continuous-control data, and a simulated decision task show favorable performance relative to the considered baselines.

AI.tldr: The paper develops a neural actor-critic method for continuous-action policies, combining a regularized minimax Bellman estimator over sigmoid networks with a reflected Langevin sampler driven by the fitted critic gradient, and gives finite-sample guarantees on value and action-gradient errors.
AI.motivation: Actor-critic methods depend on critic gradients for continuous actions, yet finite-sample guarantees have to control both value and gradient errors and how they propagate through the actor.
AI.method: A regularized minimax Bellman estimator with a high-order action-derivative penalty is fit over sigmoid networks. A finite reflected Langevin sampler uses the fitted critic gradient to draw actions. Estimation, mixing, discretization, temperature and policy-iteration errors are propagated to return guarantees.
AI.result: Under uniform Bellman regularity and covered reset sampling, value and action-gradient risks achieve classical nonparametric minimax exponents up to logarithmic factors. Refinements apply to bounded multimodal potentials and strongly concave regimes. Experiments on simulations, logged continuous-control data and a simulated decision task show favorable performance against the baselines considered.
AI.conclusion: Critic-gradient-driven sampling with minimax estimation gives theoretically grounded and empirically competitive actor-critic learning for continuous actions.

title: Subpolynomial-Query Proximal Sampling Beyond Log-Concavity
summary:
We study the gradient query complexity of sampling from a density $\pi(x)\propto\mathrm{e}^{-V(x)}$ on $\mathbb{R}^d$, where $V$ has a $ eta$-Lipschitz gradient but need not be convex. Our approach uses the proximal sampler, which alternates Gaussian perturbation with sampling a position conditional on the noisy observation. We implement its observation chain using the high-order noisy conditional sampler of [OpenAI 2026], obtaining improved dimension dependence under functional inequalities. If $\pi$ satisfies a log-Sobolev inequality (LSI) with constant $\alpha$, then for every fixed $
u>0$, there is a finite constant $C_
u$ depending only on $
u$ such that the algorithm returns a sample within total-variation distance $\varepsilon$ using at most $C_
u\kappa(d+\kappa+\varepsilon^{-1}+\|
abla V(x_0)\|^2/ eta)^
u$ queries, where $\kappa= eta/\alpha$ and $x_0$ is an arbitrary reference point for initialization. The analysis controls center-dependent local errors along exact proximal histories and removes the final observation noise by conditional decoding. Under a Poincaré inequality (PI), we obtain a corresponding guarantee from a warm start with a known bound on its Rényi divergence. An oracle lower bound shows that a stationary point alone, which suffices under LSI, is insufficient under PI.

AI.tldr: The paper gives a sampler for densities proportional to exp(-V) with Lipschitz gradient but possibly nonconvex V, whose gradient query complexity is subpolynomial in the dimension and the condition number under a log-Sobolev inequality, and gives a corresponding guarantee under a Poincare inequality with a warm start.
AI.motivation: Existing proximal sampler analyses for non-log-concave targets do not achieve these dimension and query dependencies, and the observation step needs a more efficient conditional sampler.
AI.method: The proximal sampler alternates Gaussian perturbation with conditional sampling of the position given the noisy observation. The observation chain is implemented with a high-order noisy conditional sampler from the cited OpenAI 2026 work, and the final observation noise is removed by conditional decoding. Local errors are controlled along exact proximal histories.
AI.result: Under an LSI with constant alpha, for every fixed nu > 0 there is a constant C_nu such that the algorithm reaches total variation epsilon with at most C_nu kappa (d + kappa + 1/epsilon + ||grad V(x_0)||^2 / beta)^nu queries, where kappa = beta/alpha. Under a PI, a corresponding guarantee holds from a warm start with a known Renyi bound. An oracle lower bound shows that a stationary point is insufficient under PI.
AI.conclusion: Under LSI the sampler achieves polynomial-in-dimension complexity with exponent arbitrarily close to a fixed bound, and under PI a stationary point alone cannot suffice.

title: Error Accumulation in Second-Order Sequential Machine Unlearning
summary: Machine unlearning seeks to remove the influence of deleted training data without full retraining. In the sequential setting, deletion requests arrive over time, and repeated updates can accumulate approximation errors. In this paper, we study error accumulation in high dimensions, where parameter count $p$ is proportional to sample size $n$, for second-order unlearning methods under two privacy settings: (i) \emph{partial unlearning}, which allows unpublished internal states to be retained while certified versions of the model are released; and (ii) \emph{perfect unlearning}, which retains only published models and no hidden states. We also distinguish pointwise and pathwise certification, depending on whether the certification guarantee applies to each released model or the whole released sequence. We analyze conjugate gradient (CG) as an efficient solver for the inverse Hessian-vector product (IHVP) in Newton iterations. Our theory shows that a maximum of 1/2/2/3 Newton--CG updates suffice for successful certification and vanishing population-risk degradation of the published model, for pointwise partial, pathwise partial, pointwise perfect and pathwise perfect certification, respectively. Numerical experiments demonstrate accurate sequential tracking and substantial computational gains of Newton-based methods combined with conjugate gradient, over gradient-based updates, especially for ill-conditioned problems.

AI.tldr: The paper analyzes error accumulation in sequential second-order machine unlearning when parameter count is proportional to sample size, showing that a small fixed number of Newton-CG updates suffices for certification and vanishing population-risk degradation under four certification settings.
AI.motivation: Sequential deletion requests can accumulate approximation errors in second-order unlearning, and this accumulation had not been analyzed in high dimensions with proportional parameter and sample sizes.
AI.method: Two privacy settings are studied: partial unlearning, which retains unpublished internal states while releasing certified models, and perfect unlearning, which retains only published models. Pointwise and pathwise certification are distinguished. Conjugate gradient solves the inverse Hessian-vector products in Newton iterations.
AI.result: At most 1, 2, 2 and 3 Newton-CG updates suffice for pointwise partial, pathwise partial, pointwise perfect and pathwise perfect certification, respectively, with vanishing population-risk degradation. Experiments show accurate sequential tracking and computational gains over gradient-based updates, especially for ill-conditioned problems.
AI.conclusion: Newton-CG unlearning with a few updates per deletion is theoretically certified in high dimensions, and the required updates grow with the stringency of the certification.

title: ProLand: A New Infeasible Manifold Optimization Method for LoRA Fine-Tuning
summary: Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) enables parameter-efficient fine-tuning but can suffer from redundant basis directions. Constraining the basis factor to the Stiefel manifold addresses this redundancy through orthonormality. Landing methods allow temporarily infeasible iterates to explore a neighborhood of the manifold while progressively restoring orthogonality without per-step retractions. To improve optimization efficiency while retaining this flexibility, we introduce ProLand (Product-space Landing), a retraction-free optimizer that combines coordinated factor updates with Muon-style spectral directions. By designing the updates in the space of the represented weight increment, ProLand separates objective optimization from orthogonality restoration, supporting efficient feasibility recovery. This coordinated construction also enables Muon-style directions to guide objective optimization while preserving that separation. Experiments cover four GLUE validation tasks on DeBERTa-v3-base and seven language benchmarks on Qwen2.5-3B, Llama-3.2-3B, and Moonlight-16B-A3B across multiple adapter ranks. Across these 11 tasks, ProLand achieves the highest average score among the compared methods in every tested encoder and decoder model-rank configuration.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes ProLand, a retraction-free optimizer for LoRA fine-tuning that constrains the low-rank basis factor near the Stiefel manifold, combining coordinated factor updates with Muon-style spectral directions.
AI.motivation: LoRA can have redundant basis directions, and landing methods that allow infeasible iterates still need efficient objective updates while restoring orthogonality.
AI.method: ProLand designs updates in the space of the represented weight increment, which separates objective optimization from orthogonality restoration. Muon-style spectral directions guide the objective while preserving this separation, with no per-step retraction.
AI.result: Across four GLUE validation tasks on DeBERTa-v3-base and seven language benchmarks on Qwen2.5-3B, Llama-3.2-3B and Moonlight-16B-A3B at several ranks, ProLand achieves the highest average score among compared methods in every tested encoder and decoder configuration.
AI.conclusion: Retraction-free landing with spectral directions is a competitive option for parameter-efficient fine-tuning across encoder and decoder models.

title: KINDER: Kernel-based Independence for Fair Representation Learning via Prototype-space Erasure
summary: Concept erasure is a prominent approach to achieving fairness in machine learning through the removal of sensitive attributes from learned representations. Prior concept erasure methods typically define debiasing indirectly through the failure of a chosen adversary, probe, or fairness penalty, which makes the target of erasure dependent on a particular decoder family or optimization setup. We introduce KINDER, which directly removes sensitive-attribute information from intermediate representations with respect to a chosen family of prototype functionals, and is compatible with any deep model containing an intermediate feature space, independent of the architecture, task type, or training paradigm. KINDER operates in a random Fourier feature space, where it estimates a sensitive subspace from protected group prototypes and projects representations onto its orthogonal complement. Thus, it forms an explicit representation cleaning mechanism distinct from prior fairness control studies. We conduct extensive experiments across diverse settings and show the effectiveness of KINDER on (i) supervised and self-supervised settings, (ii) classification, regression, and image segmentation tasks, and (iii) diverse data modalities, including visual, textual, and tabular data. Code and trained models are available at: this https URL

AI.tldr: The paper proposes KINDER, a concept-erasure method that removes sensitive-attribute information from intermediate representations by estimating a sensitive subspace from protected-group prototypes in a random Fourier feature space and projecting onto its orthogonal complement.
AI.motivation: Prior concept-erasure methods define debiasing indirectly through an adversary, probe or fairness penalty, which ties the erasure target to a particular decoder family or optimization setup.
AI.method: KINDER works in a random Fourier feature space, estimates a sensitive subspace from prototypes of protected groups with respect to a chosen family of prototype functionals, and projects representations onto its orthogonal complement. It applies to any model with an intermediate feature space.
AI.result: Experiments cover supervised and self-supervised settings, classification, regression and image segmentation, and visual, textual and tabular data.
AI.conclusion: Direct subspace-based representation cleaning offers an architecture- and training-agnostic alternative to adversarial concept erasure.

title: Optimistic Gradient Algorithms with Randomized Coordinate and Variance Reduction Strategies for Composite Inclusions
summary: In this paper, we consider a class of possibly nonmonotone finite-sum composite inclusions in which evaluating all components or updating all coordinates at every iteration can be computationally expensive. We develop two optimistic gradient frameworks that combine variance reduction with randomized block-coordinate updates. The first framework applies under a blockwise average Lipschitz continuity condition and the existence of a weak-Minty solution. It achieves an $\mathcal{O}(1/k)$ convergence rate for the expected squared residual, and its iterates converge almost surely under mild additional conditions. The second framework relies on a backward-forward reformulation under average co-coercivity and co-hypomonotonicity. It achieves faster $\mathcal{O}(1/k^2)$ and $o(1/k^2)$ rates for the expected squared residual, as well as $o(1/k^2)$ almost-sure rates. For both frameworks, we provide a generic condition on the stochastic estimator that covers mini-batch, loopless SVRG, and a generalized JacSketch-type estimator, and we derive the corresponding oracle complexities under importance-based block sampling. In particular, in highly heterogeneous regimes, the L-SVRG and JacSketch variants attain $\mathcal{O}\big(n + n^{2/3}\epsilon^{-2}\big)$ and $\mathcal{O}\big(n + n^{2/3}\epsilon^{-1}\big)$ oracle complexities for the nonaccelerated and accelerated methods, respectively. Numerical experiments illustrate the effects of variance reduction and block-coordinate sampling, and compare the proposed methods with existing baselines.

AI.tldr: The paper develops two optimistic gradient frameworks for nonmonotone finite-sum composite inclusions that combine variance reduction with randomized block-coordinate updates, achieving O(1/k) and O(1/k^2) rates for the expected squared residual under different assumptions.
AI.motivation: When evaluating all components or updating all coordinates is expensive, full-gradient methods for nonmonotone composite inclusions are costly, so randomized block-coordinate variants with variance reduction are needed.
AI.method: The first framework assumes blockwise average Lipschitz continuity and a weak-Minty solution. The second uses a backward-forward reformulation under average co-coercivity and co-hypomonotonicity. Both accommodate mini-batch, loopless SVRG and generalized JacSketch estimators under importance-based block sampling.
AI.result: The first framework achieves O(1/k) for the expected squared residual with almost sure iterate convergence, and the second achieves O(1/k^2) and o(1/k^2) rates. In highly heterogeneous regimes, L-SVRG and JacSketch variants reach O(n + n^{2/3} eps^{-2}) and O(n + n^{2/3} eps^{-1}) oracle complexities, nonaccelerated and accelerated respectively. Numerical experiments compare with baselines.
AI.conclusion: Randomized block variance reduction in optimistic gradient methods improves convergence and oracle complexity for nonmonotone composite problems under heterogeneity.

title: Statistical Inference under Performativity: From Policy Feedback to Self-Evolving Systems
comment: Extended version of the NeurIPS 2025 paper "Statistical Inference under Performativity" (arXiv:2505.18493)
summary: Performativity arises when prediction-informed decisions change the data-generating process, creating feedback between deployment and learning. This phenomenon occurs in policy-making and in self-evolving AI systems that shape their own future training data. Statistical inference is challenging because estimation errors in earlier predictors affect subsequent data distributions and propagate into later updates. We develop an end-to-end framework for statistical inference under performativity. For repeated risk minimization and repeated gradient descent, we establish central limit theorems at fixed deployment rounds and derive covariance recursions that capture both current-round sampling variation and uncertainty inherited from earlier deployments. We develop consistent covariance estimators using policy perturbations and score matching. These results can yield asymptotically valid confidence regions for population iterates and the performative stable point. We further extend prediction-powered inference to this dynamic setting, combining labeled observations with predictions on additional unlabeled data to improve statistical efficiency. We evaluate our framework in synthetic, semi-synthetic educational, and self-evolving large language model routing settings. Our experiments demonstrate that ignoring propagated uncertainty can lead to substantial undercoverage even after repeated retraining. Together, these results provide statistical tools for learning systems that help determine the distributions from which they learn. Our work establish a complete statistical inference under performativity, introducing new challenges and inference settings that we believe will provide substantial value to policy-making, statistics, and machine learning.

AI.tldr: The paper develops statistical inference for performative prediction, where deployed predictions change the data distribution, giving central limit theorems and covariance recursions for repeated risk minimization and gradient descent, and extending prediction-powered inference to this dynamic setting.
AI.motivation: Estimation errors in earlier predictors propagate into later data distributions and updates, so standard inference is invalid, and this arises in policy-making and in self-evolving AI systems.
AI.method: Central limit theorems are established at fixed deployment rounds, and covariance recursions capture both current-round sampling variation and inherited uncertainty. Consistent covariance estimators are built with policy perturbations and score matching, and prediction-powered inference combines labeled data with unlabeled predictions.
AI.result: The framework yields asymptotically valid confidence regions for population iterates and the performative stable point. In synthetic, semi-synthetic educational and self-evolving LLM routing settings, ignoring propagated uncertainty causes substantial undercoverage even after repeated retraining.
AI.conclusion: Inference under performativity must account for uncertainty propagated across deployment rounds, and the proposed tools enable valid confidence regions in such feedback systems.

title: Mutual Information Estimation via Triangular Transport Maps: Finite Sample Guarantees and Sample Allocation
summary: We study finite sample guarantees for transport based mutual information estimation. Mutual information can be estimated by first learning the conditional and marginal densities and then evaluating their log-density ratio by Monte Carlo. Given training samples, we use triangular transport maps to learn these densities and then compute the mutual information estimate on an independent batch of evaluation samples. For conditional density estimation using triangular transport maps, we establish non-asymptotic guarantees over realizable Hölder classes by viewing the conditional density as an ordinary density with respect to the product of the law of the conditioning variable and Lebesgue measure. This allows standard density estimation techniques to be applied directly to the conditional density estimation. These results yield finite sample guarantees for the resulting mutual information estimator and characterize how a fixed sample budget should be allocated between training and evaluation in order to minimize the mean squared error. Numerical experiments support the predicted training and evaluation error rates and illustrate the resulting sample allocation tradeoff.

AI.tldr: The paper gives finite-sample guarantees for mutual information estimation using triangular transport maps, learning conditional and marginal densities and evaluating their log-density ratio on an independent evaluation batch, and characterizes how to split a fixed sample budget between training and evaluation.
AI.motivation: Transport-based mutual information estimators lacked non-asymptotic guarantees, and the trade-off between training and evaluation samples for minimizing mean squared error was not characterized.
AI.method: Conditional density estimation with triangular transport maps is recast as ordinary density estimation with respect to the product of the conditioning law and Lebesgue measure, so standard techniques apply. Guarantees are established over realizable Holder classes and combined with Monte Carlo evaluation on separate samples.
AI.result: The resulting estimator has finite-sample error guarantees, and the paper characterizes the optimal allocation of the fixed sample budget between training and evaluation to minimize mean squared error. Numerical experiments support the predicted training and evaluation error rates and the allocation trade-off.
AI.conclusion: Transport-based mutual information estimation admits finite-sample theory, and sample allocation between fitting and evaluation can be chosen to minimize error.

title: Power-Optimal Risk Control via Standardized Margin Calibration
summary: Machine learning can screen far more candidates than can be experimentally validated, creating a need for selection procedures that identify promising candidates while controlling risk before costly experimental validation. We propose Uncertainty-Normalized Empirical Calibration (UNEC), a p-value-free framework that ranks candidates by uncertainty-normalized predictive margins and directly calibrates a selection cutoff using held-out losses. UNEC supports flexible prediction models, general bounded losses, and diverse selection targets. We study marginal discovery risk (MDR) and selective discovery risk (SDR), with SDR reducing to the false discovery rate under binary loss. We establish finite-sample MDR control for an adjusted rule and asymptotic SDR control with explicit limiting risk and power. Under a location--scale model with a common one-sided binary target, we further show that UNEC asymptotically attains the oracle power benchmark among observation-wise selection rules. Simulations and molecular screening applications in solubility, toxicity, and lipophilicity demonstrate favorable risk--power trade-offs and substantial computational gains across binary and graded-loss settings.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes Uncertainty-Normalized Empirical Calibration (UNEC), a p-value-free selection framework that ranks candidates by uncertainty-normalized predictive margins and calibrates the cutoff with held-out losses to control marginal and selective discovery risk.
AI.motivation: Screening far more candidates than can be validated experimentally requires selection procedures that control risk without p-values and support flexible models and bounded losses.
AI.method: Candidates are ranked by uncertainty-normalized margins, and the selection cutoff is calibrated directly on held-out losses. Marginal discovery risk (MDR) and selective discovery risk (SDR) are studied, with SDR reducing to the false discovery rate under binary loss.
AI.result: Finite-sample MDR control is established for an adjusted rule, and asymptotic SDR control holds with explicit limiting risk and power. Under a location-scale model with a common one-sided binary target, UNEC asymptotically attains the oracle power among observation-wise rules. Simulations and molecular screening for solubility, toxicity and lipophilicity show favorable risk-power trade-offs and computational gains.
AI.conclusion: UNEC gives p-value-free risk control for candidate selection with asymptotically optimal power in a canonical model and practical gains in molecular screening.

title: Where Causal Discovery Breaks on Real Data: Measuring the Assumptions One Property at a Time
summary: Causal discovery is usually evaluated on simulators or on systems whose ground truth follows from physics or design. When it fails on other real data, the failure is attributed to assumptions that may not hold, but which ones fail, and by how much, is rarely measured. We measure the observable properties of the data they bear on, one property at a time, on a real panel. The case study follows 2,901 US public firms over 31 quarters, with 71 types of corporate action from SEC 8-K filings, 11 financial-statement items, and an expert graph over 651 action-state pairs. The panel breaks measurable requirements of discovery: tails that survive winsorisation, balance-sheet items and revenue close to random walks, and interventions too rare to detect effects of a tenth of a standard deviation in 40 of 71 actions. Even so, a marginal test ranks expert-labelled direct above not-direct pairs within each action (AUROC 0.658) better than every null we built, so the panel does carry information about which pairs are direct. Tuned discovery methods, in configurations feasible at this panel size, recover less of it than a simple pairwise cross-correlation when pairs are ranked within each action, and no more when they are ranked within each target, which removes what the target alone predicts. Most direct pairs (132 of 222) involve actions below the support needed for 80% power against a 0.1-SD effect. For flow targets, conditioning on the target's other expert-labelled parents, often filed alongside the action, erodes the marginal discrimination, and most not-direct associations survive it: even with the graph's parent sets supplied, the expected separation does not emerge. For each property, we give a diagnostic computable before any discovery method is run.

AI.tldr: The paper measures, one property at a time, which assumptions of causal discovery fail on a real panel of 2,901 US public firms over 31 quarters, finding that some properties break discovery requirements and that tuned methods recover less signal than a simple pairwise cross-correlation.
AI.motivation: Causal discovery is usually evaluated on simulators or systems with known ground truth, and when it fails on real data the responsible assumptions are rarely measured.
AI.method: The authors measure observable properties of the data one at a time, using 71 types of corporate action from SEC 8-K filings, 11 financial-statement items and an expert graph over 651 action-state pairs. They also compare a marginal test, tuned discovery methods, and a pairwise cross-correlation baseline, with conditioning on expert-labelled parents for flow targets.
AI.result: Tails survive winsorisation, balance-sheet items and revenue are close to random walks, and 40 of 71 actions are too rare to detect a 0.1 SD effect. A marginal test ranks expert-labelled direct pairs above non-direct pairs (AUROC 0.658), better than every null built. Tuned methods recover less than a simple pairwise cross-correlation when ranked within each action, and most direct pairs (132 of 222) involve actions with insufficient power. Conditioning on other parents erodes the discrimination for flow targets.
AI.conclusion: Real-panel causal discovery is limited by measurable property violations and low power, and per-property diagnostics should be computed before running discovery methods.

title: The Statistical Geometry of Latent Recovery in Hidden Markov Models
comment: Trang Pham and Dung Le contributed equally to this work
summary: Hidden Markov models (HMMs) offer an important capability to interpret fitted latent states and transitions. When emission distributions nearly coincide, a small observation-density error does not ensure accurate estimation of the latent quantities needed for interpretation. This motivates us to characterize convergence rates for latent recovery that account for emission separation. Our main contribution lies in deriving deterministic inverse inequalities that convert Hellinger error between fitted and true densities into bounds on latent recovery errors. We develop these bounds for multivariate Gaussian HMMs with a common, known emission covariance matrix and combine them with a Hellinger estimation guarantee for the global maximum likelihood estimator to obtain latent recovery rates. Although the joint observation distribution is a Gaussian mixture with exponentially many path components, they share the same emission centers across time. Leveraging this shared structure, we show that the separation exponents are governed by the maximum number of simultaneously approaching centers rather than the number of path components. Under exact specification, the global bounds on state-sequence probability discrepancies and the 1-Wasserstein loss for latent location distributions exhibit sharp separation exponents that do not increase with the number of selected times. Moreover, sufficiently small observation-density error guarantees unique matching between fitted and true emission centers, which yields error bounds for individual emission centers and transition rows. Under over-specification, individual split-state transition rows are not necessarily identifiable, so we quantify aggregate latent recovery errors and show that state-sequence probability bounds incur larger separation exponents compared to exact specification. We conduct synthetic experiments to validate our theoretical results.

AI.tldr: The paper derives inverse inequalities that turn Hellinger estimation error into latent recovery error bounds for Gaussian HMMs with a common known emission covariance, showing that recovery is governed by how many emission centers approach each other at once rather than by the number of path components.
AI.motivation: When emission distributions nearly coincide, a small observation-density error does not guarantee accurate estimation of the latent states and transitions needed for interpretation, and existing guarantees do not account for emission separation.
AI.method: The authors prove deterministic inverse inequalities from Hellinger error to latent recovery error, apply them to multivariate Gaussian HMMs with a common known covariance, and combine them with a Hellinger guarantee for the global maximum likelihood estimator; they exploit the shared emission centers across time to bound separation exponents by the maximum number of simultaneously approaching centers.
AI.result: Under exact specification, bounds on state-sequence probability discrepancies and on the 1-Wasserstein loss for latent location distributions have sharp separation exponents that do not grow with the number of selected times; under over-specification, state-sequence bounds have larger exponents and individual split-state transition rows are not necessarily identifiable; synthetic experiments validate the theory.
AI.conclusion: Latent recovery in HMMs is characterised by emission separation with rates that depend on local center crowding rather than the combinatorial number of path components, clarifying when fitted HMMs can be interpreted reliably.

title: ALDER: A Single-Loop Augmented-Lagrangian Damped Extragradient Method for Nonconvex--Concave Minimax Problems with Nonlinear Coupled Constraints
summary: ALDER, a single-loop augmented-Lagrangian damped extragradient method, is proposed for smooth nonconvex--concave minimax problems with nonlinear coupled inequality constraints. Within an augmented-Lagrangian framework, ALDER combines prediction--correction steps for the primal variables with explicit projected-and-relaxed multiplier updates in a single loop. The penalty parameter is fixed throughout each run, eliminating inner-loop subproblem solves and iterative penalty updates. We establish uniform boundedness of the relaxed multiplier sequence and, under an extended Mangasarian--Fromovitz constraint qualification, boundedness of the projected output multiplier. Building on these bounds, we show that ALDER finds an $\varepsilon$-KKT point within $\mathcal{O}(\varepsilon^{-7/2})$ complete first-order oracle evaluations in the strongly concave setting and $\mathcal{O}(\varepsilon^{-4})$ in the concave setting. These bounds improve upon the best known complexity bounds for multi-loop algorithms for this problem class, achieved by FAL, by removing a $\log(1/\varepsilon)$ factor, while retaining a single-loop update structure.

AI.tldr: ALDER is a single-loop augmented-Lagrangian damped extragradient method for smooth nonconvex-concave minimax problems with nonlinear coupled inequality constraints that finds an epsilon-KKT point with improved complexity over the best multi-loop methods.
AI.motivation: Existing multi-loop algorithms for this problem class need inner-loop subproblem solves and penalty updates, and the best known complexity for them carries an extra log(1/epsilon) factor.
AI.method: ALDER fixes the penalty parameter throughout a run and combines prediction-correction steps on the primal variables with explicit projected and relaxed multiplier updates in a single loop, avoiding inner subproblems and iterative penalty updates.
AI.result: The method keeps the relaxed multiplier sequence uniformly bounded and, under an extended Mangasarian-Fromovitz constraint qualification, bounds the projected output multiplier; it finds an epsilon-KKT point in O(epsilon^(-7/2)) first-order oracle evaluations in the strongly concave setting and O(epsilon^(-4)) in the concave setting, improving on FAL by a log(1/epsilon) factor.
AI.conclusion: A single-loop augmented-Lagrangian scheme can match or beat multi-loop complexity for constrained nonconvex-concave minimax problems while keeping a simpler update structure.

title: Estimating Average Treatment Effects with Projected Instrumental Variables
summary: In this paper, we develop a projected instrumental variable framework that relaxes conventional assumptions for causal identification with instrumental variables. Building on the interpretation of conditional expectation as an orthogonal projection in a Hilbert space, the framework replaces the conditional expectation operator with a general projection operator. We provide an alternative inverse problem formulation based on the Riesz representation. Drawing on semiparametric efficiency theory, we further develop debiased and adaptive machine learning methods for estimation and inference. The proposed framework connects invalid instrumental variables to instrumented difference-in-differences. We also examine invalid projected instrumental variables and discuss their relationship to existing methods. Simulation studies and real data analysis demonstrate that the proposed methods perform favorably compared with existing approaches.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a projected instrumental variable framework that replaces conditional expectation with a general projection operator to identify average treatment effects under relaxed instrument assumptions, together with debiased machine learning estimators.
AI.motivation: Conventional instrumental variable identification requires strong assumptions, and existing methods do not cover invalid instruments in a unified way or connect them clearly to instrumented difference-in-differences.
AI.method: Viewing conditional expectation as an orthogonal projection in a Hilbert space, the authors generalise it to an arbitrary projection, give an inverse problem formulation based on the Riesz representation, and use semiparametric efficiency theory to build debiased and adaptive machine learning estimators and inference procedures.
AI.result: The framework links invalid instrumental variables to instrumented difference-in-differences and examines invalid projected instruments; simulations and a real data analysis show the proposed methods perform favourably against existing approaches.
AI.conclusion: Projection-based instrumental variables offer a flexible route to causal identification with relaxed assumptions, combined with efficient machine learning inference.

title: Tight Stochastic Sequential Covers for General VC Classes with Unknown i.i.d. Features
summary: We study hybrid online learning with stochastic features and adversarial labels when the feature distribution is unknown. Prior work gave stochastic sequential covers of log-size $O(d\log^2 T)$ for a general VC class and logarithmic bounds only under stronger star-type structure. We show that finite VC dimension alone is enough: every binary class of VC dimension $d$ admits a distribution-blind exact cover with log-size $O(d\log T+\log(1/\delta))$, matching the worst-case $\Omega(d\log(T/d))$ dependence on the horizon. The key ingredient is a new local cube weight that counts Boolean subcubes incident to each realizable trace. Unlike the equal splits used in earlier constructions, we split mass unevenly according to these cube weights; a coordinate-deletion inequality shows that VC dimension controls the total cost of these splits. This yields, to our knowledge, the first tight $O((d+1)\log T)$ expected worst-case log-loss regret for general VC partitions with unknown i.i.d. features, and an exact polynomial-time implementation for planar affine halfspaces. We also show that the binary phenomenon does not extend from VC dimension to pseudo-dimension: a fixed pseudo-dimension-one sigmoid class requires $\Omega(\log^2 T)$ bits for uniform sequential approximation at accuracy $1/T$.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that every binary class of VC dimension d admits a distribution-blind exact stochastic sequential cover of log-size O(d log T + log(1/delta)), which is tight, and yields the first tight O((d+1) log T) expected log-loss regret for general VC partitions with unknown i.i.d. features.
AI.motivation: Earlier stochastic sequential covers for general VC classes had log-size O(d log^2 T), and logarithmic bounds were known only under stronger star-type structure; it was unclear whether finite VC dimension alone suffices.
AI.method: The key ingredient is a new local cube weight that counts Boolean subcubes incident to each realisable trace, and the construction splits probability mass unevenly according to these weights rather than equally; a coordinate-deletion inequality shows that VC dimension controls the total cost of the splits.
AI.result: The cover has log-size O(d log T + log(1/delta)), matching the worst-case Omega(d log(T/d)) dependence on the horizon, and gives O((d+1) log T) expected worst-case log-loss regret with an exact polynomial-time implementation for planar affine halfspaces; a fixed pseudo-dimension-one sigmoid class needs Omega(log^2 T) bits for uniform sequential approximation at accuracy 1/T, so the binary phenomenon does not carry over to pseudo-dimension.
AI.conclusion: Finite VC dimension alone is enough for tight stochastic sequential covers and regret, but the analogous result fails for pseudo-dimension, so the VC characterisation does not extend to real-valued classes.

title: Optimal Learning in Fairness-Aware Contextual Bandits
summary: Mitigating unfair disparities in sequential decision-making is a growing concern in machine learning. We study contextual bandits under a global covariate-based Lipschitz fairness constraint, pioneered by \cite{dwork2012fairness}, requiring individuals with similar contexts to receive similar action distributions. We show that this constraint induces a randomisation region near the decision boundary and explicitly quantify the population level cost of fairness. We further establish a canonical representation of the optimal fair policy, which reduces the fair policy design to a lower-dimensional boundary optimisation problem. We develop a lazy fair greedy algorithm that exploits fairness-induced covariate diversity under continuous contexts, with policy updates computed via finite-dimensional linear programming. For general context distributions, including discrete and mixed contexts, we propose a lazy polyhedral upper confidence bound (UCB) algorithm, whose optimistic optimisation reduces to finitely many linear programs over confidence-set vertices. Both methods satisfy fairness at every round and achieve regret of order $O(\sqrt{T} + T^{(d-2)/(d-1)}{\indc\{d\geq 4\}})$ up to poly-logarithmic factors, where $d$ is the dimension of the contexts. A matching minimax lower bound for $\ell_1$-based fairness establishes optimality, and reveals an unavoidable nonparametric cost of learning the decision boundary, which dominates the parametric learning cost when $d \geq 4$. Experiments on synthetic and real data support our theoretical findings and demonstrate the practical effectiveness of our methods.

AI.tldr: The paper studies contextual bandits under a global Lipschitz fairness constraint and gives algorithms that satisfy fairness at every round with regret of order sqrt(T) plus a nonparametric term, together with a matching minimax lower bound for l1-based fairness.
AI.motivation: Fairness constraints requiring similar individuals to receive similar action distributions change the bandit problem near the decision boundary, and the population-level cost of fairness and the optimal fair policy were not well characterised.
AI.method: The authors show the constraint induces a randomisation region near the boundary, derive a canonical form of the optimal fair policy that reduces design to a lower-dimensional boundary optimisation, and propose a lazy fair greedy algorithm for continuous contexts and a lazy polyhedral UCB algorithm for discrete and mixed contexts, with policy updates computed by linear programs.
AI.result: Both methods are fair in every round and achieve regret of order O(sqrt(T) + T^((d-2)/(d-1))) for d at least 4 up to polylogarithmic factors, where d is the context dimension; a matching minimax lower bound for l1 fairness establishes optimality, and experiments on synthetic and real data support the theory.
AI.conclusion: Fairness imposes an unavoidable nonparametric cost of learning the decision boundary that dominates the parametric cost when the context dimension is at least 4.

title: HALO: Hierarchical Evidence Selection and Reinforcement Learning for Allocating Budgeted Label Optimization from Longitudinal Clinical Records
summary: Learning from extensive longitudinal clinical records--spanning repeated encounters, evolving conditions, and heterogeneous documentation--under a finite labeling budget requires solving two coupled problems: deciding what evidence to keep and deciding which patients deserve higher-fidelity labels. Prior work on active learning and multi-fidelity label acquisition mainly addresses the second problem, while treating the evidence presented to the acquisition policy as fixed. We present HALO, a Hierarchical Evidence Selection and Reinforcement Learning pipeline for Allocating Budgeted Label Optimization from Longitudinal Clinical Records. This framework jointly learns what to read and what label source to acquire under budget. HALO first selects informative evidence from longitudinal records and then uses a budget-aware policy to allocate free-, silver-, and gold-fidelity label sources. For frozen policies, our theory characterizes asymmetric acquired-label channels and gives a budget-constrained finite-sample gold-risk bound for a common downstream logistic model. In a heart-failure case study, HALO attained the highest MedAlign acquired-label F1 at six of eight target budgets. A downstream classifier trained on HALO-acquired labels attained the highest external MGB F1 at budgets 15-60 and remained within 0.01 of the best comparator at budgets 75-120.

AI.tldr: HALO is a hierarchical pipeline that jointly selects informative evidence from longitudinal clinical records and uses a budget-aware reinforcement learning policy to allocate free, silver and gold label sources under a finite labelling budget.
AI.motivation: Prior active learning and multi-fidelity label acquisition methods focus on which patients to label while treating the evidence shown to the acquisition policy as fixed.
AI.method: HALO first selects evidence from longitudinal records and then uses a budget-aware policy to allocate label sources of three fidelities, free, silver and gold; for frozen policies the theory characterises asymmetric acquired-label channels and gives a budget-constrained finite-sample gold-risk bound for a common downstream logistic model.
AI.result: In a heart-failure case study, HALO attains the highest MedAlign acquired-label F1 at six of eight target budgets, and a classifier trained on HALO-acquired labels attains the highest external MGB F1 at budgets 15 to 60 and stays within 0.01 of the best comparator at budgets 75 to 120.
AI.conclusion: Jointly learning what evidence to read and which label source to acquire improves label efficiency under budget in clinical settings, although gains are not uniform across all budgets.

title: Minimum-Norm Interpolation in Weighted Variation Spaces: Direct and Inverse Problems
summary: We study minimum-norm interpolation in weighted variation spaces generated by ReLU$^s$ ridge functions on the unit ball, where $s$ is a positive integer. For a target $f$ in the weighted variation space and a node set with sufficiently small fill distance $h$, every minimum-norm interpolant satisfies the direct bound $\|f-\mathscr{I}_{X_h}f\|_{L_2(\mathbb{B}^d)}\lesssim_{d,s}h^{(2s+1)/4}\|f\|_{\mathcal{V}_s}$. Under a boundary separation condition on the nodes, we construct a matching lower bound for the worst-case interpolation error. For the inverse problem, we introduce dual certificates and derive an estimate analogous to a Bernstein inequality. Under suitable upper bounds on dictionary size and spectral lower bounds for the atomic Gram matrices, sufficiently fast $L_2$ convergence of minimum-norm interpolants along geometrically decreasing fill distances implies that the target belongs to $\mathcal{V}_s$. As a byproduct, the best $L_2$ approximation error $E_n(f)_{L_2(\mathbb{B}^d)}$ for shallow ReLU$^s$ networks of width at most $n$ satisfies $E_n(f)_{L_2(\mathbb{B}^d)}\lesssim_{d,s}n^{-1/2-(2s+1)/(2d)}\|f\|_{\mathcal{V}_s}$, with the weighted atomic cost of an approximating network bounded by a constant multiple of $\|f\|_{\mathcal{V}_s}$, independently of $n$.

AI.tldr: The paper proves direct and inverse approximation results for minimum-norm interpolation in weighted variation spaces generated by ReLU^s ridge functions on the unit ball, including a matching lower bound and a Bernstein-type inequality.
AI.motivation: Approximation rates for shallow ReLU^s networks in weighted variation spaces, and characterisations of which targets belong to these spaces from interpolation behaviour, needed sharper analysis.
AI.method: For nodes with small fill distance h, the authors bound the L2 error of minimum-norm interpolants directly, prove a matching worst-case lower bound under a boundary separation condition on the nodes, and introduce dual certificates to obtain a Bernstein-type estimate for the inverse problem.
AI.result: The direct bound is O(h^((2s+1)/4)) times the variation norm of the target; sufficiently fast L2 convergence of interpolants along geometrically decreasing fill distances implies membership in the variation space under dictionary-size and Gram-matrix conditions; as a byproduct, shallow ReLU^s networks of width n achieve best L2 error O(n^(-1/2-(2s+1)/(2d))) times the variation norm.
AI.conclusion: Minimum-norm interpolation achieves rates that are both sharp and characterising for weighted variation spaces, giving a two-sided description of approximation by shallow ReLU^s networks.

title: Selective inference for pruned interaction trees with known unequal variances in randomized trials
summary: Interaction trees reuse outcomes to discover treatment-effect heterogeneity, complicating inference after growth and pruning. We develop selective inference for generalized least-squares (GLS) interaction trees with a common covariate basis and known unequal variances. Under a conditional Gaussian model with positive diagonal covariance, weighted orthogonality reduces survival under additive fixed-penalty pruning to one quadratic inequality supplementing the growth event. This yields exact finite-sample conditional tests and confidence intervals, with retained-path and complete-tree inference agreeing on compatible sections. Under causal identification and a correct reference prognosis, the pruning-invariant GLS target is a signed finite-design weighted contrast of conditional average treatment effects. Simulations at $n=100,200,400,800$ and maximum depths one to three search all adjacent-observation midpoints, support calibration and demonstrate over-rejection when pruning survival is omitted. Compared with a 50:50 honest procedure, full-data learning improves reference-split recovery in some small-sample settings. Root-level median intervals can be shorter, while deep-node intervals and upper tails can be much wider; these comparisons concern each procedure's selected targets. Estimating a common scale with the variance ratio fixed produces modest changes in Selective coverage in the settings examined, without extending the exact guarantee. An exploratory ACTG 175 analysis provides a working-model illustration with estimated arm variances.

AI.tldr: The paper develops exact finite-sample selective inference for pruned generalised least-squares interaction trees with known unequal variances, so that conditional tests and confidence intervals account for both growth and pruning.
AI.motivation: Interaction trees reuse outcomes to find treatment effect heterogeneity, which invalidates naive inference after growing and pruning, and the abstract compares against a 50:50 honest procedure that splits the data.
AI.method: Under a conditional Gaussian model with positive diagonal covariance, weighted orthogonality reduces survival under additive fixed-penalty pruning to one quadratic inequality added to the growth event, giving exact conditional tests and intervals; the target is a signed weighted contrast of conditional average treatment effects under causal identification.
AI.result: Retained-path and complete-tree inference agree on compatible sections; simulations at n = 100, 200, 400 and 800 with depth one to three show calibration and over-rejection when pruning survival is omitted; full-data learning improves reference-split recovery in some small samples, root-level intervals can be shorter, deep-node intervals can be much wider, and an exploratory ACTG 175 analysis is given.
AI.conclusion: Accounting for pruning survival is necessary for valid inference in interaction trees, and full-data learning with exact selective inference can trade interval width across tree levels relative to honest splitting.

title: Accelerating posterior sampling in Bayesian inverse problems with diffusion models: an online-offline perspective
summary: Bayesian inverse problems require both informative prior models and computationally feasible posterior inference. Score-based diffusion models provide expressive learned priors, but their use for inversion introduces a conditioning problem: the score of a noised posterior is generally unavailable from a prior score alone. This selective survey reviews the principal approaches to that problem, including likelihood guidance, spectral and projection methods, sequential Monte Carlo corrections, and amortized conditional training. We organize methods by how they split cost between offline preparation and online inference, and compare their assumptions, advantages and limitations, with emphasis on computational speedups. Some ongoing directions and open questions are gathered at the end.

AI.tldr: This selective survey reviews methods for posterior sampling in Bayesian inverse problems with score-based diffusion priors, organised by how they split computation between offline preparation and online inference.
AI.motivation: The score of a noised posterior is generally unavailable from a prior score alone, so using diffusion models as priors for inversion requires approaches that handle this conditioning problem efficiently.
AI.method: The survey covers likelihood guidance, spectral and projection methods, sequential Monte Carlo corrections and amortised conditional training, comparing their assumptions, advantages and limitations with emphasis on computational speedups.
AI.result: The survey gives no new numerical results; it classifies the approaches by offline and online cost and summarises their trade-offs.
AI.conclusion: Offline-online cost allocation is a useful lens for comparing diffusion-based posterior samplers, and the authors list ongoing directions and open questions.

title: Variational learning of energy-stable macroscopic flow equations from microscopic laws
summary: We present a generalized variational approach for constructing energy-stable macroscopic partial differential equations (PDEs) directly from microscopic physical laws. Rather than fitting the PDE evolution for prescribed variables from macroscopic trajectories, we construct an extendable variational structure by adjoining auxiliary variables to seek autonomous reduced dynamics in an enlarged state space. By defining these variables as micro--macro encoders with explicit microscopic counterparts, we cast the learning problem as the sample-wise joint identification of the reduced state representation and the variational ingredients from time-discrete data, enabling systematic law-level transfer across scales. The resulting PDEs preserve frame indifference, physical constraints, and energy stability by construction, and admit a fluctuation--dissipation-consistent stochastic extension. Numerical results for the non-Newtonian hydrodynamics of polymeric fluids show that the learned models capture the viscoelastic responses induced by nonlinear and heterogeneous molecular interactions beyond empirical closures.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a variational method that builds energy-stable macroscopic PDEs directly from microscopic laws by adjoining auxiliary micro-macro encoder variables to find autonomous reduced dynamics, applied to the non-Newtonian hydrodynamics of polymeric fluids.
AI.motivation: Macroscopic PDEs are usually fitted to macroscopic trajectories, which gives no guarantee of physical structure or transfer across scales and misses effects of molecular interactions beyond empirical closures.
AI.method: The authors enlarge the state space with auxiliary variables defined as micro-macro encoders with explicit microscopic counterparts, then learn the reduced state representation and variational ingredients jointly from time-discrete data in a sample-wise identification.
AI.result: The learned PDEs preserve frame indifference, physical constraints and energy stability by construction and admit a fluctuation-dissipation-consistent stochastic extension; numerical results for polymeric fluids capture viscoelastic responses arising from nonlinear and heterogeneous molecular interactions beyond empirical closures.
AI.conclusion: Variational structure built into the reduced dynamics allows law-level transfer from microscopic to macroscopic models with guaranteed physical properties.

title: Transport for Conditional Sampling: Foundations and Applications
summary: Conditional sampling is central to Bayesian inference, generative modeling, and causal inference: given a joint law for random variables $X$ and $Y$ and an observation $Y=y$, one seeks to sample from the conditional law of $X\mid Y=y$. Even when the joint distribution is accurately represented, this task can be computationally difficult as it may require evaluating intractable normalizing constants or solving a new inference problem for each observation. Measure transport provides an approach to this problem by identifying a map with triangular structure that directly pushes forward a reference to the conditional of a joint distribution for any observation. This article reviews the theoretical, methodological, and algorithmic foundations of triangular transports, with the Knothe-Rosenblatt rearrangement as a canonical construction. We discuss methods for estimating triangular maps from finite samples, as well as their use in simulation-based inference and causal inference. While our primary aim is to review existing formulations, we also present new ideas and open questions for conditional sampling using transport.

AI.tldr: This review surveys the theory, methods and algorithms of triangular measure transport, centred on the Knothe-Rosenblatt rearrangement, for sampling from conditional distributions, with applications to simulation-based and causal inference.
AI.motivation: Conditional sampling is central to Bayesian inference, generative modelling and causal inference, but it can require intractable normalising constants or a new inference problem for each observation.
AI.method: The article reviews triangular transport maps that push a reference distribution forward to the conditional law for any observation, discusses estimating such maps from finite samples, and covers their use in simulation-based and causal inference.
AI.result: The article is a review, but it also presents new ideas and open questions for conditional sampling using transport.
AI.conclusion: Triangular transport provides a unified framework for conditional sampling, and its estimation and applications remain active open problems.

title: Correctness and Predictive Uncertainty in Bayesian TSK Fuzzy Regression: A Reproducible Evaluation on Tabular and Building-Meter Data
comment: 21 pages, 3 figures. Supplementary material is included as an ancillary PDF
summary: Uncertainty estimates from fuzzy regression are informative only when the implementation is correct and the comparison protocol makes the sources of variation visible. We revisit a first-order Takagi--Sugeno--Kang (TSK) regression implementation and rebuild its dense, conjugate Bayesian, BIC-based, and rule-level spike-and-slab estimators using corrected code. The corrected pipeline freezes the Gaussian membership partition at training time, uses a scaled conjugate prior, evaluates firing strengths in the log domain, and reports direct posterior-predictive quantiles for Bayesian methods. Across 30 outer 80/20 splits on three targets from two UCI regression datasets, corrected TSK-LS obtains $R^2=0.957$, $0.923$, and $0.786$ on Energy-Heating, Energy-Cooling, and Concrete, respectively; rule-level Gibbs sampling with Bayesian model averaging obtains $0.957$, $0.922$, and $0.784$. We then evaluate the same workflow on a bounded chronological sample of the Building Data Genome 2 meter data that covers 158 buildings across 17 sites. In a common-unit evaluation, every method is scored on the same 47,400 test rows and every trained model uses 94,800 train--validation rows. Persistence has RMSE $27.710$, compared with $29.083$ for both TSK-LS and Bayesian TSK; the pre-specified building-level mean RMSE difference between Bayesian TSK and persistence is $+0.0447$ with a 95% site-cluster bootstrap interval of $[-1.5536,1.5665]$. The Bayesian TSK 90% intervals have PICP $0.980$ and MPIW $116.469$. Taken together, the evidence supports a narrower conclusion: spike-and-slab model averaging is a reproducible implementation option, but it does not provide a demonstrated accuracy or calibration advantage across the tested tabular and building-meter settings.

AI.tldr: A reproducibility study of Bayesian TSK fuzzy regression finds that corrected implementations are sound, but spike-and-slab model averaging gives no demonstrated accuracy or calibration advantage on tabular and building-meter data.
AI.motivation: Uncertainty estimates from fuzzy regression are only informative when the implementation is correct and the comparison protocol exposes sources of variation, so the authors revisit a first-order TSK implementation.
AI.method: The authors rebuild dense, conjugate Bayesian, BIC-based and rule-level spike-and-slab estimators with corrected code that freezes the Gaussian membership partition at training time, uses a scaled conjugate prior, evaluates firing strengths in the log domain and reports posterior predictive quantiles, and evaluate over 30 outer 80/20 splits on UCI datasets and a chronological sample of Building Data Genome 2 meter data.
AI.result: On UCI targets, corrected TSK-LS obtains R^2 of 0.957, 0.923 and 0.786 on Energy-Heating, Energy-Cooling and Concrete, and rule-level Gibbs sampling with model averaging obtains 0.957, 0.922 and 0.784; on the building data across 158 buildings, persistence has RMSE 27.710 versus 29.083 for TSK-LS and Bayesian TSK, and the Bayesian TSK 90% intervals have PICP 0.980 and MPIW 116.469.
AI.conclusion: Spike-and-slab model averaging is a reproducible implementation option but does not show a demonstrated accuracy or calibration advantage across the tested settings.

title: Abstention Spends Its Budget on Local Label Variance More Than on Novelty: Auditing Conformal Calibration and Selective Prediction under Molecular Scaffold Shift
summary: Selective prediction with split conformal calibration promises a post-hoc fix for molecular property prediction: abstain on the least reliable compounds, ideally out-of-distribution chemistry, and the retained set becomes trustworthy without retraining. We audit this recipe for a gradient-boosted fingerprint model on lipophilicity (regression) and BBBP (classification) under a Bemis-Murcko scaffold split, holding the fitted model and evaluation molecules fixed while varying only the calibration fold (18 replicates). (i) On lipophilicity, coverage depends on calibration provenance: calibrating on held-out training-scaffold molecules falls below nominal (PICP 0.841 at a 0.90 target), while novel-scaffold calibration recovers it (0.904); on BBBP, coverage stays above nominal in every regime. (ii) For split conformalized quantile regression (CQR) the conformal correction is a constant, so conformalization does not change what is abstained on. (iii) The abstention score (CQR width; effectively ensemble variance on BBBP) tracks local label variance more than chemical novelty: controlling for local label variance largely explains away the novelty association (partial Spearman 0.067 and 0.047). (iv) At a fixed assay budget, gating on interval width or ensemble variance never improves hit precision over ranking by point prediction, at the pre-specified operating point or across 20 exploratory settings; a plain novelty gate shows small, uncorrected gains at the smallest budgets. (v) In an exploratory analysis, exact conformal selection exceeds its false discovery rate target under training-scaffold calibration (0.303 at q=0.2) and is consistent with it under novel-scaffold calibration, contributing a data-driven batch size rather than a better ranking. Conformalization earns its keep through guarantees whose validity hinges on calibration provenance, not by choosing what to abstain on.

AI.tldr: An audit of split conformal selective prediction for molecular property prediction finds that abstention tracks local label variance more than chemical novelty, that calibration provenance determines coverage, and that interval-based gating does not improve hit precision over point-prediction ranking.
AI.motivation: Conformal selective prediction is often promoted as a post-hoc way to abstain on unreliable out-of-distribution molecules, and this recipe has not been checked under scaffold shift.
AI.method: Holding a gradient-boosted fingerprint model and evaluation molecules fixed under a Bemis-Murcko scaffold split, the authors vary only the calibration fold over 18 replicates on lipophilicity and BBBP, and analyse CQR widths, ensemble variance, partial Spearman correlations and fixed-budget hit precision.
AI.result: On lipophilicity, PICP is 0.841 at a 0.90 target with training-scaffold calibration and 0.904 with novel-scaffold calibration, while BBBP coverage stays above nominal; partial Spearman correlations after controlling for local label variance are 0.067 and 0.047; gating on interval width or ensemble variance never improves hit precision over point-prediction ranking across the settings examined; exact conformal selection exceeds its false discovery rate target under training-scaffold calibration at 0.303 for q = 0.2.
AI.conclusion: Conformalisation is valuable for its guarantees, whose validity depends on calibration provenance, but it does not improve which compounds are abstained on.

title: Near-Optimal $\sqrt{K}$-Regret for Online Learning in Uninformed Markov Games
summary: We study online learning in two-player uninformed Markov games, where the opponent may follow an arbitrary, unknown policy in each episode and the learner does not observe the opponent's actions. [TWYS21] showed that achieving sublinear external regret requires an exponential dependence on the episode length $H$. Motivated by this limitation, they studied the weaker notion of Nash-value regret and obtained an $\widetilde{O}(K^{2/3})$ regret bound, where $K$ is the number of episodes. More recently, [LLZR26] introduced a stronger notion called empirical Nash-value regret and achieved an $\widetilde{O}(\sqrt{K})$ bound when the opponent's non-stationarity is moderate, including the case where the opponent follows a fixed policy. However, whether the $\sqrt{K}$ rate is achievable in the worst case remained open. In this paper, we resolve this open question by developing an algorithm that achieves $\widetilde{O}(H^{3/2}S\sqrt{AK})$ empirical Nash-value regret against arbitrary opponent policies, where $S$ is the number of states and $A$ is the number of learner's actions. Specifically, our algorithm combines global and local planning by maintaining a collection of candidate predictions of future losses, each associated with a policy. Global planning learns which candidates to favor across episodes, while local planning combines their policies differently at each state to make decisions. A key ingredient is to coordinate these two components to control the discrepancy between local loss estimates and the total loss of the executed policy, using only the learner's observed trajectories.

AI.tldr: The paper resolves an open question by giving an algorithm with O~(H^(3/2) S sqrt(AK)) empirical Nash-value regret against arbitrary opponent policies in uninformed Markov games, achieving the sqrt(K) rate in the worst case.
AI.motivation: Prior work showed sublinear external regret needs exponential dependence on episode length, and the sqrt(K) rate for empirical Nash-value regret was known only when the opponent's non-stationarity is moderate, leaving the worst case open.
AI.method: The algorithm combines global planning, which learns which candidate loss predictions to favour across episodes, with local planning, which mixes their associated policies differently at each state, and coordinates the two to control the discrepancy between local loss estimates and the executed policy's total loss using only observed trajectories.
AI.result: The regret bound is O~(H^(3/2) S sqrt(AK)), where H is episode length, S the number of states, A the number of learner actions and K the number of episodes, which matches the sqrt(K) rate in the worst case.
AI.conclusion: The sqrt(K) rate is achievable against arbitrary opponents in uninformed Markov games, closing the gap left by earlier Nash-value regret results.

title: How Does Chain-of-Thought Supervision Teach Models to Reason? A Theoretical Analysis
summary: Training with chain-of-thought (CoT) supervision is an effective approach for teaching models multi-step reasoning procedures. At inference time, however, models may need to continue reasoning beyond the finite teacher CoT sequences observed during training, and longer reasoning can instead degrade performance, a phenomenon known as overthinking. How the amount and structure of training-time CoT give rise to such failures remains theoretically poorly understood. To study this problem, we introduce an in-context weight prediction model trained on finite gradient descent trajectories for linear regression. Using high-dimensional asymptotic analysis, we show that the success and failure modes of long-horizon reasoning undergo phase transitions depending on the context length and the total amount of training CoT. We further distinguish two mechanisms of overthinking, error accumulation and error amplification, and show that with short training contexts, increasing the training CoT budget can worsen long-horizon error before eventually stabilizing reasoning. Experiments with fully trained linear and multi-head softmax attention further show that these qualitative behaviors persist. Our results provide a theoretical account linking properties of training-time CoT to inference-time failures and offer guidance for designing teacher CoT that supports stable reasoning.

AI.tldr: The paper analyses theoretically how training-time chain-of-thought supervision leads to overthinking at inference, showing phase transitions in long-horizon reasoning depending on context length and training CoT budget, and identifying error accumulation and error amplification as two mechanisms.
AI.motivation: Models may need to reason beyond the finite teacher CoT seen in training, and longer reasoning can degrade performance, but how the amount and structure of training CoT produce this failure was poorly understood.
AI.method: The authors introduce an in-context weight prediction model trained on finite gradient descent trajectories for linear regression and use high-dimensional asymptotic analysis; they also run experiments with fully trained linear and multi-head softmax attention models.
AI.result: Success and failure modes of long-horizon reasoning undergo phase transitions in context length and total training CoT; with short training contexts, increasing the training CoT budget can worsen long-horizon error before it stabilises; the qualitative behaviours persist in the attention experiments.
AI.conclusion: Properties of training CoT, such as its length and structure, link directly to inference-time overthinking, and the analysis offers guidance for designing teacher CoT that supports stable reasoning.

title: Federated Estimation of Loading Spaces in Tensor Factor Models under Differential Privacy
summary: Tensor factor models provide low-dimensional representations of tensor-valued observations while preserving their multiway structure. When these observations are held by different clients, privacy constraints may prevent them from being pooled for centralized analysis. We study estimation of common loading spaces in Tucker tensor factor models under federated differential privacy, allowing heterogeneous sample sizes, privacy budgets, and factor strengths. The proposed method combines private stability testing, Huber aggregation, and Gaussian perturbation at each client with weighted aggregation at the server. We establish non-asymptotic upper bounds governed by a scaled harmonic mean of the squared local error rates, and prove minimax optimality up to logarithmic factors under strong factors, fixed factor ranks, and fixed noise variance. We further develop a private calibration procedure that selects the local tuning parameters and aggregation weights without knowledge of the noise level or client-specific factor strengths. The resulting adaptive estimator preserves the privacy guarantee and attains the error rate obtained with oracle tuning. We illustrate the finite-sample performance of the proposed estimators through simulation experiments and an application to a Meditation Traits EEG dataset.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a federated differentially private method for estimating common loading spaces in Tucker tensor factor models, with a private calibration procedure that attains oracle-level error without knowing the noise level or client factor strengths.
AI.motivation: Tensor observations held by different clients often cannot be pooled because of privacy constraints, and federated estimation of shared loading spaces under heterogeneous sample sizes, privacy budgets and factor strengths was not well developed.
AI.method: Each client combines private stability testing, Huber aggregation and Gaussian perturbation, and the server performs weighted aggregation; a private calibration step selects local tuning parameters and aggregation weights.
AI.result: The non-asymptotic error bound is governed by a scaled harmonic mean of squared local error rates, the rate is minimax optimal up to logarithmic factors under strong factors, fixed ranks and fixed noise variance, and the adaptive estimator preserves privacy and attains the oracle-tuned rate; simulations and an application to a Meditation Traits EEG dataset illustrate finite-sample performance.
AI.conclusion: Adaptive federated estimation under differential privacy can reach the optimal rate without oracle knowledge of noise or client-specific strengths.

title: Watch Your Step: Adam's Margin Maximization Bias Depends on the Learning Rate Schedule
summary: We study the implicit bias of Adam and its similarity to sign gradient descent on homogeneous models in binary classification tasks. Perhaps surprisingly, we uncover that these depend on the learning rate schedule. While previous works studied strongly decaying learning rate schedules $\eta(t)=\mathrm o \left(t^{1/L-1}\right)$, where $L$ is the homogeneity degree, and showed $\ell_\infty$-margin-maximization biases, we focus on the more common complementary regime, including constant and weakly decaying schedules.
