For a polynomial schedule $t^{\alpha}$ and homogeneity degree $L$, we show that when $\alpha > \frac 1L - \frac12$, Adam has no trajectory-independent margin-maximization bias for deep linear networks (in the KKT sense): first, there is no non-trivial, locally Lipschitz, convex implicit regularizer in this setting, including any squared norm. Second, on width-$1$ networks, the result holds without requiring convexity, implying that any implicit regularizer for wide networks must be trivial when restricted to a width-$1$ network. Nevertheless, we positively characterize the implicit bias in this regime as maximizing a trajectory-dependent weighted-$\ell_2$ margin for any $L$-homogeneous model. The fundamental mechanism behind our results is convergence of Adam's preconditioner to a trajectory-dependent vector, which also allows showing that the limiting parameter direction depends on initialization. In the intermediate regime $\frac 1L - 1 \leq \alpha \leq \frac1L - \frac12$ we prove an $\ell_\infty$ bias, conditional on gradient directional convergence to a full-support vector. Of independent interest, we establish a loss decay rate for full batch Adam on general homogeneous models, whose leading order depends only on the second-moment parameter.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that for Adam with polynomial learning rate schedules t^alpha on homogeneous models, the implicit bias depends on the schedule: for alpha above 1/L - 1/2 there is no trajectory-independent margin-maximisation bias, and the bias is instead a trajectory-dependent weighted l2 margin.
AI.motivation: Earlier work on the implicit bias of Adam and sign gradient descent studied strongly decaying learning rate schedules, while constant and weakly decaying schedules, which are more common in practice, were not understood.
AI.method: The authors show that Adam's preconditioner converges to a trajectory-dependent vector, prove that no non-trivial locally Lipschitz convex implicit regulariser exists for deep linear networks in this regime, and for width-one networks establish the result without convexity; they also prove a loss decay rate for full-batch Adam on general homogeneous models.
AI.result: For alpha above 1/L - 1/2 the implicit bias is a trajectory-dependent weighted l2 margin; in the intermediate regime an l-infinity bias holds conditional on gradient directional convergence to a full-support vector; the limiting direction depends on initialisation, and the loss decay rate depends only on the second-moment parameter.
AI.conclusion: The learning rate schedule determines the implicit bias of Adam, so conclusions drawn from strongly decaying schedules do not transfer to the schedules used in practice.

title: Large Geometry Models Are Priors For Fast Physics Pretraining
summary: Language and vision models became data-efficient by pretraining on plentiful unlabelled data; physical field models have such data, over ten million 3D shapes, but geometry pretraining designs its targets rather than deriving them from the physics. Euler-Lagrange geometry pretraining derives them: for attached flow, a shape enters the flow's Euler-Lagrange equation only through coefficients that distance and normal line (the normal up to sign) fix to first order. Their reconstruction error therefore bounds what a representation loses about any field, and fine-tuning on costly simulations need only assemble the global field. We realise it in AREALS, a masked surface autoencoder whose areal tokens carry position, normal and area, pretrained self-supervised and sign-free on 61,822 raw meshes. Because the operating condition enters only through the far field, sensors can supply it: AREALS completes a hidden field in one forward pass without condition labels. It matches the accuracy of the same architecture trained from scratch with half the simulations on DrivAerML and DrivAerNet++ and about a quarter on WindsorML. On DoubleDelta wings, 20 sensors give $3.9\times$ and $4.0\times$ lower field and force error than GABI, a Bayesian inversion method with a learned prior, and beyond the training angles pretraining halves the error.

AI.tldr: AREALS is a masked surface autoencoder pretrained without labels on raw meshes using areal tokens with position, normal and area, derived from Euler-Lagrange geometry pretraining, and it reduces the simulations needed for physics field prediction.
AI.motivation: Geometry pretraining designs its targets rather than deriving them from the physics, whereas the Euler-Lagrange equation for attached flow depends on a shape only through coefficients fixed by distance and normal line to first order.
AI.method: The authors pretrain a sign-free masked surface autoencoder on 61,822 raw meshes, with areal tokens carrying position, normal and area; because operating conditions enter only through the far field, sensors can supply the condition, so the model completes a hidden field in one forward pass without condition labels.
AI.result: AREALS matches the accuracy of the same architecture trained from scratch with about half the simulations on DrivAerML and DrivAerNet++ and about a quarter on WindsorML; on DoubleDelta wings, 20 sensors give 3.9 times and 4.0 times lower field and force error than GABI, a Bayesian inversion method with a learned prior, and pretraining halves the error beyond the training angles.
AI.conclusion: Physically derived self-supervised targets can make physical field models data-efficient, reducing the need for costly simulations.

title: Optimal spectral shrinkage via Krylov approximation
summary: Spectral shrinkage encompasses a broad family of estimators for high-dimensional linear regression that regularize estimation and prediction by applying spectral filters to the sample covariance matrix. Despite its widespread use, achieving oracle-optimal prediction risk under general covariance structures remains challenging, as the oracle filter requires unknown population quantities and has a closed form only for specific covariance models such as isotropic and spiked models. We propose \textit{risk-targeted Krylov fitting} (RTK), a data-driven spectral estimator that adapts to the unknown covariance structure and attains the oracle risk asymptotically. Like partial least squares, RTK operates in an $m$-dimensional Krylov space, but it targets the oracle risk directly by minimizing the leave-one-out risk, which we compute exactly without refitting the model $n$ times. Under general distributions and covariance structures, RTK attains the optimal prediction risk in the Krylov space up to $O(1/n)$. Furthermore, its risk approaches that of the optimal analytic filter with $m$ of order $\log n$. In simulations over a wide range of covariance structures, RTK and a truncated variant were robust to the choice of $m$ and consistently among the spectral estimators closest to the oracle. In applications to single-cell sequencing data and large-scale neural recordings, the proposed methods achieved higher prediction accuracy than competing estimators on most tasks.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes risk-targeted Krylov fitting (RTK), a data-driven spectral shrinkage estimator that minimises exact leave-one-out risk within a Krylov subspace and attains the oracle prediction risk asymptotically.
AI.motivation: Spectral shrinkage with oracle-optimal risk requires population quantities and has closed forms only for special covariance models such as isotropic and spiked ones, so general covariance structures remained challenging.
AI.method: RTK operates in an m-dimensional Krylov space like partial least squares but targets the oracle risk by minimising a leave-one-out risk computed exactly without refitting n times.
AI.result: Under general distributions and covariance structures RTK attains the optimal prediction risk in the Krylov space up to O(1/n), and its risk approaches the optimal analytic filter with m of order log n; in simulations it is robust to the choice of m and among the closest to the oracle, and it gives higher prediction accuracy than competing estimators on most single-cell sequencing and large-scale neural recording tasks.
AI.conclusion: A risk-targeted Krylov estimator can adapt to unknown covariance structure and approach oracle prediction performance with modest subspace dimension.

title: Beyond least-favorable distribution pairs: asymptotically instance-optimal robust hypothesis testing
summary: When testing a composite null $\mathcal{P}$ against a composite alternative $\mathcal{Q}$, it has been known since Huber and Strassen (1973) that if a least favorable distribution (LFD) pair exists, then a version of its likelihood ratio yields a minimax optimal test, and Huber (1965) derived a similar result in the sequential setting for a specific robust testing problem that is the focus of the current paper; the same likelihood ratio is log-optimal in the worst case; its expected logarithm under the alternative equals $\inf_{P \in \mathcal{P},S \in \mathcal{Q}} KL(S\|P)$, whose inverse also determines the stopping time of the test under the alternative. These results focus on optimizing worst-case performance, but the resulting methods have lower power if the data come from simpler alternatives. This paper studies an arguably more practical goal of achieving asymptotic \emph{instance optimality} for ``power-one'' sequential tests, which remarkably may even be possible when $\mathcal{Q} = \mathcal{P}^c$. This means that when the data are drawn from any $S \in \mathcal{P}^c$, the test has power one, and its stopping time is determined by the larger information number $\inf_{P \in \mathcal{P}} KL(S\|P)$, which governs the performance of an oracle that knows $S$. To demonstrate this point, our paper focuses on the case of testing a TV ball around a discrete distribution with $d$ components, and designs a computationally and memory efficient algorithm that is also asymptotically instance-optimal. Specifically, we consider two different asymptotic settings: one is the "Wald setting", where the type-1 error level $\alpha$ approaches zero for a fixed alternative $S$ and the second is the "Farrell setting", where $\alpha$ is fixed and $\inf_{P \in \mathcal{P}} KL(S\|P)$ approaches $0$. Our sequential test is simultaneously optimal in both regimes.

AI.tldr: The paper constructs an asymptotically instance-optimal sequential power-one test for a total variation ball around a discrete distribution, showing that instance optimality can hold even when the alternative is the complement of the null.
AI.motivation: Least-favourable-distribution likelihood ratio tests are minimax optimal but can have low power when data come from simpler alternatives, and the paper seeks a test that adapts to each alternative.
AI.method: The authors test a TV ball around a discrete distribution with d components and design an efficient sequential algorithm, analysing it in two regimes: the Wald setting where the type-1 error level goes to zero for a fixed alternative, and the Farrell setting where the information number goes to zero.
AI.result: The test is asymptotically instance-optimal, with stopping time governed by the information number inf over P in the null of KL(S||P), and is simultaneously optimal in both regimes; when the alternative is the complement of the null, data from any alternative give power one.
AI.conclusion: Instance-optimal sequential testing is achievable without least-favourable pairs, and the resulting stopping behaviour matches an oracle that knows the alternative.

title: Invertible Graph Aggregation Can Increase ReLU Readout Width
comment: 12 pages, 4 figures. Code and reproducibility materials: this https URL
summary: An invertible graph aggregation preserves the complete feature table, but can increase the size of a classifier that reads one node at a time. For every even $N\ge4$, we construct a labeled tree with $2N$ vertices and maximum degree three. A shared one-hidden-layer rectified linear unit (ReLU) classifier needs one hidden unit on the raw scalar features and exactly $N$ units after one lazy neighborhood mean. All aggregate values are distinct, and the mixing matrix has condition number at most 8. We determine the complete error curve for heads with a free affine term. The width separation persists under scalar perturbations. Under a specified bounded uniform-noise model with one nuisance coordinate, every one-unit aggregate head has expected error at least $1/12$, while a fixed $N$-unit head has zero error. Controlled fits compare trained heads with these explicit feasible scores. On Roman-empire and Tolokers, aggregation improves fitted prediction, and retaining raw features helps at the largest tested parameter budget. Training-only diagnostics include conditional output-layer optimality bounds for eight fixed runs.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that an invertible graph aggregation can increase the width needed by a one-node-at-a-time ReLU classifier, constructing trees where a shared one-hidden-layer classifier needs N units after one neighbourhood mean but only one unit on raw features.
AI.motivation: Invertible aggregation preserves the full feature table, yet it was unclear whether the classifier size needed to read node representations could be increased by it.
AI.method: For every even N at least 4, the authors build a labelled tree with 2N vertices and maximum degree three, analyse a shared one-hidden-layer ReLU classifier on raw scalar features and after one lazy neighbourhood mean, bound the condition number of the mixing matrix by 8, and derive the error curve for heads with a free affine term.
AI.result: The width separation persists under scalar perturbations, and under a bounded uniform-noise model every one-unit aggregate head has expected error at least 1/12 while a fixed N-unit head has zero error; on Roman-empire and Tolokers, aggregation improves fitted prediction and retaining raw features helps at the largest tested parameter budget.
AI.conclusion: Aggregation that is invertible in principle can make simple classifiers need more capacity, so retaining raw features can matter for parameter-limited heads.

title: Near-Quadratic Error-Free Graph Matching above Otter's Threshold via Approximate Local Tree Correlation Testing
summary: This paper presents a near-quadratic-time algorithm that correctly matches almost all nodes of two correlated Erdős-Rényi graphs without any incorrect matches. Each graph has average degree $\lambda$ and its edges are subsampled from a common parent Erdős-Rényi graph with $n$ nodes, with subsampling probability $s$. The nodes of one graph are then relabeled by an unknown permutation. The algorithm is built on a test for correlated versus independent Galton-Watson trees with approximated likelihood ratios. For every constant $s>\sqrt{C_{\mathrm{Otter}}}$, where $C_{\mathrm{Otter}}\approx0.338$ is Otter's tree-counting constant, and every $\lambda=\omega(1)$ with $\lambda=(\log n)^{O(1)}$, the algorithm outputs a partial matching of size $n-o(n)$ that contains no incorrect matches with high probability. If, in addition, $\lambda s\ge(1+\epsilon)\log n$ for a constant $\epsilon>0$, a seeded completion step recovers the permutation exactly. In both cases, the time complexity of the algorithm is $n^{2+o(1)}$ with high probability, whereas previous polynomial-time algorithms with the same guarantees either have a time-complexity bound whose exponent goes to $\infty$ as $s$ approaches $\sqrt{C_{\mathrm{Otter}}}$ from above, or apply only when $s$ is close to $1$.

AI.tldr: The paper gives a near-quadratic-time algorithm that matches almost all nodes of two correlated Erdos-Renyi graphs with no incorrect matches above Otter's threshold, and exactly recovers the permutation with a seeded completion step under an extra condition.
AI.motivation: Earlier polynomial-time algorithms for error-free matching in this regime either had running-time exponents that diverge as the subsampling probability approaches the Otter threshold, or applied only when the subsampling probability is close to one.
AI.method: The algorithm uses a test distinguishing correlated from independent Galton-Watson trees with approximated likelihood ratios to build a partial matching, followed by a seeded completion step when lambda s is at least (1 + epsilon) log n.
AI.result: For every constant s greater than the square root of Otter's constant, about 0.338, and average degree lambda that is omega(1) and polylogarithmic in n, the algorithm outputs a partial matching of size n - o(n) with no incorrect matches with high probability, and with lambda s at least (1 + epsilon) log n it recovers the permutation exactly, in n^(2+o(1)) time.
AI.conclusion: Error-free graph matching is achievable in near-quadratic time throughout the regime above Otter's threshold, improving on prior polynomial-time guarantees.

title: Efficient Proper Agnostic Learning of Halfspaces
summary: We give a proper membership-query algorithm for agnostically learning halfspaces under the uniform distribution on $\{\pm1\}^n$. Given query access to an arbitrary function $f:\{\pm1\}^n \to \{\pm1\}$, our algorithm runs in time $\mathrm{poly}(n)+2^{\mathrm{poly}(1/\varepsilon)}$ and outputs a halfspace with error at most $\mathrm{OPT}+\varepsilon$, where $\mathrm{OPT}$ is the error of the best-fitting halfspace for $f$. Previously, even with membership queries, the best known running time was $n^{\mathrm{poly}(1/\varepsilon)}$, achieved by the sample-based algorithm of Kalai, Klivans, Mansour, and Servedio (FOCS 2005). Our algorithm is the first agnostic halfspace learner under the uniform distribution on $\{\pm1\}^n$ whose running time is polynomial in $n$ with an exponent independent of $\varepsilon$. Combining our algorithm with a boosting argument yields a proper agnostic learner using only random examples. It achieves the same $\mathrm{OPT}+\varepsilon$ guarantee, with running time matching that of Kalai et al.\ up to an additive term depending only on $\varepsilon$. To our knowledge, this is the first sample-based proper agnostic learner in the Boolean setting with running time $2^{o(n)}$ for every fixed $\varepsilon>0$.

AI.tldr: The paper gives a proper membership-query algorithm for agnostically learning halfspaces under the uniform distribution on the Boolean cube whose running time is polynomial in n with an exponent independent of epsilon, and a sample-based proper agnostic learner via boosting.
AI.motivation: The best known running time for this problem with membership queries was n^(poly(1/epsilon)), achieved by the sample-based algorithm of Kalai, Klivans, Mansour and Servedio, so the dependence of the exponent on epsilon was the bottleneck.
AI.method: Given query access to an arbitrary Boolean function, the algorithm outputs a halfspace with error at most OPT plus epsilon in time poly(n) plus 2^(poly(1/epsilon)), and combining it with boosting yields a sample-based proper agnostic learner.
AI.result: The membership-query algorithm runs in poly(n) plus 2^(poly(1/epsilon)) time, and the boosted sample-based learner achieves the same OPT plus epsilon guarantee with running time matching Kalai et al. up to an additive term depending only on epsilon, giving 2^(o(n)) time for each fixed epsilon.
AI.conclusion: The exponent of n in agnostic halfspace learning under the uniform distribution can be made independent of epsilon, removing a long-standing barrier for proper learners.

title: Where Is a Prediction Model Miscalibrated, and for Whom? Local Audits in Outcome-Learned Pockets
comment: 16 pages, 3 figures, 2 tables; supplement (15 pages) as an ancillary file. Code: this https URL
summary: Overall and group-level averages, and ranking metrics such as the AUC, can hide sets of observations for which a prediction model systematically over- or under-predicts. We present an audit that asks where a model is miscalibrated (in which sets of similar observations it over- or under-predicts on average) and for whom (whether its average prediction error differs between demographic groups, such as by race or sex, within the same set). It groups observations into pockets using random-forest similarity, which weighs each feature by its importance for predicting the outcome, with a ridge-regression grouping alongside. Pockets are learned on one sample and tested on another, with simultaneous confidence intervals that allow for correlation within units such as hospitals; the audit needs only features, outcomes and fixed predictions. In 17 simulation scenarios with an error planted for one group, the combined audit located it better than the strongest alternative grouping in 15, with false-alarm rates near or below 5%; with a local error planted for everyone, it won in 12 of 15 scenarios at the smaller error size and lost when the error was unrelated to the outcome. In public synthetic data from the care-management algorithm studied by Obermeyer et al., it found no detectable overall error but under-prediction of illness in the sickest pockets and over-prediction elsewhere, and distinguished Black patients' concentration where the score under-predicted for everyone from a Black-White gap within pockets. For APACHE IVa, an exploratory analysis located its previously reported over-prediction of ICU mortality in a mostly ventilated pocket and a low-risk pocket, with none detected in a moderate-risk one. Two chest X-ray classifiers showed offsetting local errors behind no detectable overall error. Code: this https URL

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a local audit that groups observations into pockets using random-forest similarity and tests where a prediction model is miscalibrated and whether its error differs between demographic groups within the same pocket, with simultaneous confidence intervals that allow for within-unit correlation.
AI.motivation: Overall calibration, group-level averages and AUC can hide subsets where a model systematically over- or under-predicts, and existing audits do not jointly ask where a model is miscalibrated and for whom.
AI.method: Pockets are learned on one sample from features weighted by importance for the outcome, using random-forest similarity alongside ridge-regression grouping, and tested on another sample with simultaneous intervals that allow correlation within units such as hospitals; the audit requires only features, outcomes and fixed predictions.
AI.result: In 17 simulation scenarios with an error planted in one group, the combined audit located it better than the strongest alternative in 15, with false-alarm rates near or below 5%; in the Obermeyer et al. care-management data it found under-prediction in the sickest pockets and over-prediction elsewhere, with no detectable overall error; for APACHE IVa it located over-prediction of ICU mortality in one pocket and a low-risk pocket, and two chest X-ray classifiers showed offsetting local errors.
AI.conclusion: Local, pocket-level audits can reveal miscalibration and group disparities that overall metrics hide, with the caveat that some analyses are exploratory.

title: The Staged Pandora's Box: Reservation Indices for Multi-Fidelity Bayesian Optimization
summary: A staged search must decide which candidate to advance next and when to stop. Some observations only inform later decisions; others can be kept as results. We formulate these choices as a staged Pandora's box with a designated set of collectable stages. For independent finite-stage candidates with bounded readings and positive bounded own-history costs, an exact covered-call recursion gives the reservation index, the optimal value and the loss of every advance or stop; advancing an index-maximal candidate while its index exceeds the incumbent is optimal. The representation recovers classical single-stage search, nested inspection and the all-collectable Markov setting, and prices changes in the problem: enlarging the collectable set or lowering costs raises the value by an explicit covered-call overshoot. Resumption can be valuable even when future reward laws do not change, but has no value for deterministic readings. With information sharing across candidates, no rule using only their separate remaining-reading laws is universally optimal, and making an intermediate reading collectable can change which candidate is inspected first. Under a coherent joint path law with own-history costs, an approximate-planning bound controls the recomputed index's regret by changes in untouched candidates' local values; a common-component specialization bounds those changes through predictive total-variation dispersion. Exact finite-law experiments check the representation, the loss accounting and the bounds.

AI.tldr: The paper formulates staged search as a Pandora's box with collectable stages and derives an exact reservation index via a covered-call recursion, showing that advancing the index-maximal candidate is optimal when information is not shared across candidates.
AI.motivation: In multi-fidelity search, some observations only inform later decisions while others can be kept as results, and the classical Pandora's box does not capture this choice of which stages to advance and when to stop.
AI.method: For independent finite-stage candidates with bounded readings and positive bounded own-history costs, the authors compute the reservation index, optimal value and loss of each advance or stop through an exact covered-call recursion, and analyse changes to the collectable set and costs.
AI.result: Advancing an index-maximal candidate while its index exceeds the incumbent is optimal; enlarging the collectable set or lowering costs raises value by an explicit covered-call overshoot; with information sharing, no rule using only separate remaining-reading laws is universally optimal; under a coherent joint path law, an approximate-planning bound controls regret of the recomputed index, and exact finite-law experiments verify the representation and bounds.
AI.conclusion: Reservation indices extend Pandora's box to staged multi-fidelity search, but information sharing breaks the simple optimality of index rules.

title: Spectral Degeneration of Self-Attention under Isotropic Score Geometry
summary: We study the spectral structure of the self-attention matrix in Transformer models through an idealized spectral model for the pre-softmax score matrix. Motivated by the rotational isotropy of query and key representations, our model replaces the random token-space orientation of the score matrix by its canonical singular-value representative with a logarithmic spike--bulk separation. Empirical diagnostics on pretrained vision and language transformers motivate this model: token-space singular matrices have nearly uniform eigen-angle distributions, and score spectra are dominated by a small number of effective directions. We then prove that the row-wise softmax map transforms this structure into a degenerate attention matrix: dominant modes are preserved, whereas the bulk spectral distributions concentrate at zero. Stable rank remains bounded for bidirectional attention but grows logarithmically for causal attention. Within the canonical model, these results explain how attention can preserve a small number of dominant directions while compressing the remaining bulk modes.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes an idealised spectral model of pre-softmax attention scores and proves that the row-wise softmax degenerates the bulk of the spectrum to zero while preserving a few dominant directions, with stable rank bounded for bidirectional attention but growing logarithmically for causal attention.
AI.motivation: Empirical spectra of pretrained vision and language transformers show nearly uniform eigen-angle distributions and a few effective score directions, motivating a model of the attention score matrix that explains how attention compresses its remaining modes.
AI.method: The authors replace the score matrix's random token-space orientation by its canonical singular-value representative with a logarithmic spike-bulk separation, then analyse the row-wise softmax map on this model.
AI.result: Dominant modes are preserved while bulk spectral distributions concentrate at zero; stable rank remains bounded for bidirectional attention and grows logarithmically for causal attention within the canonical model.
AI.conclusion: Softmax attention can keep a small number of dominant directions while compressing bulk modes, and the model explains this behaviour for both bidirectional and causal attention.

title: When Is Tracking Affordable? A Movement-Budget Feasibility Threshold for Dynamic Regret
summary: Dynamic regret measures an online learner against a moving comparator, and standard analyses assume the learner may move freely at every round. We study what happens when it may not: the learner is given a hard budget $S$ on its total movement $\sum_t \|x_t - x_{t-1}\|$. Our main result is that a movement budget creates a feasibility barrier. On a domain of diameter $D$ with $G$-Lipschitz convex losses, for every comparator path length $P_T \in [D, DT]$ we exhibit a deterministic adversary that forces $R_d = \Omega(GDT)$ on every budget-feasible algorithm whenever $S \le c P_T$ for a universal constant $c>0$. This barrier is caused by the budget rather than by a volatile environment: for fixed $D$, it applies when $P_T = o(T)$, where the unconstrained minimax rate $\Theta(G\sqrt{D(D+P_T)T})$ is sublinear, so the same instances are learnable with an unbounded budget and unlearnable without one. Conversely, projected online gradient descent with a budget-aware step size is budget-feasible and attains $o(GDT)$ once $S = \omega(D + P_T)$. Thus the critical movement scale is $D+P_T$: linear regret is unavoidable below a sufficiently small constant multiple of $P_T$, while sublinear regret is achievable when $S/(D+P_T)\to\infty$ in the learnable regime. The construction rests on a distinction we make explicit: what makes a comparator expensive to track under a movement budget is the distance it forces the learner to travel, not its path length. Above the threshold we give a budget-dependent upper bound and identify the tight minimax rate in this region as an open problem rather than claiming a product law. Experiments support the predicted transition location and the $1/S$ decay.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that a hard movement budget on an online learner creates a feasibility barrier for dynamic regret, with linear regret forced whenever the budget is at most a constant multiple of the comparator path length, and identifies a critical movement scale of D plus P_T.
AI.motivation: Dynamic regret analyses assume the learner can move freely each round, but a limited total movement budget changes the problem and its feasibility, which was not characterised.
AI.method: The authors build a deterministic adversary for G-Lipschitz convex losses on a domain of diameter D, showing that for comparator path lengths P_T between D and DT any budget-feasible algorithm suffers linear regret when the budget S is at most c P_T, and they analyse projected online gradient descent with a budget-aware step size.
AI.result: Linear regret Omega(GDT) is unavoidable when S is at most c P_T for a universal constant c, while projected gradient descent with a budget-aware step size attains sublinear regret once S is omega(D + P_T); experiments support the predicted transition and a 1/S decay.
AI.conclusion: Tracking cost under a movement budget depends on the distance the comparator forces the learner to travel rather than its path length, and the tight minimax rate above the threshold remains open.

title: Unimodal Augmentation-based SSL Objectives Induce Cross-Modal Alignment
summary: Recent works have observed implicit cross-modal alignment between independently trained unimodal models. However, the mechanisms underlying the emergence of this phenomenon remain unresolved. In this paper, we demonstrate that unimodal augmentation-based self-supervised objectives implicitly induce cross-modal alignment. We show that low unimodal losses force high cross-modal alignment, whereas a high unimodal loss prevents such alignment. We theoretically connect the widely used InfoNCE loss to local CKA, the popular measure of cross-modal alignment. We further provide extensive empirical evidence supporting this claim, both in controlled settings and across 53 unconstrained frozen text, vision, and audio unimodal encoders. In both cases, unimodal augmentation-based objectives control cross-modal alignment. Overall, our results provide a theoretical and empirical foundation for understanding the emergence of implicit cross-modal alignment by establishing a direct connection between unimodal training objectives and cross-modal structure.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that unimodal augmentation-based self-supervised objectives implicitly induce cross-modal alignment, linking low unimodal loss to high cross-modal alignment via InfoNCE and local CKA, with evidence across 53 frozen unimodal encoders.
AI.motivation: Independently trained unimodal models have been observed to align across modalities, but the mechanism behind this emergence was unresolved.
AI.method: The authors theoretically connect the InfoNCE loss to local CKA, a measure of cross-modal alignment, and test the claim in controlled settings and across 53 unconstrained frozen text, vision and audio encoders.
AI.result: Low unimodal losses force high cross-modal alignment while high unimodal loss prevents it, and unimodal augmentation-based objectives control cross-modal alignment in both controlled and unconstrained settings.
AI.conclusion: Cross-modal structure arises directly from unimodal training objectives, giving a theoretical and empirical basis for implicit cross-modal alignment.

title: Exact Fusion of Softmax Attention Heads Can Require Exponentially Many Atoms
comment: 9 pages, 3 figures. Code and reproducibility materials: this https URL
summary: Fusing independently normalized attention heads can increase the number of explicit key-value entries, or atoms, needed to preserve their output. We prove a sharp separation for $W_d(q)=\sum_{j=1}^d\sigma(q_j)$: its $d$ two-atom heads use $2d$ head-atom terms, whereas its minimum single-head representation has exactly $2^d$ atoms, even with arbitrary fixed replacement keys, scalar values, and positive masses. The same lower bound holds for every fixed uniform error below $1/2$ on $\mathbb R^d$, and the threshold is sharp. The proof uses exposed-key normal cones; exact equality on any nonempty open query domain inherits the bound. The resulting atom bound for a fixed head count is tight when that count divides $d$. A normalized family retains its exponential exact minimum while approaching a constant on fixed-radius query balls. For pretrained-model caches, a classical affine-rank bound and a certified instance exclude exact vector preservation at a specified atom count. Learned-cache comparisons on two disjoint banks of 64 contexts show budget-dependent reversals and calibration effects.

AI.tldr: The paper proves that fusing independently normalised softmax attention heads can require exponentially many key-value atoms, showing that for the function sum of sigma(q_j) a two-atom-per-head construction uses 2d head-atom terms while any single head needs 2^d atoms.
AI.motivation: Fusing attention heads can increase the number of explicit key-value entries needed to preserve their output, and the size of this blow-up for exact fusion was not known.
AI.method: For W_d(q) equal to the sum over j of sigma(q_j), the authors prove a lower bound using exposed-key normal cones, extend exact equality to any nonempty open query domain, and analyse a normalised family and pretrained-model caches with an affine-rank bound and a certified instance.
AI.result: The single-head representation needs exactly 2^d atoms, the same lower bound holds for any fixed uniform error below 1/2, and the threshold is sharp; a normalised family keeps an exponential exact minimum while approaching a constant on fixed-radius balls; learned-cache comparisons on two disjoint banks of 64 contexts show budget-dependent reversals and calibration effects.
AI.conclusion: Exact fusion of attention heads can be exponentially costly in atom count, so approximate or budget-aware fusion may be needed in practice.

title: Diagonal Equivalence in State Space Models: Characterization, Retrieval Rank, and Selective Extensions
comment: 81 pages, 6 figures, 33 tables. Code: this https URL
summary: We classify real and complex state-space models (SSMs) with linear transitions, distinguishing fixed-basis diagonal equivalence from input-output equivalence and tracking coefficient-conditioning windows under coordinate changes. We characterize diagonal equivalence through commuting transition families whose members are diagonalizable over the chosen field. With time-shared token-local matrix maps, we identify this class's state-mediated kernels with unnormalized scalar-mode linear attention with multiplicative masks. Mamba 3's multiple-input, multiple-output (MIMO) construction lifts one value per local interface; SSD-MIMO routes independent values for local retrieval rank above one. HybridMamba combines Mamba 1's per-coordinate decay, Mamba 2-style heads and Mamba 3's complex rotations and two-endpoint writes, mixing real and rotating state blocks with different decay laws. They recover Mamba 1-3 single-input, single-output (SISO) configurations as exact special cases. On five large H100 bfloat16 workloads, our fused GPU kernels improve geometric-mean training time over official Mamba 1/3 in matched SISO recoveries, with Mamba 2 near parity at SSM-core scope. Memory tradeoffs depend on the baseline and metric: saved-for-backward versus peak allocation. In small-model multi-token recall experiments, both designs outperform Mamba 1-3 on the hardest tier; higher routing ranks perform best in gated or phase-diverse configurations. In single-seed language models with about 500M parameters, both improve on Mamba 1/2 in test loss at 2B tokens, but the routing gains do not translate into lower language-model loss. Our best configurations approach Mamba 3 SISO through 10B tokens while remaining behind it and Mamba 3 MIMO in language-model loss.

AI.tldr: The paper classifies linear state-space models into fixed-basis diagonal equivalence classes, relates them to unnormalised scalar-mode linear attention, and proposes SSD-MIMO and HybridMamba architectures that recover Mamba 1-3 as special cases and run faster on H100 kernels.
AI.motivation: Mamba variants differ in their state and write structure, and it was unclear which SSM configurations are equivalent, how they relate to attention, and what retrieval rank they support.
AI.method: The authors characterise diagonal equivalence through commuting, diagonalisable transition families and identify state-mediated kernels with linear attention with multiplicative masks; SSD-MIMO routes independent values for retrieval rank above one, and HybridMamba mixes real and complex rotating state blocks with different decay laws, with fused GPU kernels.
AI.result: On five large H100 bfloat16 workloads the fused kernels improve geometric-mean training time over official Mamba 1 and 3 in matched SISO recoveries, with Mamba 2 near parity; in small multi-token recall tests both designs beat Mamba 1-3 on the hardest tier; in single-seed models of about 500M parameters they improve test loss over Mamba 1 and 2 at 2B tokens but remain behind Mamba 3 at 10B tokens and in language-model loss.
AI.conclusion: The proposed designs improve retrieval and training efficiency in several settings, but routing gains do not yet translate into lower language-model loss than Mamba 3.

title: Bagel: A Fast Bayesian Online Changepoint Detection Algorithm for Linear Models via Posterior Merging
summary: Bayesian online changepoint detection provides a natural framework for quantifying uncertainty about whether and when a change has occurred. It also enables the use of prior information which can increase detection power. Exact Bayesian inference sequentially updates the posterior of whether and when a change has occurred. We present a unified approach to calculating and updating this posterior for a class of regression models covering standard changepoint scenarios, such as changes in mean and slope, whilst also allowing common structure such as seasonal effects. However, naive implementation has a computational cost that increases linearly over time. We, further, introduce approximate updates that keep this cost constant. These are based on novel ideas of merging changepoint times, and are an alternative to existing pruning approaches. We show that merging enables better approximations of the posterior of when a change occurs. Furthermore, we introduce a novel condition for merging that accounts for both the posterior probability of the changepoint times and the similarity of their corresponding post-change parameters. We show that this is more accurate than conditions that only consider the former. We demonstrate the advantage of our approach on simulated data, and the Azure LLM inference traces.

AI.tldr: The paper presents Bagel, an approximate Bayesian online changepoint detection method for linear regression models that merges changepoint candidates so that per-step cost stays constant rather than growing linearly over time.
AI.motivation: Exact Bayesian online changepoint detection has a computational cost that grows linearly with time, and existing approximations rely on pruning.
AI.method: The authors give a unified posterior update for regression models covering changes in mean and slope and seasonal effects, and propose merging changepoint times with a condition that accounts for both posterior probability and similarity of post-change parameters.
AI.result: Merging gives better approximations of the changepoint posterior than pruning, and the merging condition is more accurate than conditions based only on posterior probability; the method is demonstrated on simulated data and on Azure LLM inference traces.
AI.conclusion: Merging changepoint candidates offers a constant-cost alternative to pruning for online changepoint detection in regression models.

title: Strictly proper scoring rules for node selection tasks on graphs
summary: In node selection tasks, the goal is to identify a single unknown target node in a graph. We consider probabilistic supervised node selection, where the estimator outputs a probability distribution over the nodes of the graph and the ground-truth node is available for evaluation. Classical evaluation metrics for such tasks are either statistically ill-conceived or blind to the graph structure. To fill this gap, we introduce two strictly proper scoring rules that are explicitly graph-aware: the Resistance score, which is parameter-free, and the Diffusion score, which operates at an adjustable coarse-graining resolution. We show that the Diffusion score interpolates between the multi-category Brier score and a cluster-level weighted Brier score. The Resistance score generalises two classical scoring rules: the multi-category Brier score and the Ranked probability score. Applied to rooted trees, it also serves as the strictly proper version of the improper Hierarchical error distance used in hierarchical classification. In the same setting, we furthermore establish strict propriety of the Hierarchical cross-entropy family, a recently introduced separate class of hierarchy-aware scoring rules. Experiments on epidemic source detection and on ImageNet classification confirm that the proposed scores detect meaningful differences in estimation quality that classical metrics miss.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces two strictly proper, graph-aware scoring rules for probabilistic node selection, the parameter-free Resistance score and the coarse-graining Diffusion score, which generalise classical Brier and ranked probability scores and are demonstrated on epidemic source detection and ImageNet classification.
AI.motivation: Classical metrics for identifying a single target node in a graph are either statistically improper or ignore graph structure, so they can miss meaningful differences in estimation quality.
AI.method: The authors define the Resistance score and the Diffusion score, show that the Diffusion score interpolates between the multi-category Brier score and a cluster-level weighted Brier score, show that the Resistance score generalises the Brier and ranked probability scores, and prove strict propriety for the Hierarchical cross-entropy family on rooted trees.
AI.result: On rooted trees the Resistance score is the strictly proper version of the hierarchical error distance; experiments on epidemic source detection and ImageNet classification confirm that the proposed scores detect differences in estimation quality that classical metrics miss.
AI.conclusion: Graph-aware strictly proper scores give a principled evaluation for probabilistic node selection and hierarchical classification.

title: On a Class of Non-Local Elliptic-Transport Systems in Score-Guided Probability Flow on $SE(3)$: Score-Singularity Resolution, Space-Time ADN Shift, and Markov Mean-Field Games
summary: We establish mathematical foundations for optimal spatiotemporal vector fields governing continuous score-guided probability flows over bounded submanifolds $M \subset SE(3)$ on the Special Euclidean group $SE(3) \cong \mathbb{R}^3 \times SO(3)$. Modeling dynamic density evolution via a score-perturbed Lie-algebraic continuity equation under zero-flux boundary conditions, we resolve the non-local score drift singularity $s(g,t) = \nabla_{SE(3)} \log \rho(g,t)$ as $\rho \rightarrow 0^+$ via weighted parabolic flux dissipation bounds. Using left-invariant exponential group mollifiers, we derive boundary-preserving DiPerna--Lions commutator estimates tracking structure constants $\{c_{ij}^k\}$. Second, interpreting the optimality system as a 7D space-time elliptic operator $L_{7D} = -\Delta_{SE(3)} - \partial_t^2$ with zero-order corner compatibility on $\partial M \times \{0,T\}$, we establish Agmon--Douglis--Nirenberg $W_p^2(Q_T)$ shift estimates tracking Lie algebra constants, boundary geometry $\|\partial M\|_{C^2}$, and Ricci curvature $\|Ric_{SE(3)}\|_{L^\infty}$, yielding a full $C^\infty(\overline{Q}_T)$ Schauder bootstrap expansion. Third, we extend this system to non-cooperative Markov Mean-Field Games (MFGs) on $SE(3)$, establishing score-guided Nash equilibria via Schauder--Tychonoff fixed points. Crucially, the constant diagonal Ricci curvature $Ric_{SE(3)} = \mathrm{diag}(0,0,0,1/2,1/2,1/2)$ from $SO(3)$ induces a sharp Bochner--Weitzenböck spectral gap boost $\lambda_1(-\Delta_{SE(3)}) \ge \lambda_1(-\Delta_{\mathbb{R}^3}) + 1/2 > 0$. This positive rotational curvature enhances the Lie-algebraic Poincaré coercivity constant, demonstrating that intrinsic group curvature stabilizes score-guided flows against dispersion and expands the critical Nash uniqueness horizon $T_{SE(3)}^*$ beyond flat Euclidean limits.

AI.tldr: The paper develops mathematical foundations for score-guided probability flows on bounded submanifolds of SE(3), covering singularity resolution, Agmon-Douglis-Nirenberg regularity for a 7D space-time elliptic operator, and Nash equilibria in Markov mean-field games.
AI.motivation: Score-guided probability flows on bounded submanifolds of SE(3) require control of the score singularity where the density vanishes and regularity of the associated optimality system, which the abstract presents as needing mathematical foundations.
AI.method: The authors model density evolution with a score-perturbed Lie-algebraic continuity equation under zero-flux boundary conditions, use left-invariant exponential group mollifiers for commutator estimates, interpret the optimality system as a 7D space-time elliptic operator for Schauder-type bootstrap estimates, and extend to non-cooperative Markov mean-field games via Schauder-Tychonoff fixed points.
AI.result: The paper claims the score singularity is resolved as the density tends to zero, that Schauder bootstrap regularity holds up to C-infinity on the closure of the space-time domain, that score-guided Nash equilibria exist, and that the constant diagonal Ricci curvature of SO(3) gives a spectral gap bound of lambda_1 at least lambda_1 of the Euclidean Laplacian plus 1/2; no numerical experiments are reported in the abstract.
AI.conclusion: The authors argue that intrinsic group curvature stabilises score-guided flows and enlarges the Nash uniqueness horizon beyond flat Euclidean limits, although these claims rest on the analytic arguments stated in the abstract.

authors: Devesh Shah Antonio H. de O. Fonseca
title: LLMs Depend on Specialist Tools for Out-of-Distribution Generalization in MS/MS Structural Elucidation
comment: Accepted at "NeurIPS 2026 Workshop on Agentic Systems for Molecular Sciences" and "I Can't Believe It's Not Better: Failure Modes of AI in Biology Workshop at NeurIPS 2026"
summary: A frontier language model was recently reported to solve 1D NMR structural elucidation without tools. We ask whether this capability transfers to tandem mass spectrometry (MS/MS) in the de novo setting, where the model must propose a structure directly from the spectrum without a candidate list or reference library. To separate reasoning from recall, we build a 100-analyte benchmark from MassSpecGym, split by each analyte's textual footprint into in-distribution (well documented in literature) and out-of-distribution (essentially undocumented) arms. We hold the model, harness, and output format fixed and vary only the LLM's access to domain-specific tools. Without tools, a frontier LLM reaches 52% Top-1 accuracy in-distribution but only 2% out-of-distribution. Only access to de novo structure generators improves out-of-distribution accuracy, raising it to as much as 38% Top-1, and the resulting agent outperforms the standalone de novo models both in and out of distribution. These results suggest that LLMs are not effective at de novo MS/MS structural elucidation on their own, and that further gains depend on the specialist tools available to the agent rather than on the LLM itself.

AI.tldr: On a 100-analyte MS/MS benchmark, a frontier LLM alone solves structure elucidation well only for in-distribution compounds, and its out-of-distribution accuracy rises to 38 percent Top-1 only when it can call de novo structure generators.
AI.motivation: A frontier model was reported to solve 1D NMR elucidation without tools, and the authors ask whether this ability transfers to de novo tandem mass spectrometry without candidate lists or reference libraries, where recall must be separated from reasoning.
AI.method: From MassSpecGym they build a 100-analyte benchmark split by textual footprint into in-distribution and out-of-distribution arms, hold the model, harness and output format fixed, and vary only access to domain-specific tools.
AI.result: Without tools the LLM reaches 52 percent Top-1 accuracy in-distribution but only 2 percent out-of-distribution; access to de novo structure generators raises out-of-distribution accuracy to as much as 38 percent Top-1, and the resulting agent outperforms the standalone de novo models both in and out of distribution.
AI.conclusion: LLMs are not effective at de novo MS/MS structure elucidation on their own, and further gains depend on specialist tools rather than the language model itself.

title: Tilted Convexity and an Exact Offline-Online Separation
summary: Convexity has three equivalent descriptions: support by affine functions, monotonicity of the subdifferential, and increasing secant slopes. We weaken all three by one distortion with parameter $\gamma\in(0,1]$, which multiplies positive changes by $\gamma$ and divides negative ones by $\gamma$. The resulting classes are the convex functions at $\gamma=1$ and, for $\gamma<1$, are distinct and nested, with the parameter dropping by at most a square along the chain. For proper lower semicontinuous functions in these classes, the effective domain is convex, local minimizers are global, and the function is locally Lipschitz on the relative interior of its domain. The classes separate offline from online optimization over compact convex sets with efficient projection, with access to function values and bounded support vectors. A smooth member of any class can be minimized to additive accuracy $\varepsilon$ with $\mathrm{poly}(1/\varepsilon)$ first-order queries and projections. Online, with nonpositive losses and $\alpha$-regret measured against $\alpha$ times the best fixed point, a polynomial-time algorithm achieves $\gamma$-regret $O(\sqrt T)$ on the largest class. For every fixed, effectively specified $\gamma\in(0,1)$ and every $\alpha\in(\gamma,1]$, no randomized polynomial-time algorithm has sublinear expected $\alpha$-regret unless $\mathbf{NP}=\mathbf{RP}$, already for smooth concave polynomial losses in the smallest class, each minimized by one linear optimization. Thus, unless $\mathbf{NP}=\mathbf{RP}$, $\gamma$ is the exact online coefficient of each class, while the offline coefficient is one.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a distortion parameter gamma that weakens convexity into a nested hierarchy of classes, shows that gamma is the exact online coefficient for each class while the offline coefficient is one, unless NP equals RP.
AI.motivation: Convexity has several equivalent descriptions, and the authors ask whether weakened versions give a meaningful hierarchy separating offline from online optimisation.
AI.method: The distortion multiplies positive changes in the secant and subgradient descriptions by gamma and divides negative ones by gamma, giving classes that are nested for gamma less than one; the authors study their structure and analyse optimisation with function values and bounded support vectors.
AI.result: For proper lower semicontinuous members the effective domain is convex, local minimisers are global and the function is locally Lipschitz on the relative interior; smooth members can be minimised to additive accuracy epsilon with poly(1/epsilon) first-order queries and projections; an algorithm achieves gamma-regret O(sqrt(T)) online on the largest class; for fixed gamma in (0,1) and alpha in (gamma,1], no randomised polynomial-time algorithm has sublinear alpha-regret unless NP equals RP.
AI.conclusion: The classes separate offline from online optimisation, with gamma as the exact online coefficient under the stated complexity assumption.

title: ST-GFM: Spectral-Temporal Graph Forecasting with Measured Perturbation Bounds and Masked Spectral Reconstruction
comment: 21 Pages, 11 Figures, 12 Tables, Supplementary Materials attached, Under Review
summary: Graph forecasters for sensor networks are trained in one regime and deployed in others, where sensor coupling and signal frequency content both change. We split this spectral shift into an operator channel and a frequency channel, each with a dimensionless measure. ST-GFM (Spectral-Temporal Graph Forecasting Model) filters every input step with Chebyshev and bidirectional diffusion filters on one learned, non-symmetric operator and alternates them with per-node temporal attention. For the operator channel we prove Frobenius-norm perturbation bounds for both graph branches, show that the Chebyshev bound is attained to first order, and compute its constant from the trained weights and the measured operator norm: 17.9 on METR-LA and 21.5 on PEMS-BAY. Under random edge dropout the trained layer moves by 2.0% to 3.1% of this bound. Masked Spectral Reconstruction (MSR), a self-supervised loss active in the first 40 epochs, matches the log power spectrum of the encoder output to that of the input. For small log-spectral residuals on unclamped bins it is proportional to an Itakura-Saito divergence to leading order. Removing it raises the 60-minute MAE by 0.30 on METR-LA, close to the 0.33 lost when all three self-supervised losses go. Under one shared evaluation pipeline, the 60-minute MAE of ST-GFM is 3.5% below a retrained STAEformer on METR-LA and 13.0% below it on PEMS-BAY. Its 60-minute MAE is 3.0980.017 on METR-LA (five seeds) and 1.5760.006 on PEMS-BAY (three seeds), the lowest PEMS-BAY MAE among twelve published baselines.

AI.tldr: ST-GFM is a spectral-temporal graph forecaster for sensor networks that uses Chebyshev and bidirectional diffusion filters on a learned non-symmetric operator, with proven Frobenius perturbation bounds and a masked spectral reconstruction loss, and it reports lower 60-minute MAE than a retrained STAEformer on METR-LA and PEMS-BAY.
AI.motivation: Graph forecasters for sensor networks are trained and deployed under different sensor coupling and signal frequency content, and the operator and frequency shifts were not separated or measured with dimensionless quantities.
AI.method: ST-GFM filters each input step with Chebyshev and bidirectional diffusion filters on one learned non-symmetric operator and alternates them with per-node temporal attention; for the operator channel the authors prove Frobenius perturbation bounds and compute a constant from trained weights and the measured operator norm; the masked spectral reconstruction loss, active in the first 40 epochs, matches the log power spectrum of encoder output to that of the input.
AI.result: The Chebyshev bound constant is 17.9 on METR-LA and 21.5 on PEMS-BAY, and under random edge dropout the trained layer moves by 2.0 to 3.1 percent of this bound; removing the reconstruction loss raises the 60-minute MAE by 0.30 on METR-LA; 60-minute MAE is 3.5 percent below a retrained STAEformer on METR-LA and 13.0 percent below it on PEMS-BAY, reaching 3.098 plus or minus 0.017 on METR-LA over five seeds and 1.576 plus or minus 0.006 on PEMS-BAY over three seeds, the lowest PEMS-BAY MAE among twelve published baselines.
AI.conclusion: Separating operator and frequency shifts with measured bounds gives a principled account of graph forecaster behaviour under distribution change, alongside competitive accuracy.

title: ParaDeAl: Parallel Descent Algorithms for Sparse Statistics
summary: Best subset selection is a central problem in statistical regression, drawing increasing attention from the broader optimization and machine learning communities. Solving the hard L0 sparsity constraint directly has been computationally challenging; as a result, most existing work proposes formulations which do not enforce the constraint, but instead use a mix of L0/L1/L2 penalties to encourage sparsity. Modern methods for solving such penalized formulations are tractable for p = 100,000, but give up direct control over sparsity. In this paper, we propose a two-stage proximal gradient descent-based approach which both enforces the sparsity constraint and incorporates L1/L2 penalties, leveraging GPUs for computational acceleration to find approximate solutions. Our method, ParaDeAl, offers the user the ability to select the problem hyperparameters, solves all configurations in parallel, and obtains solutions up to 15x faster than the best state-of-the-art CPU competitors while achieving almost identical test accuracy for the same support size for large (p > 100,000) synthetic and real-world datasets.

AI.tldr: ParaDeAl is a GPU-accelerated two-stage proximal gradient method that enforces an exact L0 sparsity constraint with optional L1 and L2 penalties, solving all hyperparameter configurations in parallel for best subset selection.
AI.motivation: Most methods for best subset selection replace the hard L0 constraint with penalties and give up direct control of sparsity, while exact-constraint approaches have been computationally challenging.
AI.method: The two-stage proximal gradient descent approach enforces the sparsity constraint, incorporates L1 and L2 penalties, and runs on GPUs to find approximate solutions for all user-chosen configurations in parallel.
AI.result: ParaDeAl is up to 15 times faster than the best CPU state-of-the-art competitors on large synthetic and real-world datasets with p above 100,000, while achieving almost identical test accuracy at the same support size.
AI.conclusion: Direct sparsity control with GPU parallelism makes best subset selection practical at large scale without sacrificing accuracy.

title: Efficient Closure Learning in Dynamical Systems: A Comparison of Data-Assimilated and Embedded Approaches
summary: Increased computing power has transformed computational science and improved predictive capabilities for complex systems, but many phenomena still exceed current simulation capabilities or require rapid evaluations for fast design iterations. Closure models address this challenge by approximating unresolved effects in reduced or incomplete dynamical systems. Data-driven closures offer a flexible mechanism for improving model accuracy and applicability, but approaches that embed the closure within a computational model for construction and training phases can be computationally expensive and cause numerical instabilities in the computational model during training. To avoid the challenges posed by embedded approaches, staged approaches to closure-model learning have been developed. The first stage uses data assimilation to infer state and closure trajectories from observations. The second stage trains a machine learning closure model offline using the assimilated data, thereby avoiding repeated simulator calls during training. In this work, we investigate the cost and accuracy tradeoffs between embedded and staged data-driven closure modeling approaches for a synthetic epidemiological SIQR model with a nonlinear state-dependent quarantine closure. The results illustrate a practical accuracy-efficiency trade-off: for this exemplar, embedded training provides the strongest average accuracy, while the staged approach yields comparable qualitative behavior with a moderate increase in error, substantially fewer model evaluations, and improved optimization robustness.

AI.tldr: The paper compares embedded and staged data-driven closure learning on a synthetic SIQR epidemiological model with a nonlinear quarantine closure, finding that embedded training is most accurate on average while the staged approach is cheaper and more robust at moderate extra error.
AI.motivation: Embedded closure training within a simulator can be expensive and numerically unstable, while staged approaches that first assimilate data and then learn offline have not been compared on the cost and accuracy trade-off.
AI.method: The staged approach first uses data assimilation to infer state and closure trajectories from observations and then trains a machine learning closure offline, while the embedded approach trains the closure inside the simulator; both are compared on a synthetic SIQR model with a nonlinear state-dependent quarantine closure.
AI.result: Embedded training gives the strongest average accuracy, while the staged approach yields comparable qualitative behaviour with a moderate increase in error, substantially fewer model evaluations and improved optimisation robustness.
AI.conclusion: For this exemplar, staged closure learning offers a practical accuracy-efficiency trade-off relative to embedded training, although the result is limited to one model.

title: Benchmark Prediction with Sparse and Unpaired Cached Responses
summary: Evaluating a generative model on all queries from all available benchmark tasks is prohibitively expensive. As such, models are often evaluated on different subsets of tasks and/or different subsets of queries from a given task. The resulting collection of responses and the corresponding (model, task) score matrix are sparse and unpaired. In this paper, we introduce the Product Kernel Perspective Space (PKPS), a collection of low-dimensional representations of models based on their embedded responses. PKPS generalizes existing methods for representing black-box generative models by comparing responses to similar -- rather than just identical -- queries and is therefore able to utilize sparse and unpaired information. Theoretically, we show that benchmark prediction using PKPS is query-efficient relative to methods that only use information from dense and paired portions of the evaluation data. Empirically, we show that PKPS-based methods outperform baselines on benchmark prediction across two large benchmark suites.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces the Product Kernel Perspective Space (PKPS), a low-dimensional representation of generative models built from embedded responses to similar rather than identical queries, enabling benchmark prediction from sparse and unpaired evaluation data.
AI.motivation: Evaluating a generative model on every query of every benchmark is too expensive, so evaluation data are sparse and unpaired across models and tasks, and existing representation methods use only identical queries.
AI.method: PKPS compares model responses to similar queries, so it can use sparse and unpaired information, and the authors give a theoretical query-efficiency comparison with methods that use only dense and paired data.
AI.result: Theory shows PKPS-based benchmark prediction is query-efficient relative to dense-and-paired methods, and empirically PKPS-based methods outperform baselines on benchmark prediction across two large benchmark suites.
AI.conclusion: Using responses to similar queries extends black-box model representations to sparse evaluation data and improves benchmark prediction.

title: From Fragmentation to Fusion: A Survey and Roadmap for Omnimodal Embeddings
summary: Embedding models underpin virtually every modern AI system, from search engines to recommendation systems. Despite shared mathematical foundations, research on embedding models remains fragmented by modality: the communities develop largely in isolation, seldom exchanging insights. We argue that this fragmentation obscures a deeper convergence. Driven by contrastive learning, Transformer architectures, and a granularity shift, embedding research across modalities is converging toward a common set of principles, even as modality-specific challenges remain underexplored. To reason across this convergence without conflating it, we propose a framework of three progressively harder capabilities: coverage, comparability, and compositionality. Three paths toward unification satisfy these in turn: transformation broadens coverage, alignment enables comparability, and joint embedding, the terminus we advocate, aims at compositionality. This position paper traces the resulting evolution, providing the first unified, cross-cutting treatment of omnimodal embedding research.

AI.tldr: This position paper surveys omnimodal embedding research and argues that embedding methods across text, vision and audio are converging toward joint embeddings that support compositionality, organised by three capabilities of coverage, comparability and compositionality.
AI.motivation: Embedding research remains fragmented by modality even though shared contrastive, Transformer and granularity principles point to a common direction, and no unified cross-cutting treatment existed.
AI.method: The authors propose a framework of three progressively harder capabilities, coverage, comparability and compositionality, and map three routes to unification: transformation for coverage, alignment for comparability and joint embedding for compositionality, which they advocate.
AI.result: As a position paper it reports no experiments; it traces the evolution of omnimodal embedding research and gives what it describes as the first unified, cross-cutting treatment of the area.
AI.conclusion: Joint embedding is proposed as the target for compositional omnimodal representations, and the framework offers a common vocabulary for the field.

title: MEMENTO: Learning Context Management for Long Context Processing Agents
summary: LLM agents that operate over long inputs must perform context management: deciding what to retain in a fixed-size context window. A common approach is compaction, where the model replaces its history with a self-generated note. Yet off-the-shelf agentic models, including GPT-5.5 and GLM-5.3, often write ineffective notes, and reinforcement learning (RL) alone rarely discovers useful note-taking behavior. We present MEMENTO, a long-context agent built on Qwen3-8B and trained to manage its context through compaction. We first bootstrap note-taking by fine-tuning on synthetic trajectories annotated with notes generated in hindsight, then reinforce it with RL using a reward that combines answer correctness, note-quality heuristics, and confidence calibration. Although trained only to compact into a fresh window, MEMENTO extends at test time to strategies such as context folding and confidence-based backtracking. On book-level question answering across four benchmarks, with books of up to 2.5M tokens, MEMENTO raises Qwen3-8B's accuracy from 36.9% to 67.8% while never holding more than 20K tokens in context. It outperforms GPT-5.5 agent in the same harness (13.1%) and full book context (56.7%) at less than 1/50 the cost. It also nearly matches a ~100x larger GLM-5.3 agent (69.3%) at 1/9 the cost, and comes within 6.4 points of GLM-5.3 full context at 1/26 the cost.

AI.tldr: MEMENTO trains a Qwen3-8B long-context agent to manage its own context through learned note-taking compaction, using supervised bootstrapping on hindsight-annotated trajectories followed by RL. On book-level QA it reaches 67.8% accuracy while never holding more than 20K tokens in context.
AI.motivation: Off-the-shelf agentic models often write ineffective compaction notes, and reinforcement learning alone rarely discovers useful note-taking behavior.
AI.method: The agent is fine-tuned on synthetic trajectories annotated with notes generated in hindsight, then reinforced with RL using a reward that combines answer correctness, note-quality heuristics and confidence calibration. It is trained only to compact into a fresh window but extends at test time to context folding and confidence-based backtracking.
AI.result: On book-level QA across four benchmarks with books up to 2.5M tokens, accuracy for Qwen3-8B rises from 36.9% to 67.8%. It outperforms a GPT-5.5 agent in the same harness (13.1%) and full book context (56.7%) at less than 1/50 the cost, and nearly matches a roughly 100x larger GLM-5.3 agent (69.3%) at 1/9 the cost.
AI.conclusion: Learned context management lets a small model handle very long inputs within a bounded context window and at low cost, competing with much larger models.

title: Cross-Lingual Persona Effects in LLM Negotiation
comment: Accepted to SocialAgent Workshop at NeurIPS 2026. 13 pages, 1 figure
summary: Tell an LLM negotiator to be "headstrong" and it should hold firm on price, but does that instruction retain the same behavior in every language? To test this, we use identical buyer and seller instances of Gemini 3.6 Flash to negotiate the same 12 CraigslistBargain scenarios in English and Korean. The pilot-scale 2 x 2 x 3 design crosses interaction language, seller urgency (none or strong), and buyer persona (cooperative, neutral, or headstrong), yielding 432 attempted negotiations. We call this property cross-lingual social-policy fidelity: whether a prompt-defined social policy produces the same behavioral effect regardless of interaction language. It often does not. Korean negotiations reached agreement far more often than English (77.3% vs. 52.5%, a 24.8-point gap, Holm-adjusted p = .0039), but only for neutral and headstrong buyers; cooperative buyers were already near-ceiling in both languages. Buyers' opening offers barely differed by language; the gap instead emerged later, through larger seller concessions and a smaller final gap in Korean, and agreed prices were also lower in Korean. Repeating the full design with Qwen3.7 Flash as both agents gives directional support: agreement was again higher in Korean (+13.9 points vs. Gemini's +24.8, with an interval whose lower bound is near zero), and sellers again conceded more. Pragmatic analysis reveals why: while both languages frequently featured face-threatening acts like rejections and counter-offers, Korean dialogue softened these threats with substantially more politeness mitigation, especially among sellers (11.7% vs. 3.6%). These results show that such a policy can produce different simulated negotiation behavior, not just different wording, when only the interaction language changes.

AI.tldr: The paper tests whether a prompt-defined negotiation persona produces the same behavior in English and Korean, using Gemini 3.6 Flash agents on 12 CraigslistBargain scenarios. The same persona often yields different outcomes across languages, and Korean negotiations reach agreement more often (77.3% vs. 52.5%).
AI.motivation: Persona prompts are usually assumed to have the same behavioral effect in every language, but this has not been tested for social policy, so the paper defines cross-lingual social-policy fidelity.
AI.method: Identical buyer and seller LLM instances negotiate in English and Korean in a pilot 2 x 2 x 3 design crossing interaction language, seller urgency (none or strong) and buyer persona (cooperative, neutral or headstrong), giving 432 attempted negotiations. The design is repeated with Qwen3.7 Flash, and pragmatic analysis examines face-threatening acts and politeness mitigation.
AI.result: For Gemini, Korean agreement exceeds English by 24.8 points (Holm-adjusted p = .0039), but only for neutral and headstrong buyers, since cooperative buyers are near ceiling in both languages. Opening offers barely differ, and the gap comes from larger seller concessions and lower agreed prices in Korean. Qwen3.7 Flash shows a directionally similar gap of +13.9 points with an interval whose lower bound is near zero, and Korean dialogue uses more politeness mitigation, especially from sellers (11.7% vs. 3.6%).
AI.conclusion: Changing only the interaction language can change simulated negotiation behavior, not just wording, so social-policy prompts need cross-lingual validation.

title: GAVAGAI: Referential Alignment for Infant-Scale Vision-Language Models via Balanced Optimal Transport
comment: Accepted in NeuriPs 2026 workshop "The BabyVLM Workshop Toward Developmentally Plausible Multimodal Systems"
summary: A child learns which words name which things from roughly 100 million words of input. Vision-language models trained at a comparable scale bind words to referents far less reliably, and we argue that part of the gap is structural: the usual next-token captioning objective has no variable standing for "this word refers to that region," so training applies no direct pressure to ground words. We add such a variable by treating each scene as a small assignment problem between the content words heard and the regions seen, solved as entropic optimal transport under two constraints. First, a word may be assigned to a special NOTHING column instead of any region, which matters because most content words in caregiver speech do not name anything visible. Second, no region may receive more than a bounded share of the assignment mass, a capacity constraint that encodes mutual exclusivity. The alignment step costs about eight Sinkhorn iterations, small next to the vision encoder. In controlled simulation, the naive version of the idea, a row-wise softmax that forces every word onto some region, collapses to 0.000 word-to-picture accuracy under realistic non-reference rates, below the 0.058 of captioning alone, while our two constraints reach 0.075 in that regime and 0.700 on clean input. A one-parameter version of the model reproduces adult cross-situational learning accuracy across three ambiguity conditions (RMSE 0.024). On the SAYCam infant video corpus, adding the alignment loss to a next-token captioning model raises word-to-picture accuracy from 32.4% to 48.7% and localization IoU from 0.18 to 0.38. A contrastive model trained on the same child's data remains stronger on its own benchmark, so our claim is that the loss improves a captioning objective under high non-reference rates, not that it sets a new best.

AI.tldr: GAVAGAI adds a word-to-region assignment variable to captioning training, solved with entropic optimal transport that allows a NOTHING column and a capacity bound on regions. On the SAYCam infant video corpus it raises word-to-picture accuracy from 32.4% to 48.7%.
AI.motivation: Vision-language models trained at infant-scale data bind words to referents less reliably than children do, and next-token captioning gives no direct pressure to ground words in regions.
AI.method: Each scene is treated as an assignment problem between heard content words and seen regions, solved with about eight Sinkhorn iterations under two constraints: a NOTHING column for words that name nothing visible, and a bound on each region's share of assignment mass that encodes mutual exclusivity. A naive row-wise softmax variant is also evaluated.

A one-parameter version reproduces adult cross-situational learning accuracy (RMSE 0.024). On SAYCam, adding the alignment loss to captioning raises word-to-picture accuracy from 32.4% to 48.7% and localization IoU from 0.18 to 0.38, though a contrastive model trained on the same child's data remains stronger on its own benchmark.
AI.conclusion: The alignment loss improves a captioning objective under high non-reference rates, but the paper does not claim a new best result.

title: Queering the Audits: Community-Based Auditing of AI Harms to Queer Communities
comment: Published in Identity Aware AI workshop at LREC 2026
summary: AI systems embed majority-group defaults into training data, evaluation metrics, and category definitions, producing documented harms for queer communities including erasure, misclassification, and discrimination. Standard technical audits often rely on aggregate measures and cannot detect harms that be come visible only through the lived experience of affected communities. We conducted a participatory auditing workshop at EurIPS 2025 where 16 queer community members audited four case studies using the 4Cs harm taxonomy (Content, Conduct, Contact, Contract) applied across the AI lifecycle. Participants used structured worksheets and plenary synthesis to classify harms and trace them to their origins in the development pipeline. Across all four cases, participants traced harms to problem definition and data collection, and they identified contractual structures that extract value from vulnerable populations while providing minimal recourse. These findings illustrate that community-informed auditing surfaces concrete, identity-specific harms that aggregate evaluation methods risk overlooking.

AI.tldr: A participatory auditing workshop at EurIPS 2025 had 16 queer community members audit four AI case studies with the 4Cs harm taxonomy. Participants traced harms to problem definition and data collection, and identified contracts that extract value while offering minimal recourse.
AI.motivation: Standard technical audits rely on aggregate measures and miss harms to queer communities that become visible only through lived experience.
AI.method: Community members used structured worksheets and plenary synthesis to classify harms (Content, Conduct, Contact, Contract) across the AI lifecycle and trace them to their origins in the development pipeline.
