AI.result: Across all four cases, participants traced harms to problem definition and data collection, and identified contractual structures that extract value from vulnerable populations while providing minimal recourse.
AI.conclusion: Community-informed auditing surfaces concrete, identity-specific harms that aggregate evaluation methods risk overlooking.

title: Cross-Prompt Reuse of Entity-Replacement Responses
summary: With model weights fixed, we measure how much of an entity-replacement response transfers between English factual questions, beyond whether answers change. We add the hidden-state change from two source questions to a target question about the same entity, comparing the predicted log-probability shift between two relations' published answers, given known answer prefixes, with the measured one. Hidden reuse injects the aligned change at 50% depth before the target's remaining layers; direct reuse adds source output-score changes. With other-relation sources, hidden reuse removes 45% and 49% of no-change error on 0.5-1B Qwen and Llama. Gemma-2-2B removes 22% and passes one of three comparisons in plain text without its default beginning-of-sequence (BOS) token. A later protocol restoring it yields 58-68%, passing every comparison on three cohorts. Larger checkpoints, chat format and new entities show replication and format- or cohort-dependent failures. On small plain-format checkpoints, other-relation hidden reuse mainly reproduces the shift both relations' questions share, without reliably lowering relation-selective error. With target-relation sources, hidden reuse's post hoc advantage over direct reuse is 0.2-0.9 nats outside chat format, unconfirmed and not replacement-specific. The same relation-neutral change at both questions' entity tokens lowers relation-selective error more than random or other-replacement changes, indicating receiving-question dependence.

AI.tldr: With model weights fixed, the paper measures how much of an entity-replacement response transfers between English factual questions, by adding hidden-state or output-score changes from source questions to a target question about the same entity. With other-relation sources, hidden reuse removes 45% and 49% of no-change error on 0.5-1B Qwen and Llama, but on small plain-format checkpoints this mainly reproduces the shift both relations share.
AI.motivation: It was unclear whether an answer change induced by entity replacement transfers to other questions about the same entity, beyond whether answers change at all.
AI.method: The hidden-state change from two source questions is added at 50% depth before the target's remaining layers (hidden reuse), compared with direct reuse, which adds source output-score changes. Effects are scored as the predicted log-probability shift between two relations' published answers, given known answer prefixes, compared with the measured shift.
AI.result: With other-relation sources, hidden reuse removes 45% and 49% of no-change error on 0.5-1B Qwen and Llama, and 22% on Gemma-2-2B without its default BOS token, rising to 58-68% under a later protocol that restores it. Larger checkpoints, chat format and new entities show replication and format- or cohort-dependent failures. With target-relation sources, hidden reuse's advantage over direct reuse is 0.2-0.9 nats outside chat format, but it is unconfirmed and not replacement-specific. A relation-neutral change at both entity tokens lowers relation-selective error more than random or other-replacement changes.
AI.conclusion: Transfer depends on the receiving question; on small plain-format checkpoints hidden reuse mainly carries shared shift rather than reliable relation-selective correction.

title: Humanized but Still True? Auditing Facts and Detection in AI-Text Humanizers
comment: 11 pages, 2 figures, 4 tables. Code and data: this https URL
summary: AI "humanizers" rewrite machine-generated text so that detectors classify it as human-written. Public leaderboards score evasion and embedding similarity, but not whether checkable details survive. We check whether numbers, dates, person and organization names, and quoted spans survive each rewrite, using a rule-based checker validated by two AI annotators (precision 0.84-1.00, recall 0.93-0.95; no human annotation). In the October 2026 cycle of a public humanizer leaderboard, all 11 commercial tools changed or dropped at least one of these units in 35-65% of the documents that contained one. Most changes were to quoted spans; counting numbers and names alone, 10 of the 11 tools still altered at least one in 20% or more of the documents. The September 2026 cycle was similar (19-50%). An open 12B humanizer kept at least 97% of numbers and names in fact-dense U.S. federal agency text, but reworded 67-78% of the quoted spans, against its own prompt. Unit retention and detector evasion were not clearly related across tools (Spearman rho = -0.46, 95% CI -0.65 to 0.08), and the open model's four released files (two of them quantization-aware low-bit files) did not show the pre-registered monotone trade-off. On federal texts with matched human, AI-styled and humanized versions, a general-purpose decision model, Jev, asked a single zero-shot question, separated human originals from humanized rewrites with AUROC 0.864 (0.827-0.902), 0.18-0.22 higher than Binoculars, Fast-DetectGPT and the adversarially trained RADAR, while calling 24% of the human originals AI at a 0.5 threshold. On the AI-styled rewrites by 2026 models, both perplexity-based detectors scored below chance (AUROC 0.37 and 0.39), also with line breaks removed. Hypotheses, data rules and analyses were frozen before the main runs; two earlier data contacts are disclosed. We release the checker and the per-item results.

AI.tldr: The paper audits whether AI-text humanizers keep checkable details such as numbers, dates, names and quotes, and whether detectors still flag humanized text. Across 11 commercial tools, at least one such unit changes in 35-65% of documents that contain one, and a general-purpose decision model, Jev, separates human originals from humanized rewrites with AUROC 0.864.
AI.motivation: Public humanizer leaderboards score detector evasion and embedding similarity but not whether verifiable details survive the rewrite.
AI.method: A rule-based checker, validated by two AI annotators, checks whether numbers, dates, person and organization names, and quoted spans survive each rewrite. Matched human, AI-styled and humanized federal-agency texts are used to test Jev, asked one zero-shot question, against Binoculars, Fast-DetectGPT and RADAR. Hypotheses, data rules and analyses were frozen before the main runs.
AI.result: In the October 2026 cycle all 11 commercial tools changed or dropped at least one unit in 35-65% of documents that contained one, mostly quoted spans; the September cycle showed 19-50%. An open 12B humanizer kept at least 97% of numbers and names in federal agency text but reworded 67-78% of quoted spans. Jev reaches AUROC 0.864, 0.18-0.22 higher than the baselines, while labeling 24% of human originals as AI at a 0.5 threshold. On AI-styled rewrites by 2026 models, both perplexity-based detectors score below chance (AUROC 0.37 and 0.39).
AI.conclusion: Humanizers often alter checkable facts, and detector evasion and fact retention are not clearly related across tools, so humanized text should be evaluated on both.

title: Circuit Oracle: Automating Attribution Graph Analysis via Natural-Language Queries
comment: Extended version of a paper presented at the Mechanistic Interpretability and Compositional Learning workshops at ICML 2026
summary: Attribution graphs, an emerging tool in mechanistic interpretability, use transcoders to decompose language model computations into sparse interpretable features connected by causal edges. However, turning a graph into a safety-relevant insight requires hours of manual analysis by experts. We introduce Circuit Oracle, an off-the-shelf LLM equipped with a multi-agent harness and task-specific authored skills, which answers natural-language questions about a target model by reading the attribution graph through tool calls. We evaluate it on three safety-relevant proxy tasks: detecting spurious features in probe circuits, eliciting hidden knowledge from taboo-finetuned models, and suppression jailbreaking via feature-level interventions. Beyond task scores, the oracle produces pruned subgraphs and context-specific feature explanations that we assess qualitatively. Results are mixed. On spurious-feature detection, Circuit Oracle reaches 78.2 $\pm$ 2.4% accuracy, outperforming single-layer feature-ranking baselines. On secret elicitation, trained self-explainers like Activation Oracles remain the stronger baseline. On refusal suppression over 50 prompts, its single committed intervention is slightly below a diff-in-means baseline, and only exceeds it when allowed the best of five attempts. Results are stable across five runs and across model choices for the agents. We also release the pruned subgraphs and context-specific feature readings that revise existing global labels, and invite future work to develop evaluations that can measure their usefulness directly.

AI.tldr: Circuit Oracle is an off-the-shelf LLM with a multi-agent harness and authored skills that answers natural-language questions by reading attribution graphs through tool calls. It reaches 78.2 ± 2.4% accuracy on spurious-feature detection, but its results on the other two safety-relevant proxy tasks are mixed.
AI.motivation: Turning an attribution graph into a safety-relevant insight takes hours of expert manual analysis.
AI.method: The LLM reads the attribution graph through tool calls and is evaluated on spurious-feature detection in probe circuits, secret elicitation from taboo-finetuned models and refusal suppression via feature-level interventions. It also produces pruned subgraphs and context-specific feature explanations.
AI.result: On spurious-feature detection it reaches 78.2 ± 2.4% accuracy, above single-layer feature-ranking baselines. On secret elicitation, trained self-explainers such as Activation Oracles remain stronger. On refusal suppression over 50 prompts, its single committed intervention is slightly below a diff-in-means baseline and exceeds it only when allowed the best of five attempts. Results are stable across five runs and across agent model choices.
AI.conclusion: The approach is a useful but mixed tool for interpretability analysis, and the paper invites evaluations that measure the usefulness of its subgraphs and feature readings directly.

title: Fidelity Collapses with Table Size, Not Turn Count: Delivery Architecture in a Deployed Tool-Using Agent
comment: Non-archival paper at the Second Workshop for Research on Agent Language Models (REALM) at EMNLP 2026. 21 pages, 5 figures
summary: When a multi-turn agent delivers a tool's structured records into the model's context and re-emits them each turn, every turn can corrupt data the tool computed correctly. We measure this in a production award-travel agent: two architectures over identical frozen payloads, lineage-matched prompts and sampling, differing only in delivery architecture. SYNTHESIS feeds full record sets into the planner's context and answers follow-ups in-head; BYPASS, the deployed system, keeps records in session state, translates follow-ups into arguments for a deterministic filter, and delivers rows over a typed side channel. Across 24 dialogues (339 scored turns per condition), BYPASS scores 92.3% of turns fully correct, SYNTHESIS 45.7% (paired gap +46.6pp [+35.7, +57.1]). Varying delivered-table size by capture date, SYNTHESIS collapses from near-perfect at 10 rows or fewer to 8% or less beyond about 74 rows. On a content-controlled prefix ladder the collapse threshold orders by model capability, from under 10 rows (GPT-4o-mini) to about 198 or more (Gemini 2.5 Pro), while BYPASS stays size-flat for all four models. The collapse is expensive: beyond 100 rows, where almost no SYNTHESIS answer is correct, each correct one costs roughly 200x BYPASS's flat \$0.012. Practitioners converged on typed side-channel delivery for rendering, not correctness; we show it was, unknowingly, also a correctness decision.

AI.tldr: In a deployed award-travel agent, feeding full tool-returned record sets back into the planner's context makes answers collapse as table size grows, while a typed side channel with deterministic filtering stays correct. Across 24 dialogues, BYPASS scores 92.3% of turns fully correct against 45.7% for SYNTHESIS.
AI.motivation: Multi-turn agents that re-emit structured tool records each turn can corrupt data the tool computed correctly, but the effect of delivery architecture on correctness had not been isolated.
AI.method: Two architectures run over identical frozen payloads with lineage-matched prompts and sampling. SYNTHESIS puts full record sets in the planner's context and answers follow-ups in-head. BYPASS, the deployed system, keeps records in session state, translates follow-ups into arguments for a deterministic filter, and delivers rows over a typed side channel.
AI.result: BYPASS scores 92.3% of 339 scored turns fully correct against 45.7% for SYNTHESIS (paired gap +46.6 points, interval +35.7 to +57.1). SYNTHESIS falls from near-perfect at 10 rows or fewer to 8% or less beyond about 74 rows. The collapse threshold orders by model capability, from under 10 rows (GPT-4o-mini) to about 198 or more (Gemini 2.5 Pro), while BYPASS stays flat across table size for all four models. Beyond 100 rows, each correct SYNTHESIS answer costs roughly 200 times BYPASS's flat cost of 0.012 USD.
AI.conclusion: Delivery architecture determines correctness as well as rendering, so typed side-channel delivery was also a correctness decision.

title: From Lookups to Lessons: Turning Retrieved Knowledge into Parametric Memory
summary: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) helps large language models (LLMs) answer factual questions beyond their training data, but it adds storage and inference costs. Distilling previously retrieved information into parametric memories enables reuse without online retrieval. However, training the memory to mimic a retriever rewards accurate independent predictions, which do not necessarily improve the final output quality when combined with the LLM's existing predictions. To address this, we introduce ResMem, in which the LLM reads retrieved text offline to generate teacher targets. This design avoids storing massive token representations, unlike existing parametric memory approaches such as MLP Memory, which relies on k-nearest neighbor (kNN) datastores. Furthermore, by using the LLM as an offline teacher that reads privileged retrieved evidence alongside the input, we train a parametric memory to learn an additive logit residual. This residual aligns the predictions of a student sharing the same backbone with the teacher distribution, while self-distillation updates remain confined to the parametric memory. On a Wikipedia subset, ResMem reduces the storage retained for teacher construction by 94.7% compared with the evaluated kNN pipeline. Across five question answering datasets, ResMem raises mean token F1 from 32.83% for the frozen LLM to 34.48%. It also breaks 21% fewer of the LLM's correct answers than a kNN-trained memory. These findings validate our motivation of treating retrieval as a learning resource, with parametric memory shaped by how retrieved knowledge is used to inform the model's future predictions. Code and model weights are available at this https URL and this https URL.

AI.tldr: ResMem distills retrieved knowledge into a parametric memory by having the LLM read retrieved text offline and produce teacher targets, so the memory learns an additive logit residual rather than an independent retriever-matching prediction. It cuts stored teacher-construction data by 94.7% relative to a kNN pipeline and raises mean token F1 from 32.83% to 34.48% across five QA datasets.
AI.motivation: RAG adds storage and inference costs, and training a memory to mimic a retriever rewards accurate independent predictions that do not necessarily improve the LLM's final output.
AI.method: The LLM reads privileged retrieved evidence offline to generate teacher targets, and a parametric memory learns an additive logit residual that aligns a same-backbone student with the teacher distribution. Self-distillation updates are confined to the parametric memory, and the design avoids storing token representations as kNN datastores do.
AI.result: On a Wikipedia subset, ResMem reduces the storage retained for teacher construction by 94.7% relative to the evaluated kNN pipeline. Across five QA datasets, mean token F1 rises from 32.83% for the frozen LLM to 34.48%, and it breaks 21% fewer of the LLM's correct answers than a kNN-trained memory.
AI.conclusion: Treating retrieval as a learning resource, with memory shaped by how retrieved knowledge informs future predictions, gives a cheaper and less disruptive alternative to kNN parametric memory.

title: Steering Readerly Dynamics: Trajectory-Guided Story Generation with Large Language Models
comment: 55 pages, 20 figures, 18 tables, including references and the appendix
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to generate stories, but these stories struggle to reproduce engaging readerly dynamics, the evolving reader responses that shape narrative experience. To address this challenge, we propose a framework that learns readerly dynamics from high-quality human-written stories and uses them to guide story generation. Instead of directly modeling high-dimensional story content, we train a small LLM to predict future reader responses as low-dimensional trajectories. We then leverage the strong instruction-following capability of a larger, off-the-shelf writer LLM to generate story segments that follow these predicted trajectories within a given story setting. Our framework improves trajectory-based fidelity to human-written stories by 12%-35% while largely preserving story coherence.

AI.tldr: The framework learns readerly dynamics from human-written stories, trains a small LLM to predict future reader responses as low-dimensional trajectories, and uses a larger writer LLM to generate story segments that follow them. It improves trajectory-based fidelity to human-written stories by 12%-35% while largely preserving coherence.
AI.motivation: LLM-generated stories struggle to reproduce the evolving reader responses that make narratives engaging.
AI.method: Instead of modeling high-dimensional story content directly, a small LLM predicts future reader responses as low-dimensional trajectories, and an off-the-shelf instruction-following writer LLM generates story segments that follow the predicted trajectories within a given story setting.
AI.result: The framework improves trajectory-based fidelity to human-written stories by 12%-35% while largely preserving story coherence.
AI.conclusion: Predicting reader-response trajectories offers a way to steer story generation toward human-like readerly dynamics while keeping coherence.

title: Spotting the Artificial: Dialogic Humor Improvisation in Humans and LLMs
summary: We propose a methodology for investigating the differences between natural and synthetic language in a challenging setting: humorous improvisational dialogue. Our experimental setting compares human-produced comedy improvisations with the dialogues generated by LLMs in a multi-agent environment that we designed. The analysis combines automated linguistic measures with manual annotation grounded in Systemic Functional Linguistics (SFL). The results show that, although LLMs can create coherent and creative scenes, they often fail to reproduce key characteristics of spontaneous spoken interaction. In addition, LLM-generated interactions display a strong tendency toward politeness and positive evaluations, contrasting with the broader range of attitudes found in human humorous improvisation. Our evidence highlights both the strengths and limitations of current LLMs in modeling dialogic humor and demonstrate the value of integrating linguistic theory with NLP methods for the analysis of machine-generated language

AI.tldr: The paper compares human improvised humorous dialogue with LLM-generated dialogue from a designed multi-agent setup, using automated linguistic measures and manual annotation grounded in Systemic Functional Linguistics. LLM scenes are coherent and creative but lack key features of spontaneous spoken interaction and skew toward politeness and positive evaluation.
AI.motivation: It is unclear how natural and synthetic language differ in a demanding setting such as humorous improvisation, and how to analyze that difference with linguistic theory.
AI.method: Human comedy improvisations are compared with dialogues generated by LLMs in a multi-agent environment the authors designed. The analysis combines automated linguistic measures with manual annotation grounded in Systemic Functional Linguistics.
AI.result: Although LLMs create coherent and creative scenes, they often fail to reproduce key characteristics of spontaneous spoken interaction. LLM interactions show a strong tendency toward politeness and positive evaluations, whereas human humorous improvisation displays a broader range of attitudes.
AI.conclusion: Current LLMs have both strengths and limits in modeling dialogic humor, and integrating linguistic theory with NLP methods is valuable for analyzing machine-generated language.

title: AStockArena: Beyond Returns, Can We Entrust Real Capital to the Decisions of Financial Agents?
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used in dynamic financial trading, yet real-time trading benchmarks mainly evaluate agents by cumulative returns and risk-adjusted performance. Such outcome metrics cannot show whether trades are faithfully reported, supported by available evidence, and consistent with account states. We introduce AStockArena, a real-time decision-auditing benchmark for continuous trading in China's A-share market. Under shared market conditions and execution constraints, we evaluate 13 open- and closed-source models over 3,198 sequential decisions. AStockArena reconstructsthe actions actually posted to accounts by aligning reports, trade requests, execution responses, and account states, and audits them with eight checks spanning execution traceability (O), evidence sufficiency (RK), and financial meta-awareness (B), combining record verification with consensus expert annotation. Of 1,070 trading points, 72.99% exhibit at least one audit gap; model-level rates range from52.2% to 91.2%, with evidence gaps most prevalent. Historical trade-filtering replay further shows thatportfolio outcomes are sensitive to these flagged trades. Decision-process auditing thus offers a verifiable complement to return-based evaluation of financial agents.

AI.tldr: AStockArena is a real-time decision-auditing benchmark for continuous trading in China's A-share market that reconstructs the actions actually posted to accounts and audits them with eight checks. Of 1,070 trading points across 13 models, 72.99% show at least one audit gap.
AI.motivation: Return-based benchmarks cannot show whether trades are faithfully reported, supported by available evidence, and consistent with account states.
AI.method: Under shared market conditions and execution constraints, 13 open and closed models make 3,198 sequential decisions. Actions are reconstructed by aligning reports, trade requests, execution responses and account states, then audited with eight checks spanning execution traceability (O), evidence sufficiency (RK) and financial meta-awareness (B), combining record verification with consensus expert annotation. Historical trade-filtering replay tests how sensitive portfolio outcomes are to flagged trades.
AI.result: 72.99% of 1,070 trading points exhibit at least one audit gap. Model-level rates range from 52.2% to 91.2%, with evidence gaps most prevalent. In historical replay, portfolio outcomes are sensitive to the flagged trades.
AI.conclusion: Decision-process auditing offers a verifiable complement to return-based evaluation of financial agents.

title: Dual-Axis Policy Entailment: A Benchmark for Policy-Change Reasoning
summary: Whether a policy shifts domains and, by extension, continues, broadens, narrows, or reverses previous policy is of paramount importance to the study of public policy. We propose Dual-Axis Policy Entailment (DAPE), which evaluates an ordered pair of policy directives on both dimensions at once: a binary judgment determines whether the two directives govern the same policy domain, and a five-way judgment determines whether the later directive continues, broadens, narrows, or reverses the earlier policy, or governs a different domain altogether. Read together, the two judgments form one five-category label, our primary metric. The two-axis design captures two central dimensions of policy change without conflating errors on either dimension into a generic "irrelevant" label, and it makes annotation more rigorous: a coder cannot dismiss a difficult pair as domain-irrelevant without an explicit, checkable decision. We introduce an expert-annotated benchmark of 1,000 ordered directive pairs drawn from a large corpus of Chinese government policy, together with an annotation-calibration protocol (an adjudication packet with pre/post agreement measurement) that we contribute as a methodological artifact. Fourteen open-weight models and four frontier API flagships fail the task zero-shot: even the best frontier flagship's chance-corrected agreement with expert labels is far below the human ceiling (Cohen's $\kappa \approx 0.29$ vs. $0.53$). A fine-tuned open-weight model (LoRA SFT of Qwen3-14B, five-fold cross-validation) closes this gap, reaching the coder-mutual human ceiling ($\kappa = 0.524$ vs. $0.527$). Finally, we apply our method to China's AI policy (1980-2024) and map the direction of policy change across eras.

AI.tldr: Dual-Axis Policy Entailment (DAPE) is a benchmark for policy-change reasoning that asks whether two ordered policy directives share a domain and how the later one relates to the earlier, combined into a five-way label. A LoRA-fine-tuned Qwen3-14B reaches the human coder ceiling (kappa 0.524 vs. 0.527), while the best zero-shot frontier flagship reaches about 0.29.
AI.motivation: Whether a policy shifts domains and whether it continues, broadens, narrows or reverses earlier policy both matter for public policy study, and a single generic irrelevant label would conflate domain mismatch with unrelatedness.
AI.method: A binary domain judgment and a five-way judgment are combined into one primary label. A 1,000-pair expert-annotated benchmark is drawn from Chinese government policy, with an annotation-calibration protocol using adjudication and pre/post agreement measurement. Fourteen open-weight and four frontier API models are evaluated zero-shot, and Qwen3-14B is fine-tuned with LoRA under five-fold cross-validation.
AI.result: Zero-shot models fail: the best frontier flagship reaches Cohen's kappa of about 0.29 against expert labels, far below the human ceiling of 0.53. LoRA fine-tuning of Qwen3-14B reaches kappa 0.524 against a coder-mutual ceiling of 0.527. The method is applied to China's AI policy from 1980 to 2024 to map the direction of policy change across eras.
AI.conclusion: Policy-change reasoning remains hard zero-shot, but a fine-tuned model matches human agreement, and the benchmark and calibration protocol are contributed as methodological artifacts.

title: Distinguishing among reasoning levels of GPT 5.5 Pro via a grammar lens benchmark
summary: Does the level of test-time processing effort affect a language model's computational capability? A formal grammar-lens benchmark method, derived from the theory of computation, generates novel data at specified levels, each successively more computationally powerful than the levels below. Using this data, we tested GPT-5.5, and GPT-5.5-Pro-Medium, -High, and -XHigh, showing incrementally increased acceptance of test data: 16, 40, 43, and 52\%, respectively, illustrating the benchmark's ability to discern fine-grained differences among models' added test-time reasoning levels. Additionally, as test-time compute effort increases, model responses diverge from human responses to the same data. This increasing disagreement may turn out to be broadly characteristic of more capable language models, introducing the potential of a general capability-versus-alignment conflict.

AI.tldr: A grammar-lens benchmark derived from the theory of computation generates novel data at successively more computationally powerful levels and is used to test GPT-5.5 and its Pro variants at increasing test-time effort. Acceptance rises from 16% to 52% across the levels, and model responses diverge further from human responses as effort increases.
AI.motivation: It is unclear whether more test-time processing effort increases a language model's computational capability, and whether that gain aligns with human judgments.
AI.method: Novel test data are generated from formal grammars at specified levels, each more powerful than the one below. GPT-5.5 and GPT-5.5-Pro at Medium, High and XHigh effort are evaluated on this data and compared with human responses to the same items.
AI.result: Acceptance of test data increases incrementally: 16%, 40%, 43% and 52% for GPT-5.5, GPT-5.5-Pro-Medium, -High and -XHigh respectively. As test-time effort increases, model responses diverge from human responses to the same data.
AI.conclusion: The benchmark distinguishes fine-grained reasoning levels, and the growing disagreement with humans may signal a broader capability-versus-alignment conflict in more capable models.

title: From Apparent Search Gains to Selection Failures: Auditing Test-Time Inference in Structured Workflow Planning
comment: 37 pages. Code and reproducibility artifacts: this https URL
summary: Test-time search can improve structured planning, but when methods differ in prompts, post-processing, and selection, it is unclear what an observed gain should be attributed to. We study this question on DisasterBench, where models compose typed multi-tool workflows, by decomposing inference into three observable stages: whether a correct workflow is discovered, whether it survives structural validation, and whether it is finally selected. Comparing independent sampling, a nominal tree-search configuration, and multi-operator search under controlled inference budgets on two model families, we find that (i) the nominal tree-search configuration realizes non-adaptive complete-workflow sampling, and independent sampling with its expansion prompt reproduces its candidate discovery without constructing a tree; (ii) structural validation never removes the last correct workflow in our evaluated candidate pools, whereas majority voting leaves a discovered correct workflow unselected on 10-19% of tasks per pool, with an audit confirming substantive tool-choice or information-flow errors in 57 of 60 examined cases; and (iii) a tool-specification-aware verifier recovers some of these losses but overturns more correct decisions than it fixes. Our results motivate auditing realized rather than nominal inference pipelines, and reporting discovery, validity, and selection separately.

AI.tldr: On DisasterBench structured workflow planning, the paper decomposes test-time inference into discovery, structural validity and final selection. It finds that the nominal tree-search configuration is effectively non-adaptive sampling, and that majority voting leaves a discovered correct workflow unselected on 10-19% of tasks per pool.
AI.motivation: When test-time search methods differ in prompts, post-processing and selection, it is unclear what an observed gain should be attributed to.
AI.method: Independent sampling, a nominal tree-search configuration and multi-operator search are compared under controlled inference budgets on two model families. Each run is decomposed into whether a correct workflow is discovered, whether it survives structural validation and whether it is finally selected. A tool-specification-aware verifier is also tested, and an audit examines 60 cases.
AI.result: The tree-search configuration realizes non-adaptive complete-workflow sampling, and independent sampling with its expansion prompt reproduces its candidate discovery. Structural validation never removes the last correct workflow in the evaluated pools, while majority voting leaves a discovered correct workflow unselected on 10-19% of tasks per pool. The audit confirms substantive tool-choice or information-flow errors in 57 of 60 examined cases. The verifier recovers some losses but overturns more correct decisions than it fixes.
AI.conclusion: Inference pipelines should be audited by their realized behavior rather than nominal design, and discovery, validity and selection should be reported separately.

title: Saidzoda-Tajik-E5-Large: Fine-Tuning a 560M Embedder for Tajik Retrieval
comment: 10 pages, 5 tables, 1 figure. Technical report. Model: this https URL
summary: Finding the passage that answers a question is the first step of most practical systems built on documents, and for Tajik we found no openly described model for it. We present Saidzoda-Tajik-E5-Large, a Tajik text embedder built from multilingual-e5-large-instruct (560M parameters). We asked our own Tajik language model to write questions for passages from Tajik laws, tax documents, Wikipedia and web text, and trained on 235,140 question and passage pairs for one epoch, with hard negatives chosen by another embedder and English and Russian pairs mixed in so the model would not forget those languages. On laws the model had never seen, the right passage is among the top ten results for 93.6% of questions, up from 80.2%; on tax documents, 94.5% against 82.6%. On Belebele, the one test we have that was written by people, the gain is smaller and not confirmed (92.2% to 95.2%, with touching intervals), and Russian and English do not change. On law and tax questions written in the same style as its training questions, it is tied with Giga-Embeddings-3B, a model five times its size; on Belebele the 3B and 8B models score slightly higher, and only after we fine-tuned them on our data are they clearly ahead. We also report what failed: training in bfloat16 broke the model, and replacing Tajik letters with similar Russian ones did not help. Our law, tax and Wikipedia test questions come from the same model that wrote the training questions, so we treat those scores as an upper limit until questions written by Tajik speakers are available.

AI.tldr: The paper fine-tunes multilingual-e5-large-instruct (560M parameters) into a Tajik passage embedder trained on 235,140 question-passage pairs. On questions about unseen laws the right passage is in the top ten for 93.6% of questions, up from 80.2%, while the Belebele gain is smaller and unconfirmed.
AI.motivation: No openly described embedding model for Tajik retrieval existed.
AI.method: Questions for Tajik laws, tax documents, Wikipedia and web text are written by the authors' own Tajik language model. The embedder is trained for one epoch with hard negatives chosen by another embedder, with English and Russian pairs mixed in so those languages are not forgotten.
AI.result: On unseen laws, top-ten accuracy rises from 80.2% to 93.6%, and on tax documents from 82.6% to 94.5%. On Belebele, the gain is smaller and not confirmed (92.2% to 95.2%, with touching intervals), and Russian and English do not change. On questions written in the training style, the model ties with Giga-Embeddings-3B, which is five times its size. Training in bfloat16 broke the model. The test questions come from the same model that wrote the training questions, so the scores are treated as an upper limit.
AI.conclusion: The model is a useful Tajik retriever on in-style questions, but its gains on human-written data remain unconfirmed until Tajik speakers write test questions.

title: Multi-Estimate Elicitation Does Not Uniformly Debias Language Model Judgments
summary: Does eliciting five weighted estimates within a single response change how a language model responds to information? Across anchoring, hindsight, base-rate, conjunction, and status-quo/default tasks, we compare direct numerical answers with a multi-estimate response format, contrasting source framings, explicitly random cues, and probability-consistency constraints. We evaluate three completed configurations--gpt-6.1-sol, claude-sonnet-5.5, and Qwen3-8B (reasoning disabled, analyzed descriptively). In the first two configurations, direct elicitation yielded near-zero irrelevant-anchor indices and status-quo effects, while remaining responsive to informative sources and informed advice. Of 23 preregistered confirmatory tests, six rejected after Holm adjustment; however, all six absolute point estimates fell below their prespecified smallest effect sizes of interest without establishing equivalence. Moreover, while separate versus joint elicitation shifted conjunction judgments, interpretation is constrained by between-call noise. Ultimately, multi-estimate elicitation failed to produce uniform debiasing or response attenuation across tasks and models, though post hoc correlations between candidate spread and anchoring error motivate independent predictive validation. Materials: this https URL

AI.tldr: Eliciting five weighted estimates within one response does not uniformly debias LLM judgments across anchoring, hindsight, base-rate, conjunction and status-quo tasks. Six of 23 preregistered tests reject after Holm adjustment, but all six absolute point estimates fall below their smallest effect sizes of interest.
AI.motivation: Multi-estimate response formats might reduce biases such as anchoring, but whether they change how models respond to information was unknown.
AI.method: Direct numerical answers are compared with a multi-estimate format across five task families, with source framings, explicitly random cues and probability-consistency constraints. Two configurations, gpt-6.1-sol and claude-sonnet-5.5, are analyzed in full, and Qwen3-8B with reasoning disabled is analyzed descriptively.
AI.result: In the first two configurations, direct elicitation yields near-zero irrelevant-anchor indices and status-quo effects while remaining responsive to informative sources and informed advice. Of 23 preregistered confirmatory tests, six reject after Holm adjustment, but all six absolute point estimates fall below their prespecified smallest effect sizes of interest without establishing equivalence. Separate versus joint elicitation shifts conjunction judgments, but between-call noise constrains interpretation.
AI.conclusion: Multi-estimate elicitation does not produce uniform debiasing or response attenuation across tasks and models, and the post hoc link between candidate spread and anchoring error needs independent predictive validation.

title: Enhancing Language Model Reasoning with Structured Multi-Level Modeling
summary: Inference-time scaling enhances a model's reasoning by extending its chain-of-thought (CoT). However, existing approaches typically rely on a single policy trained with outcome-reward reinforcement learning (RL), which often suffers from long-horizon plan failures where the implicit plan drifts from valid strategies, especially for small LMs with limited capacity. To address this, we propose Multi-Level Reasoning (MLR), which reformulates long-CoT generation as a two-level stochastic process. A high-level planner generates structured step descriptors specifying both the reasoning mode and the semantic subgoal. The low-level executor then produces detailed reasoning conditioned on these descriptors, forming an alternating plan--execute loop. To maintain scalability, we adopt a minimal design where the base model serves as the low-level policy and a lightweight LoRA module implements the high-level policy. For training, we observe that outcome-reward RL provides sparse and delayed feedback for long trajectories (e.g., several thousand tokens), hindering credit assignment. We therefore introduce iterative Step-DPO, a process-level preference optimization scheme that leverages Twisted Sequential Monte Carlo (TSMC) to provide scalable stepwise supervision. This yields more effective training, improved stability, and higher accuracy. Extensive experiments on challenging math, science, and logical reasoning benchmarks show that, under the same reduced data budget (10% SFT and 5% preference relative to the DeepSeek-R1 distillation setup), MLR outperforms both SFT-based distillation and strong RL/preference-optimization baselines across multiple base models and tasks. Moreover, MLR exhibits slower performance degradation on long-horizon reasoning, demonstrating stronger robustness under extended CoT generation.

AI.tldr: Multi-Level Reasoning (MLR) splits long chain-of-thought generation into a high-level planner that emits structured step descriptors and a low-level executor that reasons under them. With iterative Step-DPO, a process-level preference method using Twisted Sequential Monte Carlo for stepwise supervision, it outperforms SFT distillation and RL baselines under a reduced data budget and degrades more slowly on long reasoning.
AI.motivation: Single-policy outcome-reward RL suffers from long-horizon plan drift in small LMs, and sparse, delayed feedback over several thousand tokens hinders credit assignment.
AI.method: A high-level planner generates structured step descriptors specifying reasoning mode and semantic subgoal, forming an alternating plan-execute loop. The base model serves as the low-level policy, and a lightweight LoRA module implements the high-level policy. Training uses iterative Step-DPO with Twisted Sequential Monte Carlo for scalable stepwise supervision.
AI.result: Under 10% SFT and 5% preference data relative to the DeepSeek-R1 distillation setup, MLR outperforms SFT distillation and strong RL and preference-optimization baselines across multiple base models and tasks in math, science and logical reasoning. It shows slower performance degradation on long-horizon reasoning.
AI.conclusion: Structured two-level planning with process-level preference training improves the accuracy and robustness of small reasoning models under extended chain-of-thought generation.

title: ElectroChemLLM: A Multimodal LLM Pipeline for High-Fidelity Electrochemical Informatics
summary: Electrochemistry is central to solving many modern-day challenges, including energy storage systems for a sustainable future, and its advancement relies heavily on the data from past findings. Existing automated pipelines are limited by text-only architectures, context fragmentation, and numerical hallucinations - collectively preventing accurate, large-scale curation of property databases. We introduce ElectrochemLLM, a multimodal information extraction pipeline that jointly identifies structured electrochemical records encompassing electrolyte compositions, electrode materials, cell configurations, and their measured physicochemical properties from unstructured scientific PDFs at scale. By combining hybrid document parsing with vision-capable LLM orchestration, the pipeline extracts verifiable, structured data across text, tables, and figures. Evaluated on the battery-electrolyte subset of our manually annotated benchmark of 232 papers, ElectrochemLLM achieves an F-1 score of 0.97, and has been applied to curate ElectroChemDB, a structured database spanning 15,000 electrochemical research articles. We demonstrate the utility of this resource by training machine learning models for electrolyte property prediction, illustrating a complete pathway from unstructured literature to predictive materials discovery.

AI.tldr: ElectrochemLLM is a multimodal LLM pipeline that extracts structured electrochemical records from scientific PDFs by combining hybrid document parsing with vision-capable LLM orchestration. It achieves an F-1 score of 0.97 on the battery-electrolyte subset of a 232-paper benchmark and has been used to build ElectroChemDB from 15,000 articles.
AI.motivation: Text-only extraction pipelines suffer from context fragmentation and numerical hallucinations, which prevent accurate large-scale curation of electrochemical property databases.
AI.method: Hybrid document parsing is combined with vision-capable LLM orchestration to jointly extract electrolyte compositions, electrode materials, cell configurations and measured properties across text, tables and figures.
AI.result: The F-1 score is 0.97 on the battery-electrolyte subset of a manually annotated benchmark of 232 papers. The pipeline has been applied to curate ElectroChemDB, which spans 15,000 electrochemical research articles, and models trained on it predict electrolyte properties.
AI.conclusion: The pipeline turns unstructured literature into a database that supports predictive materials discovery.

title: Audit at the Precision You Deploy: Quantization Reshapes a Subliminally Learned Preference
summary: Subliminal learning allows AI models to inherit hidden preferences from seemingly unrelated training data, such as number sequences. Safety audits may evaluate models at standard 16-bit precision, while deployments may use compressed, quantized weights. We ask whether quantization changes the expression of a subliminal preference and what drives any resulting change. To investigate, we implant a "favourite animal: panda" preference into Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct. We define its net strength as the difference in mean panda-answer probability between subliminal models and neutrally trained controls under the same quantization setting. Applying this metric across different compression levels reveals a stark contrast. While behaviour remains stable at 8 bits, 4-bit quantization triggers severe, opposing shifts depending on the quantizer. Half-Quadratic Quantization (HQQ) amplifies the preference, raising the subliminally trained model's panda probability from roughly 55% at 16 bits to 64% at 4 bits, while the controls stay near 17%. This raises the trait's net strength ~1.3 times its 16-bit value. In contrast, NormalFloat (NF4) at 4-bit suppresses it, shrinking the net strength to just ~0.3 times its 16-bit value, despite producing rounding errors of the same size to within 4%. We examine the structure of the rounding errors and find that their arrangement drives the divergence. Randomly shuffling HQQ's errors within each quantization group, without changing their magnitude, shifts the trait's net strength between 0.2 and 1.6 times its 16-bit value. Despite these opposing shifts, the underlying fine-tuning signal remains largely intact. Because a model's internal state and outward behaviour diverge so unpredictably under compression, a 16-bit audit cannot reliably bound real-world risks. Safety evaluations must test the exact quantized weights intended for deployment.

AI.tldr: A "favourite animal: panda" preference implanted into Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct is expressed very differently under 4-bit quantization depending on the quantizer: HQQ amplifies it to about 1.3 times its 16-bit net strength, while NF4 suppresses it to about 0.3 times. Safety audits at 16 bits therefore cannot bound the risk of the deployed quantized weights.
AI.motivation: Safety audits typically evaluate models at 16-bit precision, but deployments may use compressed weights, and it is unknown whether quantization changes subliminally learned preferences.
AI.method: The panda preference is implanted by subliminal learning from number sequences. Net strength is the difference in mean panda-answer probability between subliminal models and neutrally trained controls under the same quantization setting. Compression levels are compared, and the structure of rounding errors is examined, including by shuffling HQQ's errors within each quantization group.
AI.result: At 8 bits behavior remains stable. At 4 bits HQQ raises the subliminally trained model's panda probability from about 55% at 16 bits to 64%, while controls stay near 17%, giving a net strength about 1.3 times the 16-bit value. NF4 shrinks net strength to about 0.3 times despite rounding errors of the same size, within 4%. Shuffling HQQ's errors shifts net strength between 0.2 and 1.6 times, and the underlying fine-tuning signal remains largely intact.
AI.conclusion: The arrangement of rounding errors drives the divergence, so a 16-bit audit cannot reliably bound real-world risk, and safety evaluations must test the exact quantized weights intended for deployment.

title: Precedent Labels and Facts Shift LLM Approval Decisions in Opposite Directions
summary: When a language model decides refund or claim requests under written policies, the system can show it similar past cases. Each past case has two parts: its facts and the decision recorded for it. We separate the two. A model sees a policy, a request and three past cases, and we change either the recorded decisions or the facts, keeping the request fixed. We select requests that are close calls: deciding without past cases, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash approved each in some of four tries and denied it in others. When the past cases are near-copies of the request (its facts with a few details changed), switching their recorded decisions from DENY to APPROVE raises approval by about 30 to 55 percentage points in DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, GPT-5.6 Luna and Claude Haiku 5.5 on policies written for the study, and DeepSeek and Luna show the same on nine public policies paraphrased from real ones. The facts push the other way: shown without their recorded decisions, past cases whose facts support approval make these two models approve less often than past cases whose facts support denial. One reading is that the request looks weaker next to them. This push is not just a correction toward the right answer: in an additional DeepSeek analysis, it was of similar estimated size on requests that human annotators judged approvable and on those they judged deniable. In a separate DeepSeek run on the public policies, when the past cases are near-copies of a different request, switching their decisions moves approval by 9 points instead of 43, while facts that support approval still lower it by 22 points against facts that support denial. Systems that retrieve past decisions should test the two parts separately.

AI.tldr: When a model decides refund or claim requests with retrieved past cases, switching the recorded decisions of near-copy past cases shifts approval by about 30 to 55 points, while the facts of those cases push approval the other way. Systems that retrieve past decisions should test the recorded decisions and the facts separately.
AI.motivation: Retrieval-augmented decision systems show past cases that combine facts and recorded decisions, but the separate effects of each part on LLM approval decisions were unknown.
AI.method: A model sees a policy, a request and three past cases, while either the recorded decisions or the facts are varied and the request is held fixed. Close-call requests are selected where DeepSeek V4.1 Flash approved in some of four tries and denied in others. Experiments use study-written policies and nine public policies paraphrased from real ones.
AI.result: With near-copy past cases, switching recorded decisions from DENY to APPROVE raises approval by about 30 to 55 points for DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, GPT-5.6 Luna and Claude Haiku 5.5 on study-written policies, and DeepSeek and Luna show the same on public policies. Facts supporting approval, shown without their decisions, make approval less frequent than facts supporting denial, and this push is of similar estimated size on requests human annotators judged approvable and deniable. On public policies with near-copies of a different request, switching decisions moves approval by 9 points instead of 43, while facts supporting approval still lower it by 22 points against facts supporting denial.
AI.conclusion: The two parts of a precedent have separable and opposite effects on LLM approvals, so retrieval systems should test each part separately.

title: Constructing Budgeted KGW Evasion through Token-Event Evidence Replacement
summary: KGW watermarks bias sampling to accumulate keyed detection evidence. We construct budgeted evasion through token-event evidence replacement using ordinary phrase rewrites. Our construction jointly selects compositions of LLM-proposed alternatives from an independent model and measures global token-edit distance on complete outputs. At the largest attainable cost within the budget, exact coverage search maximizes removal of original scored token pairs. It uses a known tokenizer without the key, detector feedback or queries to the watermarked model. Exact accounting separates source evidence removed, evidence created and length effects, with initial strength setting the required reduction. Separate signed-event analysis found that mean suppression arose mainly from removing watermark-enriched source events. In controlled, occurrence-counted, one-token-context KGW tests on short passages, 39 of 82 qualified, initially detected sources yielded rewrites with terminal detector score Z < 4 that passed blinded source-relative model review, at a mean actual token-edit cost of 16.0% under a 20% allowance. To examine whether this initial requirement can be inferred, a separate historical 95-passage study estimated initial detector score Z0 from generation traces with correlation 0.793 and an in-sample association beyond length. This aggregate information did not establish improved allocation, and the separate no-trace stopping test did not reliably exploit cheaper reviewed crossings in the candidate bank. Comparisons did not establish an advantage over simpler selection and ordinary constrained rewriting. The construction makes budgeted evidence replacement executable while exposing limits in signed reduction and recognition of sufficient editing.

AI.tldr: The paper constructs budgeted evasion of KGW watermarks by replacing token-level detection evidence with ordinary phrase rewrites chosen from LLM-proposed alternatives under a token-edit budget. In controlled short-passage tests, 39 of 82 initially detected sources were rewritten to a terminal detector score below 4 and passed blinded model review, at a mean actual token-edit cost of 16.0% under a 20% allowance.
AI.motivation: Robustness of watermarks to ordinary editing has been studied, but a budgeted construction that targets the specific scored token pairs of KGW watermarks, without the key or detector access, had not been established.
AI.method: Compositions of LLM-proposed alternatives from an independent model are jointly selected, and global token-edit distance is measured on complete outputs. Exact coverage search maximizes removal of original scored token pairs at the largest attainable cost within the budget. Signed-event accounting separates removed source evidence, created evidence and length effects. The approach uses a known tokenizer, without the key, detector feedback or queries to the watermarked model.
AI.result: In controlled, occurrence-counted, one-token-context tests on short passages, 39 of 82 qualified, initially detected sources yielded rewrites with terminal Z below 4 that passed blinded source-relative model review, at a mean actual token-edit cost of 16.0% under a 20% allowance. Mean suppression arose mainly from removing watermark-enriched source events. Estimating initial detector score from generation traces reached correlation 0.793, but this did not establish improved allocation, and comparisons did not establish an advantage over simpler selection or ordinary constrained rewriting.
AI.conclusion: The construction makes budgeted evidence replacement executable and exposes limits in signed reduction and in recognizing sufficient editing.

title: DuSE-Bench: Benchmarking Joint Reasoning over Evolving Dialogue and Documents
summary: Persistent Web information assistants must combine evolving document facts with user requirements established and revised across sessions. Yet systematic evaluation of how changes in both sources affect response requirements and evidence attribution remains limited. To address this gap, we introduce Dual-Source Evolution Benchmark (DuSE-Bench), a benchmark comprising 1,000 tasks across five scenarios, including 700 whose required premises originate in both dialogue and documents. An evolving Support Graph guides task construction and preserves links from updated facts and reused conclusions to original turns and passages. Task annotations distinguish grounding source from state dependence and enable separate evaluation of response content, response type, and source attribution. Experiments across 11 baseline configurations reveal persistent challenges in joint reasoning over evolving dialogue and documents, with content accuracy on jointly grounded tasks reaching at most 56.7%. Moreover, improvements in content accuracy can coincide with poorer response choice, while content-correct responses frequently lack complete attribution to original evidence. Matched evidence substitutions further show that the effect of replacing one source's evidence depends on support from the other. These findings motivate coordinating dialogue memory and document retrieval to apply current user requirements and document facts together while preserving their original support. The data are available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: DuSE-Bench is a benchmark of 1,000 tasks for joint reasoning over evolving dialogue and documents, 700 of which require premises from both sources. Across 11 baseline configurations, content accuracy on jointly grounded tasks reaches at most 56.7%.
AI.motivation: Persistent web information assistants must combine evolving document facts with user requirements revised across sessions, but systematic evaluation of how changes in both sources affect responses and attribution remains limited.
AI.method: An evolving Support Graph guides task construction and links updated facts and reused conclusions to original turns and passages. Annotations distinguish grounding source from state dependence, enabling separate evaluation of response content, response type and source attribution. Matched evidence substitutions test how the effect of replacing one source's evidence depends on support from the other.
AI.result: Across 11 baseline configurations, content accuracy on jointly grounded tasks reaches at most 56.7%. Improvements in content accuracy can coincide with poorer response choice, and content-correct responses often lack complete attribution to original evidence. The effect of replacing one source's evidence depends on support from the other source.
AI.conclusion: Dialogue memory and document retrieval need to be coordinated to apply current user requirements and document facts together while preserving their original support.

title: CheXPoT: Post-Hoc Visual Verification and Correction of VLM-Generated Radiology Reports
summary: Vision-language models (VLMs) have shown promise for chest radiograph report generation, but adoption remains limited because of hallucinated findings that are not grounded in the image. Correcting these hallucinations and improving overall report quality remains a significant challenge. Prior work has addressed this problem by refining models with reinforcement learning, preference optimization, or chain-of-thought supervision, often at substantial compute cost. To address this gap, we introduce CheXPoT, a program-of-thought (PoT) framework that verifies each generated finding against image features and removes those it cannot ground. CheXPoT decomposes generated reports into predicates with RadGraph and an LLM, grounds these predicates against a DenseNet-121 and Grad-CAM visual evidence table, executes PoT verification code, and rewrites reports after removing unsupported predicates. On a 4,145-image held-out split, CheXPoT yields statistically significant precision gains on 8 of 14 CheXpert classes and F1 gains on 5, with no significant decreases in either metric. CheXPoT lifts micro-average precision from 19.2% (MedGemma-4B) to 46.8% (MedGemma-4B + CheXPoT) and micro-average F1 from 23.0% to 49.4%, absolute gains of 27.6% and 26.4% respectively. We also tested CheXPoT on other VLM report generators. On LLaVA-Med, CheXPoT lifts micro-average precision from 4.5% to 17.7% and micro-average F1 from 6.3% to 19.4%. On MAIRA-2, CheXPoT lifts micro-average precision from 15.6% to 42.1% and micro-average F1 from 21.0% to 45.3%. Our results suggest that inexpensive post-hoc visual verification may improve VLM trustworthiness by correcting unsupported findings from generated reports. CheXPoT lays a foundation for tools that help validate VLM-generated radiology reports and reduce unsupported findings. These innovations may subsequently help increase trust and adoption of VLM tools in Medicine.

AI.tldr: CheXPoT is a program-of-thought framework that verifies each finding in a VLM-generated chest radiograph report against image features and removes findings it cannot ground. It lifts micro-average precision for MedGemma-4B from 19.2% to 46.8% and micro-average F1 from 23.0% to 49.4%.
AI.motivation: Hallucinated findings not grounded in the image limit adoption of VLM-generated radiology reports, and existing fixes such as RL refinement, preference optimization or chain-of-thought supervision are costly.
AI.method: Reports are decomposed into predicates with RadGraph and an LLM, which are grounded against a DenseNet-121 and Grad-CAM visual evidence table. PoT verification code is executed, and reports are rewritten after removing unsupported predicates.
AI.result: On a 4,145-image held-out split, CheXPoT yields statistically significant precision gains on 8 of 14 CheXpert classes and F1 gains on 5, with no significant decreases in either metric. Micro-average precision for MedGemma-4B rises from 19.2% to 46.8% and F1 from 23.0% to 49.4%. On LLaVA-Med, precision rises from 4.5% to 17.7% and F1 from 6.3% to 19.4%; on MAIRA-2, from 15.6% to 42.1% and from 21.0% to 45.3%.
AI.conclusion: Inexpensive post-hoc visual verification may improve the trustworthiness of VLM-generated radiology reports by correcting unsupported findings.

title: Steer, Don't Tell: Breaking Reasoning Plateaus with Reachability-Aligned Self-Distillation
summary: Post training for large reasoning models remains insufficient on challenging problems, whose correct trajectories are hard to sample. Though prior works address this difficulty by integrating supervised fine tuning on expert trajectories with reinforcement learning, such external experts are not always available. Existing self improvement methods instead use reference solutions to create a privileged self-teacher. Yet privileged teacher correctness does not imply student reachability. Solution conditioning shifts the teacher distribution toward actions unlikely under the unprivileged student, producing seemingly "correct" trajectories that are unreachable or even mal-formed learning targets. Accordingly, we identify reachability alignment as the key to self constructed supervision and propose Self-Steered Reasoner (SSR). SSR realizes this principle through student support projection, which transforms the privileged teacher distribution into a directional signal only over reasoning actions locally reachable under the unguided student. Verification then retains correct trajectories sampled from this reachable space. To further boost the sampling efficiency, an iterative refinement framework is adopted, using diagnostic guidance based on current trajectories. On problems with pass@64 = 0 even after extensive RL, SSR recovers correct and learnable trajectories for 74.6% without parameter updates. Fine tuning on these trajectories followed by resumed reinforcement learning improves aggregate accuracy by 4.9 percentage points on AIME25/26 and HMMT26. These results show that privileged guidance becomes effective self-improvement data when aligned with the reasoning actions the student can reach.

AI.tldr: Self-Steered Reasoner (SSR) recovers correct and learnable trajectories for 74.6% of problems with pass@64 = 0 even after extensive RL, by projecting the privileged teacher distribution onto reasoning actions the unguided student can reach. Fine-tuning on these trajectories and resuming RL improves aggregate accuracy by 4.9 points on AIME25/26 and HMMT26.
AI.motivation: Self-improvement with privileged reference solutions creates teachers whose correct trajectories are unreachable for the student, because solution conditioning shifts the teacher toward actions the student rarely takes.
AI.method: Student support projection transforms the privileged teacher distribution into a directional signal only over reasoning actions locally reachable under the unguided student. Verification retains correct trajectories sampled from this reachable space, and an iterative refinement uses diagnostic guidance from current trajectories to improve sampling efficiency. Trajectory recovery requires no parameter updates.
AI.result: On problems with pass@64 = 0 after extensive RL, SSR recovers correct and learnable trajectories for 74.6%. Fine-tuning on these trajectories followed by resumed RL improves aggregate accuracy by 4.9 percentage points on AIME25/26 and HMMT26.
AI.conclusion: Privileged guidance becomes effective self-improvement data when aligned with the reasoning actions the student can reach.

title: Adaptive-Policy Distillation: Knowledge Injection under Information Asymmetry
summary: On-policy distillation (OPD), which uses reverse-KL supervision on student rollouts to transfer a context-conditioned model's behavior into student model parameters for closed-book inference, has shown strong results. However, we find that this success does not translate to knowledge injection: across two document-QA benchmarks, OPD injects document knowledge far less efficiently than simple off-policy distillation. We trace this reversal to two failures that are structural, yet sparse across token positions. Reverse KL weights its gradient by the student distribution and therefore barely lifts document-specific tokens the student considers unlikely; after forward KL restores this signal, student rollouts expose later positions on the target trajectory only after generating the preceding tokens correctly, so coverage deteriorates with target length. Motivated by the concentration of teacher-student divergence at these hard positions, we propose Adaptive-Policy Distillation (APD), whose per-token gate jointly shifts the rollout toward the teacher and the objective toward forward KL where needed, withdrawing both interventions as the student learns. Without labels or a verifier, APD improves over OPD by up to 54.6%, achieving the best scores of 0.558 F1 on QASPER and 0.486 MRR on BioASQ.

AI.tldr: Adaptive-Policy Distillation (APD) addresses why on-policy distillation injects document knowledge less efficiently than off-policy distillation: its per-token gate shifts rollouts toward the teacher and the objective toward forward KL at hard positions. Without labels or a verifier it improves over OPD by up to 54.6%, reaching 0.558 F1 on QASPER and 0.486 MRR on BioASQ.
AI.motivation: On-policy distillation with reverse KL works for behavior transfer but injects document knowledge less efficiently than simple off-policy distillation on document-QA benchmarks.
AI.method: The authors attribute the failure to two structural problems: reverse KL weights gradients by the student distribution, which barely lifts document-specific tokens the student finds unlikely, and student rollouts reach later target positions only after generating preceding tokens correctly, so coverage deteriorates with target length. APD uses a per-token gate that jointly shifts the rollout toward the teacher and the objective toward forward KL where needed, and withdraws both as the student learns.
AI.result: APD improves over OPD by up to 54.6% on two document-QA benchmarks, reaching 0.558 F1 on QASPER and 0.486 MRR on BioASQ, without labels or a verifier.
AI.conclusion: Knowledge injection under information asymmetry needs interventions targeted at the sparse hard token positions where teacher-student divergence concentrates.

title: ShiftRAG: Bypassing the Textual Bottleneck via Decoupled Learning and Continuous Soft Tokens
summary: Despite advances in retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), suppressing hallucinations during complex reasoning remains a persistent challenge. We identify that existing RAG pipelines suffer from a textual bottleneck: by passing only raw text to the generator, they discard discriminative signals of the retriever. Furthermore, recent attempts to unify retrieval and generation within a single LLM induce severe objective conflict and exacerbate the rank collapse of decoder-only architectures, degrading performance on both tasks. To address these limitations, we introduce ShiftRAG, a decoupled RAG framework that employs a single LLM backbone but isolates discriminative retrieval learning from autoregressive generation. To bridge these decoupled modes, we project retrieval alignments into continuous soft tokens, establishing a high-bandwidth interface that infuses the generator with retrieval-side signals. Concurrently, our soft orthogonality objective mitigates rank collapse, while layer-wise relevance dynamics preserve the fine-grained latent space required for highly discriminative evidence separation. Extensive evaluations demonstrate that ShiftRAG significantly improves retrieval and question answering performance over state-of-the-art baselines. ShiftRAG preserves foundational capabilities of the backbone while maintaining a favorable efficiency-performance trade-off on general text encoding and generative tasks.

AI.tldr: ShiftRAG is a decoupled RAG framework that uses one LLM backbone but separates discriminative retrieval learning from autoregressive generation, passing retrieval alignments to the generator as continuous soft tokens. It improves retrieval and question answering over state-of-the-art baselines while preserving the backbone's general capabilities.
AI.motivation: Existing RAG pipelines pass only raw text to the generator, discarding retriever signals, and unifying retrieval and generation in one LLM induces objective conflict and rank collapse in decoder-only architectures.
AI.method: Retrieval alignments are projected into continuous soft tokens as a high-bandwidth interface to the generator. A soft orthogonality objective mitigates rank collapse, and layer-wise relevance dynamics preserve the fine-grained latent space needed to separate evidence.
AI.result: The abstract reports significant improvements in retrieval and question answering over state-of-the-art baselines, and a favorable efficiency-performance trade-off on general text encoding and generative tasks. No specific numbers are given in the abstract.
AI.conclusion: Decoupling retrieval learning from generation and conveying retrieval signals as soft tokens offers a route past the textual bottleneck without degrading the backbone.

title: What Breaks and What Comes Back: Capability Damage and Recovery in Depth-Pruned Small Language Models
summary: Depth pruning removes whole Transformer blocks to make a language model smaller and faster, but the damage is not spread evenly across what the model can do, and a short fine-tuning run, called healing, decides what comes back. We measure this for small models used as agents. Four instruction-tuned models of 1.2-1.7B parameters (Llama-3.2-1B, Qwen2.5-1.5B, SmolLM2-1.7B and OLMo-2-1B) are pruned and healed, and six capabilities are tracked: structured output, function calling, instruction following, mathematical reasoning, safety refusal and knowledge. Three results hold across the families. First, function calling and math collapse in every model (retention 0.00-0.07 of the unpruned score), and the order in which capabilities break agrees closely across the four (Kendall's W = 0.92; 0.62 after correcting for chance floors). Second, which parameters are trained matters as much as which data: fully tuning the last three blocks instead of adding low-rank adapters to all blocks costs up to 0.18 in capped mean retention on three families, and one 300k-token pilot per scope detects this. Third, we test a planner that allocates a 1M-token healing budget from 21 short pilot heals. At a fixed budget it raises the weakest capability on two families, although only one of these gains survives a test that also resamples training seeds. Once its 3.48M pilot tokens are counted, uniform healing with the same total number of training tokens matches or beats every planned variant on every family and retains math significantly better on three of them in an item-level test (on one when seeds are also resampled). Healing longer is a strong and simple baseline that planned recovery must beat. Code, per-item predictions and every result are public.

AI.tldr: After depth pruning four 1.2-1.7B instruction-tuned small models, function calling and math collapse in every model, and the order in which capabilities break agrees closely across models. Which parameters are tuned during healing matters as much as the data, and uniform healing with the same total number of tokens matches or beats planned variants.
AI.motivation: Depth pruning damages capabilities unevenly, and it is unclear what a short healing fine-tune recovers when the small models are used as agents.
AI.method: Llama-3.2-1B, Qwen2.5-1.5B, SmolLM2-1.7B and OLMo-2-1B are pruned and healed, and six capabilities are tracked: structured output, function calling, instruction following, math reasoning, safety refusal and knowledge. Healing scopes are compared, and a planner allocates a 1M-token healing budget from 21 short pilot heals.
AI.result: Function calling and math retain only 0.00-0.07 of the unpruned score in every model, and the break order has Kendall's W of 0.92 (0.62 after correcting for chance floors). Fully tuning the last three blocks instead of adding low-rank adapters to all blocks costs up to 0.18 in capped mean retention on three families. The planner raises the weakest capability on two families at fixed budget, but only one gain survives a test that resamples training seeds. Once its 3.48M pilot tokens are counted, uniform healing matches or beats every planned variant and retains math significantly better on three families.
AI.conclusion: Healing longer is a strong, simple baseline that planned recovery must beat.

title: Random Is Almost Enough? Stable and Low-Cost Benchmark Compression via BestRand
summary: Benchmark compression reduces the often prohibitive time and cost of model evaluation by evaluating models on a small benchmark subset that closely matches full-benchmark results. To quantify estimation error, we derive an accurate analytical approximation to the error distribution when estimating full-benchmark scores from a subset, showing that most subsets yield small errors, while a few produce much larger errors, resulting in a long-tailed distribution. This means random sampling alone can achieve surprisingly strong performance with high probability, but remains unstable due to rare large errors. We further show that this instability is inherent to modern foundation models and persists even as more models are evaluated. Based on these findings, we introduce BestRand, a stable and low-cost benchmark compression method that preserves the efficiency of random sampling while substantially reducing its high-error tail. We validate BestRand on 70+ text, multimodal, and agent benchmarks, and further extend it to VLA evaluation. Compared with competitive methods, BestRand reduces high-error risk by 50.2% and estimation error by 16.4% on average, while requiring only 51.3% of the construction cost. It further reduces OOD estimation error by 21.8% on average across score-range, model-family, and temporal shifts. Together, our theory provides practical guidance for understanding and predicting the accuracy and reliability of benchmark compression, while BestRand enables stable and accurate compression at low cost. The code and data are publicly available onhttps://github.com/George-Ling3/BestRand.

AI.tldr: BestRand is a benchmark-compression method that keeps random sampling's efficiency while reducing its high-error tail, which arises because subset-based estimates of full-benchmark scores have a long-tailed error distribution. Across 70+ benchmarks it cuts high-error risk by 50.2% and estimation error by 16.4% on average, at 51.3% of the construction cost of competitive methods.
AI.motivation: Evaluating models on full benchmarks is costly, and random subsets usually give small errors but occasionally produce large ones that make them unstable.
AI.method: An analytical approximation to the error distribution of subset-based estimates is derived, showing that the distribution is long-tailed. Building on this, BestRand preserves random sampling's efficiency while substantially reducing the high-error tail. It is validated on 70+ text, multimodal and agent benchmarks and extended to VLA evaluation.
AI.result: Compared with competitive methods, BestRand reduces high-error risk by 50.2% and estimation error by 16.4% on average, while requiring 51.3% of the construction cost. It reduces OOD estimation error by 21.8% on average across score-range, model-family and temporal shifts.
AI.conclusion: The theory gives practical guidance on the accuracy and reliability of benchmark compression, and BestRand enables stable, accurate compression at low cost.

title: S1CogBench: What System One Decision Models Can and Cannot Do on Cognitive Experiments
comment: 13 pages, 4 figures, 12 tables. Code at this https URL
summary: Language models are no longer used only to generate text. Software also asks them for decisions, in routing, guardrails, and automated gates. System One decision models, also called typed decision models, such as Jev and Laya, return one fast decision over the legal options, leaving no text to inspect. However, a fast, well-formed decision does not show that the model used the evidence. Cognitive experiments can test this, because they vary task demands and measure how behavior changes, yet existing cognitive benchmarks evaluate language and multimodal models. We introduce S1CogBench to ask what these models can and cannot do on 24 cognitive tasks, evaluating five open models and Jev and keeping conditions and scoring apart from disclosed adaptations. We find that decision models vary widely in reliability, acting well does not imply predicting humans, aggregate scores hide how decisions respond to conditions, and speed comes mainly from answering without generation. To our knowledge, S1CogBench is the first benchmark of System One decision models on established cognitive experiments, and it gives a shared test of whether their decisions respond to evidence, feedback, memory load, and future opportunities before software relies on them.

AI.tldr: S1CogBench evaluates five open models and the decision model Jev on 24 established cognitive experiments, testing whether typed System One decision models respond to evidence, feedback, memory load and future opportunities.
